title: Every auth rate limit and brute-force lockout is keyed on a client-supplied header; the network control the code relies on is not in the deploy runbook
what: clientIp() returns `req.headers['x-real-ip']` with no trust boundary, falling back to `req.ip` (which, with `app.set('trust proxy', true)` in main.ts:35, is the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry — also client-supplied). Every unauthenticated auth budget is keyed on that value: `signup:ip:${ip}` / `login:ip:${ip}` / `pwreset:ip:${ip}` / `emailverify:ip:${ip}` (auth.controller.ts:135,167,251,282), `admin-login:ip:${ip}` (admin-auth.controller.ts:73), and the per-(account+IP) login lockout `login:fail:${uid}:${ip}` / `login:lock:${uid}:${ip}` (login.service.ts:15-16). The file's own comment says spoofing is impossible because "the host firewall only admits Cloudflare ranges, so the header cannot be spoofed by hitting the origin directly (see infra/caddy/Caddyfile)" — but infra/caddy/Caddyfile contains no `remote_ip` matcher or Cloudflare allowlist anywhere; it unconditionally does `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}` (lines 177, 219, 276), i.e. it copies a header the client can set. The runbook the operator will actually follow, docs/deployment-hetzner.md:192-200, says `ufw allow 80/tcp` / `ufw allow 443/tcp` — open to the entire internet, not Cloudflare ranges — and the same document warns that Docker-published ports bypass ufw regardless. Only the aspirational checklist in docs/server-handbook.md:891 mentions restricting 80/443, and it is a manual, unautomated, never-executed step on a box that has never been deployed to.
impact: An attacker rotating CF-Connecting-IP (or X-Forwarded-For) on requests sent straight to the origin gets unlimited attempts against every unauthenticated auth endpoint: unlimited password guessing against any known library account and against admin.libriant.com, unlimited signup (each of which provisions a Postgres database), unlimited password-reset email bombing. The per-account lockout never trips because a fresh bucket is created for every attempt. Every IP recorded in supportSession.ipAddress, supportRedemptionAttempt.ipAddress and the legal-consent record is attacker-authored fiction, which also breaks the GDPR accountability record signup.service.ts writes.
evidence: RAN (integration probe): sending `X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.9` with six wrong logins created the lock under exactly that attacker-chosen key — probe output `P9 redis lock key present = true` for key `login:lock:<uid>:198.51.100.9`. READ: `grep -rn 'remote_ip|trusted_proxies' infra/caddy/Caddyfile` → no matches; `grep -n 'X-Real-IP' infra/caddy/Caddyfile` → `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}` at 177/219/276 with no origin check. READ docs/deployment-hetzner.md:195-198 → `ufw allow 80/tcp` / `ufw allow 443/tcp`.
fix: Do not trust the header unconditionally. In Caddy, wrap the reverse_proxy in a `@cf remote_ip <cloudflare-v4-and-v6-ranges>` matcher and `header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}` (not the client header) for anything that does not match; refuse or 403 non-Cloudflare origin traffic. In the app, replace `app.set('trust proxy', true)` with an explicit proxy list, and make clientIp() ignore X-Real-IP unless the immediate peer is a known proxy. Add the Cloudflare-range ufw rules to the actual deployment script (not only the checklist) and gate the deploy on an automated `nmap`/curl check that a direct-to-origin request with a forged CF-Connecting-IP does not reach the API.
verification: Re-derived from source, not the finding text. READ apps/api/src/platform/client-ip.ts:16-21 — `req.headers['x-real-ip']` is returned with no trust boundary, falling back to `req.ip`; main.ts:36 is `app.set('trust proxy', true)`. Tried to refute the 'no Cloudflare allowlist' claim by chasing the `import cloudflare_origin` snippet the Caddyfile pulls in at lines 154/213/…: infra/caddy/Caddyfile:111-121 is a `tls /etc/caddy/origin/origin.crt …` directive ONLY — no `remote_ip`, no `trusted_proxies`, no allowlist anywhere in the 359-line file. RAN two live probes against a booted app. (a) six wrong logins carrying `X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.9` produced the Redis key `login:lock:<uid>:198.51.100.9`; a correct-password login for the SAME account from `X-Real-IP: 203.0.113.7` returned 200 while the locked bucket returned 401 — i.e. the lockout follows the attacker's chosen bucket and rotating the header resets it. (b) With NO X-Real-IP at all, six wrong logins carrying `X-Forwarded-For: 192.0.2.55, 10.0.0.1` produced `lbr:login:lock:<uid>:192.0.2.55` — so the `req.ip` fallback is ALSO client-controlled under `trust proxy: true`; both spoof vectors work. Severity held at blocker for one reason the original finding did not name: infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:135-138 publishes Caddy as `80:80` / `443:443`, and docs/deployment-hetzner.md itself warns that Docker-published ports are inserted ahead of ufw's chains — so even the aspirational 'restrict 80/443 to Cloudflare ranges' checkbox in docs/server-handbook.md:891 would NOT close this. There is currently no configuration of the documented deploy that prevents a forged-header request from reaching the API.

title: With STRIPE_DRIVER=fake — what every production template writes today — the webhook verifies signatures against a hardcoded secret published in this repo
what: FakeStripeDriver hardcodes `private secret = 'fake-webhook-secret-for-dev'` and only tests ever call setSecret(). billing.module.ts:22-28 selects the driver purely on `STRIPE_DRIVER`, and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET is never handed to the fake driver. POST /webhooks/stripe is unauthenticated by design and, per SystemModeMiddleware ALWAYS_PASS (system-mode.middleware.ts:44), bypasses maintenance/read-only mode; OriginCheckMiddleware allows a missing Origin (origin-check.middleware.ts:41). So while the fake driver is in place, the signature check is satisfiable by anyone. `.env.prod.example:69` sets STRIPE_DRIVER=fake, `scripts/ensure-env.sh:100` writes it as the default, and `infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:65` defaults it to fake — and docs/billing-go-live.md tells the operator to flip the master switch from the admin panel, which requires no .env change at all, so enforcement can be turned on while this driver is still serving.
impact: Any internet host can rewrite any tenant's subscription row: grant themselves Institutional, or set another library to canceled/past_due. The victim's Stripe customer id is not even a secret in this mode — FakeStripeDriver.createCustomer mints `cus_fake_<tenantId>` and GET /t/:slug/billing returns both tenantId and stripeCustomerId to the tenant's own admin. The forged rows persist and become the truth the moment billing is enabled. Signature minting is also unlimited, so stripe_webhook_events grows without bound.
evidence:
EXECUTED, twice.
(1) Unit-level: constructing FakeStripeDriver exactly as billing.module.ts does, with STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_the_operator_set_a_real_one in the environment, prints `driver secret in use : fake-webhook-secret-for-dev` and accepts an event signed with that literal.
(2) End-to-end over HTTP against the audit Postgres, booting the real AppModule and POSTing to /webhooks/stripe with no credential of any kind, only `signFakeWebhook(body,'fake-webhook-secret-for-dev')`: HTTP 200, and the control plane moved from
  libwf-be65e9 | starter | active | (null)
to
  libwf-be65e9 | institutional | active | sub_audit
with stripe_webhook_events showing the event processed=t, error=null. An event signed with any other secret returned 400.
fix: Two independent changes. (a) Make the fake driver refuse to verify anything outside development: throw from its constructor when `loadEnv().nodeEnv !== 'development'`, or require STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET and use it instead of the literal. (b) Refuse to boot when the toggle can enforce but the driver is fake — extend the main.ts guard (which already refuses RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED in production) to reject `nodeEnv==='production' && stripeDriver!=='real'`, and have PlatformSettingsService.setBillingEnabled throw rather than log a warning (platform-settings.service.ts:60-66) in that state.
verification:
EXECUTED end-to-end. Booted the real AppModule against the audit control plane and POSTed a `customer.subscription.updated` event to /webhooks/stripe with NO credential of any kind, signed only with the literal from stripe-fake.driver.ts:32:
  B02 before: starter active null
  B02 forged POST status: 200 {"received":true}
  B02 after : institutional active sub_vfy_forged
  B02 wrong-secret POST status: 400
Refutation attempts, all failed: (a) billing.module.ts:22-28 selects the driver on STRIPE_DRIVER alone and never passes STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET to the fake — setSecret() has no non-test caller; (b) main.ts has no boot guard on stripeDriver (grep STRIPE_DRIVER over apps/api/src returns only env.ts:353); (c) the webhook controller calls no assertBillingEnabled, so the write lands even with BILLING_ENABLED=false. One correction to the original evidence: docs/billing-go-live.md step 4 DOES instruct setting STRIPE_DRIVER=real in .env.prod, so the doc is not silent on it — but the master switch is separately flippable from the admin panel (setBillingEnabled only logs a warning, platform-settings.service.ts:60-66), so the two can diverge. The finding stands regardless of the switch: an unauthenticated internet request writes the control plane today.

title: Every plan change opens a NEW Stripe subscription and abandons the old one — an upgrade double-charges the library, forever
what: startCheckout's only guard against an existing subscription is `plan.id === sub.planId && sub.status === 'active'` (line 285). Any other plan goes to `stripe.checkout.sessions.create({ mode:'subscription', ... })` (stripe-real.driver.ts:68-78), which always creates an additional subscription for that customer — it never modifies an existing one. Nothing in the codebase cancels or updates the previous subscription: the StripeDriver interface (stripe-driver.ts:93-110) has no `updateSubscription`/`subscriptions.update` and no proration parameter anywhere in the repo (`grep -rn proration_behavior apps` returns nothing). syncStripeSubscription then overwrites `stripeSubscriptionId` with the new id (line 617), so the old subscription's id is erased from our database entirely and cancelAtPeriodEnd (line 359) can only ever reach the newest one.
impact: A Community library upgrading to Municipal is charged €39 AND €79 every month, indefinitely. A library 'downgrading' from Municipal to Community adds €39 on top of the €79 it is still paying. Neither the library nor an operator can see the orphan — it exists only in Stripe. Cancelling from the app stops the newest subscription and leaves the older one billing. This is charge-back and refund territory on the first paying customers.
evidence:
EXECUTED against the audit control plane. Applied sub_A (community, active), then a second subscription sub_B (central, active) for the same customer, exactly as a second Checkout would produce:
  after checkout created sub_B while sub_A lives  plan=central  status=active  stripeSub=sub_B
  rows anywhere still referencing sub_A: 0
Read-only for the Stripe side: `mode:'subscription'` Checkout creates a new subscription; the repo contains no call that would replace the old one.
fix: Do not route plan changes through Checkout. When `sub.stripeSubscriptionId` is set, call `stripe.subscriptions.update(id, { items:[{ id: <item>, price: newPriceId }], proration_behavior:'create_prorations' })` through a new driver method and let the resulting `customer.subscription.updated` webhook do the sync; reserve Checkout for the first subscription only. Until that lands, block startCheckout with a 400 whenever `sub.stripeSubscriptionId != null`.
verification: READ-verified line by line. billing.service.ts:285 is the only existing-subscription guard (`plan.id === sub.planId && sub.status === 'active'`) — a DIFFERENT plan slug passes straight through to stripe.createCheckoutSession with mode:'subscription' (stripe-real.driver.ts:68-78). Tried to find the cancelling guard the finding says is missing and could not: the StripeDriver interface (stripe-driver.ts:93-110) exposes only createCustomer / createCheckoutSession / createBillingPortalSession / cancelSubscriptionAtPeriodEnd / resumeSubscription / verifyWebhookSignature — there is no subscriptions.update and `grep -rn 'proration_behavior' apps packages` returns nothing. syncStripeSubscription then overwrites stripeSubscriptionId (line 617), erasing the old id, so cancelAtPeriodEnd (line 359) can only ever reach the newest subscription. Stripe Checkout in subscription mode creates an additional subscription per completed session; nothing here reconciles that. Blocker upheld: this is duplicate recurring charges on real cards with no in-product way to see or stop the orphan.

title: No VAT anywhere in the billing path — Greek libraries cannot pay against the receipt, and ~24% of every euro collected is owed regardless
what: createCheckoutSession sets mode, customer, line_items, urls, client_reference_id and `customer_update`. It does NOT set `automatic_tax: { enabled: true }`, `tax_id_collection: { enabled: true }`, or `billing_address_collection: 'required'`. `customer_update:{name:'auto',address:'auto'}` is the companion parameter Stripe requires alongside automatic_tax; on its own it collects nothing. Stripe therefore charges the Price amount with no tax line and issues a receipt with no VAT and no customer VAT number. The control plane already has the columns for this — billing_accounts.taxId, taxCountry, addressLine1..country (schema.prisma:574-580) — and no code path anywhere writes them: ensureStripeCustomer (billing.service.ts:746-780) sets only billingEmail and billingName. The marketing site's own build lint forbids the words ΦΠΑ, ΑΦΜ and τιμολόγιο (apps/site/build.ts:180, reason: 'The business is not registered and nothing is trademarked'), so the advertised '390 €' carries no statement of whether VAT is included or excluded.
impact: Two separate injuries. (1) The customers are Greek municipalities and δημόσιες βιβλιοθήκες; their accounting departments cannot book a payment without a compliant invoice carrying the supplier's ΑΦΜ and the ΦΠΑ line. A Stripe card receipt with neither cannot be paid from a public budget — the deals stall after the card is entered. (2) A price advertised with no VAT statement is treated as VAT-inclusive, so of a €390 annual sale roughly €75 is owed to AADE out of money already booked as revenue; every tier is ~19.4% less profitable than the pricing model assumes. Neither problem is detectable from inside the app.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn 'automatic_tax|tax_id_collection|billing_address_collection|proration_behavior|taxCountry' apps/api/src apps/web/app apps/site packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma` returns exactly one hit — the unused schema column `packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:575: taxCountry String?`. docs/billing-go-live.md contains no occurrence of tax, VAT or ΦΠΑ; its whole configuration surface is eight price ids, a webhook URL and four env vars.
fix: Enable Stripe Tax on the account, then set `automatic_tax:{enabled:true}`, `tax_id_collection:{enabled:true}` and `billing_address_collection:'required'` on the Checkout session, and mirror the resulting `customer.tax_ids` / address back into billing_accounts on the customer.updated webhook. Decide and state on both the pricing page and the plan cards whether the figure is πλέον ΦΠΑ or συμπ. ΦΠΑ, and add that step to docs/billing-go-live.md. This is gated on the company actually being registered with an ΑΦΜ.
verification: READ-verified against the driver source. stripe-real.driver.ts:68-78 sets mode, customer, line_items, success_url, cancel_url, client_reference_id and customer_update only. Re-ran the grep across the whole repo: `grep -rn 'automatic_tax|tax_id_collection|billing_address_collection|proration_behavior' apps packages` returns ZERO hits. Confirmed the schema columns exist and are dead: schema.prisma:572-580 declares taxId/taxCountry/addressLine1..country, and the only writers of billing_accounts (auth/signup.service.ts:195 and billing.service.ts:766) set nothing but tenantId/billingEmail/billingName. Tried to downgrade this as 'not a code defect' and could not: with no tax configuration Stripe charges the bare Price and issues a receipt with no VAT line and no customer VAT id, which is not a document a Greek municipality can book. Kept at blocker, with the caveat the original finding already states: the code fix is gated on the company having an ΑΦΜ, so this is a launch prerequisite rather than a patch.

title: Redis unavailable makes EVERY request 500 — including /healthz, /readyz and the /admin/system-mode recovery lever
what: SystemModeMiddleware is mounted on '*'. Its ALWAYS_PASS branch — the one whose comment says 'infra probes keep working ... an operator never locks themselves out of the lever they need to pull to recover' — still executes `req.systemMode = await this.modes.resolveGlobal()` BEFORE calling next(). resolveGlobal() calls readCache(), which does a bare `await this.redis.client.get(key)` with no try/catch, and RedisService constructs ioredis with `enableOfflineQueue: false`. So when Redis is not reachable the GET throws synchronously ("Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false"), the middleware rejects, and the global exception filter turns it into a 500 — for every path, bypassed or not.
impact: A Redis restart, OOM, or a wrong REDIS_URL takes the whole platform down rather than degrading it. Every library gets 500s. The liveness probe cannot say 'alive but degraded', /readyz cannot say which dependency is down, and /admin/system-mode — the documented lever for putting the platform into maintenance and recovering — also 500s, so the operator has no in-band recovery path. Redis in this stack is a single container with appendonly on and no maxmemory; a restart is a routine event.
evidence: EXECUTED. Booted the API (NODE_ENV=production, live audit Postgres) with REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6399 (nothing listening). `curl /healthz` → HTTP 500 `{"statusCode":500,"error":"InternalServerError",...,"supportCode":"AYLXKPI6"}`; `curl /readyz` → HTTP 500. The logged stack is exactly: `Error: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false ... at SystemModeService.readCache (system-mode.service.ts:232:41) at SystemModeService.resolveGlobal (system-mode.service.ts:44:31) at SystemModeMiddleware.use (system-mode.middleware.ts:100:41)`. With Redis up and only Postgres unreachable, /healthz stays 200 and /readyz returns 503 — confirming Redis, not Postgres, is the single point of total failure.
fix: As stated, PLUS the same try/catch on TenantResolverService.readCache/writeCache (tenant-resolver.service.ts:94-108) — otherwise tenant routes still 500 with Redis down.
verification: RE-EXECUTED independently. Booted apps/api under NODE_ENV=production against the live audit Postgres with REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6399 (nothing listening). Results: GET /healthz -> 500 {"supportCode":"5BZQGXX6"}, GET /readyz -> 500, GET /admin/system-mode -> 500. The logged stack is verbatim the one claimed: "Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false ... at SystemModeService.readCache (system-mode.service.ts:232:41) at SystemModeService.resolveGlobal (:44:31) at SystemModeMiddleware.use (system-mode.middleware.ts:100:41)". Code re-read and matches: middleware.ts:96-101 executes `req.systemMode = await this.modes.resolveGlobal()` INSIDE the ALWAYS_PASS branch before next(); service.ts:231-233 readCache does a bare `await this.redis.client.get(key)`; redis.service.ts:25 sets `enableOfflineQueue: false`. Searched for a guard that would prevent it and found NONE — the global filter (http-exception.filter.ts:74) turns the rejection into a 500. Control test: with Redis up and only the control DB dead, /healthz stayed 200 and /readyz returned 503, so Redis is uniquely the total-failure dependency. ADDITIONAL, not in the original: TenantResolverService.readCache (apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-resolver.service.ts:94-96) has the identical unguarded `this.redis.client.get` — so a fix confined to SystemModeService still leaves every /t/<slug>/* request 500ing on a Redis outage. Severity blocker upheld: a routine Redis restart is a full-platform outage with no in-band recovery lever, and RateLimitService (rate-limit.service.ts:98-105) is the only Redis caller in the request path that actually try/catches.

title: Every file upload 500s in the launch configuration: the unlimited storage quota overflows Postgres bigint
what: `unlimitedPlan()` substitutes `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` for every int feature while billing is off. `StorageService.put` computes `limitBytes = BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n` = 9444732965739289378816 and binds it into a raw `UPDATE tenants ... AND "storageUsedBytes" + $n <= $limitBytes`. Prisma binds it as int8; the value is ~1024x the bigint maximum, so Postgres rejects with SQLSTATE 22003. The throw is outside the try/catch, which only wraps `driver.put` at line 103.
impact: With subscriptions off — the launch configuration — no tenant can upload a book cover, member photo, branding logo, PDF attachment or MARC file. Every attempt is an opaque HTTP 500. Turning billing ON is what makes it work, the opposite of what an operator would guess.
evidence: READ: effective-plan.service.ts:38 `const UNLIMITED_INT = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;`, line 52 assigns it to every int feature, line 110-111 applies `unlimitedPlan` whenever `settings.billingEnabled()` is false. features.ts:44-51 confirms `max_storage_mb` is type 'int', so `getInt` returns the sentinel unchanged. config/env.ts:366 `billingEnabled: bool('BILLING_ENABLED', false)` and .env.prod.example:65 `BILLING_ENABLED=false` confirm the launch default.
verification: Re-derived independently rather than trusting the original probe. RAN `psql -d libriant_control -c "SELECT 9007199254740991::bigint * 1024 * 1024"` -> `ERROR: bigint out of range`. Then RAN the EXACT `controlDb.$executeRaw` template from storage.service.ts:74-79 against the live audit control plane with `limitBytes = BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) * 1024n * 1024n` and a real tenant id -> `PrismaClientKnownRequestError ... Raw query failed. Code: 22003. Message: value "9444732965739289378816" is out of range for type bigint`. The claim that Prisma binds the BigInt as int8 (rather than numeric, which would not overflow) is the load-bearing step and it holds. Severity upheld: this is not a race or an edge case — it is 100% of uploads in the configuration the product ships in.
fix: Treat the sentinel as 'no ceiling' in StorageService: `const unlimited = limitMb >= Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;` and run the UPDATE without the `<=` predicate when true. Alternatively clamp UNLIMITED_INT at effective-plan.service.ts:38 to a value whose byte product fits int8 (e.g. 2**43 MB). Add an integration test with BILLING_ENABLED=false that uploads a cover — apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts:8 forces `BILLING_ENABLED ||= 'true'`, so the whole suite runs in the opposite configuration from production.

title: Every file upload returns HTTP 500 in the launch configuration (bigint overflow from the unlimited-plan sentinel)
what: When subscriptions are off, EffectivePlanService.unlimitedPlan() rewrites every int feature to UNLIMITED_INT = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991). StorageService.put then computes `const limitBytes = BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n` = 9444732965739289378816 and interpolates it into the atomic reservation `UPDATE tenants SET "storageUsedBytes" = ... WHERE "storageUsedBytes" + $n <= ${limitBytes}`. That literal exceeds Postgres bigint (max 9223372036854775807), so the statement fails with SQLSTATE 22003 before any file is written. Every upload path funnels through StorageService.put: book covers (catalog/covers.controller.ts), member photos (members/photos.controller.ts), library logos (branding/branding.controller.ts) and the generic storage endpoint. Note the switch is the platform_settings row `billing.enabled`, which is seeded to 'false' and OVERRIDES the BILLING_ENABLED env var (platform-settings.service.ts:39), so setting the env var true does not avoid it.
impact: On launch day, with subscriptions disabled as planned, no library can upload a single book cover, member photo, or their own logo. Every attempt returns the generic 'something went wrong, here is a support code' 500. This is the first thing a librarian does after adding a book. It is not degraded behaviour, it is total failure of the whole upload feature, and it will read to the customer as 'the product is broken'.
evidence: EXECUTED against the live audit env. `POST /t/probes1-x9/storage/covers` with a 7-byte image/png returned 500. API log: `Invalid prisma.$executeRaw() invocation: Raw query failed. Code: 22003. Message: value "9444732965739289378816" is out of range for type bigint ... at async StorageService.put (apps/api/src/storage/storage.service.ts:76)`. Confirmed the arithmetic: 9007199254740991 x 1048576 = 9444732965739289378816 exactly. Confirmed the source: `GET /t/probes1-x9/plan` returns `max_storage_mb = {"type":"int","value":9007199254740991,"source":"override","note":"Included - subscriptions are currently disabled."}`. Confirmed the gate: `select key,value from platform_settings` -> `billing.enabled|false`. A cover upload succeeded (201, ref covers/cmt5mnc442df6cc8c2af8.png) only during a window where the settings cache still held billing=true; once the cache re-read the DB row every upload 500s again, including a 12 MB one.
fix: Clamp the byte ceiling before it reaches SQL. In StorageService.put: `const limitBytes = limitMb >= Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER ? 9223372036854775807n : BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n;` — or better, skip the conditional UPDATE entirely and do an unconditional increment when the plan is unlimited. Add an integration test that runs the upload path with `billing.enabled=false`; the existing suite only exercises it with a real plan, which is why this was never caught.
verification: REPRODUCED END-TO-END on the live audit env, and proved causation both ways. (a) Isolated the SQL: ran the exact tagged template from storage.service.ts:76 through Prisma with limitBytes = BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)*1024n*1024n -> `Invalid prisma.$executeRaw() invocation: Raw query failed. Code: 22003. Message: value "9444732965739289378816" is out of range for type bigint`. (b) Full path with billing OFF (no platform_settings row, BILLING_ENABLED unset -> false): POST /t/ver-up/storage/covers with an image/png -> HTTP 500 {supportCode CYT36QF5}; api.log carries the 22003. (c) Flipped the switch: inserted platform_settings('billing.enabled','true'), deleted the Redis keys platform_setting:billing.enabled and plan:effective:* -> the identical upload returned 201 {"ref":"covers/cmt5nc4f35ca3306d8542.png","contentType":"image/png"}. The unlimited-plan sentinel is the cause, confirmed. TWO CORRECTIONS to the original evidence, neither of which changes the outcome: (1) the value is NOT string-interpolated into the SQL — Prisma's $executeRaw is a tagged template and ${limitBytes} is a bind parameter; Postgres rejects it as an out-of-range int8 bind, which is why the error text looks like a literal. (2) There is no seeded `billing.enabled` row: `select key,value from platform_settings` on a freshly migrated+seeded control DB returns zero rows, so the value comes from config/env.ts:366 `billingEnabled: bool('BILLING_ENABLED', false)` — the default, not a DB override. The launch configuration reaches the broken state by default rather than by a seeded row. Blocker rating upheld: all four upload entry points funnel through StorageService.put (catalog/covers.controller.ts:61, members/photos.controller.ts:59, branding/branding.controller.ts:62, storage-demo.controller.ts:92).

title: Every rate limit and the account lockout key off a client-supplied header, so all of them are bypassed by rotating X-Real-IP
what: clientIp() reads `X-Real-IP` from the request with no check on who sent it. Everything that throttles unauthenticated abuse is keyed on that value: the per-IP signup cap (5/10min), the per-IP login cap (20/5min), the per-IP password-reset cap, the /apply form cap (5/hour) and — critically — the brute-force lockout itself, which login.service.ts:15 keys as `login:fail:<uid>:<ip>` and `login:lock:<uid>:<ip>` (comment A1-01). Changing one header per request gives every request a fresh, empty bucket. The code justifies trusting the header with a comment (client-ip.ts:9, repeated in infra/caddy/Caddyfile:175): 'The host firewall only admits Cloudflare's ranges, so the header cannot be spoofed by hitting the origin directly.' No such firewall exists anywhere in the repo. There is no ufw/iptables/nftables rule in scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh, scripts/deploy-on-host.sh, infra/compose/* or infra/deploy/fleet.yml, and the one documented procedure the operator will follow (docs/deployment-hetzner.md:192-199) is `ufw allow 80/tcp` / `ufw allow 443/tcp` — open to the entire internet, not Cloudflare ranges. Caddy then does `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}`, so an attacker hitting the origin IP directly with a forged CF-Connecting-IP has Caddy stamp the forgery into X-Real-IP for them. The origin IP (195.201.13.95) is in the repo.
impact: There is no working defence against password guessing, signup flooding, or form spam. An attacker can (a) brute-force any known account without ever tripping the lockout, (b) provision unlimited tenant Postgres databases through /auth/signup, and (c) flood the marketing form. All audit-log IP attribution is also attacker-controlled: an intruder chooses what IP appears next to their actions in the audit trail.
evidence: EXECUTED against the live audit env. (1) Login limiter: 25 POSTs to /auth/login with a fixed `X-Real-IP: 9.9.9.9` -> 20x401 then 5x429, limiter works. The same 25 with `X-Real-IP: 10.0.0.$i` -> 25x401, zero 429. (2) Account lockout: 40 wrong-password POSTs against the real account owner@libwf-be65e9.test with a rotating X-Real-IP -> 40x401, no 429, and `select failedLogins, lockedUntil from users` shows failedLogins=40 with lockedUntil NULL — the lockout never fired once. (3) /apply: 8 submissions from one IP -> 5x303 then 3x429; 8 with rotating IPs -> 8x303, all persisted (applications table went to 13 rows). (4) READ: grep for ufw|iptables|nftables|firewall across scripts/, infra/ returns no rule anywhere; docs/deployment-hetzner.md:196-197 is `ufw allow 80/tcp` + `ufw allow 443/tcp`.
fix: Two changes, both needed. (a) Stop trusting the header unconditionally: in client-ip.ts, only honour X-Real-IP when the TCP peer (`req.socket.remoteAddress`) is in an allowlist of trusted proxy addresses (the Caddy container IP / a TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS env var); otherwise fall back to req.socket.remoteAddress. (b) Make the deploy actually implement the assumption the code documents: add the Cloudflare-range-restricted 80/443 rules to scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh (pull https://www.cloudflare.com/ips-v4 and -v6) so the control is code, not a sentence in a markdown file, and fix docs/deployment-hetzner.md:196-197 which currently tells the operator to do the opposite. Additionally, give the account lockout a bare-account component with a much higher threshold on top of the per-(account+IP) one, so IP rotation cannot make it unreachable.
verification: MECHANISM REPRODUCED; ONE PIECE OF THE ORIGINAL EVIDENCE IS WRONG AND ONE IS OVERSTATED, but the finding gets stronger, not weaker. Reproduced live: 25 POSTs to /auth/login with a fixed `X-Real-IP: 9.9.9.9` -> 20x401 then 5x429 (limiter works); the same 25 with `X-Real-IP: 10.0.0.$i` -> 25x401, zero 429, no lockout. Read-verified the source: client-ip.ts:16-20 returns the header with no peer check; login.service.ts:15-16 keys FAIL_KEY/LOCK_KEY on (userId, ip); admin-audit.ts:27 stores clientIp(req) on audit rows, so the attribution claim holds. CORRECTION 1 (wrong evidence, dropped): 'failedLogins=40 with lockedUntil NULL' proves nothing. Tenant login NEVER writes lockedUntil — login.service.ts:212 increments failedLogins purely for audit and the lock decision lives only in Redis (login.service.ts:224-228); lockedUntil stays NULL even when the lockout fires. Only admin-auth.service.ts:93 writes it. CORRECTION 2 (the firewall DOES exist in the repo, and it still does not save this): docs/deployment-hetzner.md:486-496 documents exactly the Cloudflare-range ufw lock the code's comment assumes, framed as 'Lock the origin to Cloudflare... which would also let them spoof the real-client-IP header'. So 'no such firewall exists anywhere in the repo' is false. It nonetheless fails as a control, for two reasons I verified: (i) it is prose in a markdown file, absent from scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh (grep for ufw|iptables|nftables returns nothing there), and it is step 4 of a LATER Cloudflare section, after the Part-2 firewall the operator actually applies (deployment-hetzner.md:192-199 = `ufw allow 80/tcp` + `443`); (ii) more importantly, the SAME document warns at line 202 that 'Docker bypasses ufw — published container ports are inserted into iptables ahead of ufw's chains', and infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:135-138 publishes Caddy on '80:80' and '443:443'. Container-published ports are DNAT'd through FORWARD, not INPUT, so `ufw allow from <cf-range> to any port 443` does not filter them. Caddy adds no second layer: the Caddyfile has no `client_auth` (Authenticated Origin Pulls) and no remote_ip matcher — infra/caddy/Caddyfile:111-121 is a bare `tls origin.crt origin.key`. A request to the origin IP with `Host: app.libriant.com` and a forged CF-Connecting-IP is served, and Caddyfile:177 stamps the forgery into X-Real-IP. Blocker upheld.

title: With EMAIL_DRIVER=console in production nothing is delivered AND the body is withheld — password reset, email verification and staff invites are dead ends, and the runbook says the opposite
what: ConsoleEmailDriver computes `isDev = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') === 'development'`. Both apps/api/Dockerfile:83 and infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:35,240 set NODE_ENV=production, so the driver takes the `else` branch and logs only `NOT delivering "<subject>" to <addr> (body withheld)`. No mail is sent and no token appears anywhere an operator would look. Three user-facing flows then have no completion path: (a) POST /auth/password-reset/request mints a token into Redis and enqueues the link (apps/api/src/auth/password-reset.service.ts:70-105) — the user never receives it and there is NO admin endpoint that can reset a tenant user's password (grep of apps/api/src/admin and apps/api/src/platform for `passwordHash` returns only the admin's own login check, admin-auth.service.ts:39); (b) email verification never arrives, so `users.emailVerifiedAt` stays NULL forever; (c) EmailVerifiedGuard (apps/api/src/auth/email-verified.guard.ts:37) is applied to POST /t/:slug/staff (apps/api/src/staff/staff.controller.ts:51), so the owner can never add a second librarian. The only recovery is an undocumented `select "bodyMarkdown" from email_outbox` in psql, inside the token's 60-minute TTL. docs/deploy-from-the-server.md:113 tells the operator the opposite — that the console driver 'writes password-reset links into `docker logs api`' — which is true only in development.
impact: On day one a librarian who forgets their password is locked out of their library permanently unless the sole operator SSHes in and runs a psql query nobody has written down, within 60 minutes of the request. A library that hires a second member of staff cannot add them at all. The one document an operator would consult during that incident gives an instruction that does not work.
evidence: READ console-driver.ts:21 `private readonly isDev = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') === 'development';` and :33 `console driver in a non-dev environment: NOT delivering ... (body withheld)`. READ Dockerfile:83 `ENV NODE_ENV=production`. EXECUTED against the live audit environment (integration probe, signup then POST /t/<slug>/staff): `### SIGNUP 201`, `### INVITE STAFF 403 {"code":"email_verification_required",...}`, `### OWNER emailVerifiedAt = null`, and the outbox showed `{"kind":"email_verification","to":"owner@lrp-6e683b.test","status":"pending"}`. EXECUTED `psql \d email_outbox` — `bodyMarkdown text not null` confirms the psql escape hatch exists but is undocumented.
fix: Do not go public on console. Either (a) provision Resend, set EMAIL_DRIVER=resend + EMAIL_FROM and the DNS in finding 03, or (b) if launching on console anyway: add an owner-only admin endpoint that force-verifies a tenant user's email and issues a one-time password-reset link returned in the HTTP response, add an 'Emails' page to the admin panel that renders the outbox body, and correct docs/deploy-from-the-server.md:113 to say the body is withheld in production and where the link actually lives.
verification: RE-DERIVED AND RE-EXECUTED. READ console-driver.ts:21 — `isDev = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') === 'development'`; :31-35 the else-branch logs `NOT delivering "<subject>" to <addr> (body withheld)` and returns a fake providerId (so the outbox row is marked delivered). READ apps/api/Dockerfile:83 `ENV NODE_ENV=production` and `grep -n NODE_ENV infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` → lines 35 and 240, both `production`. RAN my own throwaway integration probe (apps/api/test/integration/zzz-verify-launch-probe.spec.ts, since deleted) against the live audit Postgres/Redis: `SIGNUP 201` / `LOGIN 200` / `OWNER emailVerifiedAt=null` / `INVITE-STAFF 403 {"code":"email_verification_required"}` / `PWRESET-REQ 202 {"ok":true}` / outbox row `{kind: email_verification, status: pending}`. Independently reproduced, not taken on trust. CHECKED FOR A GUARD ELSEWHERE AND FOUND NONE THAT SAVES IT: `grep -rn emailVerifiedAt apps/api/src --include=*.ts` returns exactly one writer — email-verification.service.ts:150/:166 — reachable only by redeeming a token that arrives by email. There is no admin force-verify endpoint (`ls apps/api/src/admin/` has no such controller; `grep passwordHash apps/api/src/admin apps/api/src/platform apps/api/src/support` returns only admin-auth.service.ts:39/:59, the admin's own login). ONE CLAIM IN THE ORIGINAL IS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED HERE: the finding says a librarian who forgets their password is locked out permanently. `POST /t/:slug/staff/:id/reset-password` (staff.controller.ts:58) → staff.service.ts:114-132 mints a temp password and RETURNS IT IN THE HTTP RESPONSE — no email involved. So a *staff member* has a working in-app recovery. This does not rescue the finding; it sharpens it, because the same EmailVerifiedGuard means no staff member can ever be created, so the owner is the only user that exists and the owner has no such path. ONE MITIGATION THE FINDING UNDERSTATES: `bodyMarkdown` is retained on the outbox row indefinitely (no purge job exists — `grep -rn emailOutbox apps/api/src/jobs` finds only support-session-expiry), and email-verification.service.ts:173 exposes a `resend`, so the operator's psql escape hatch can be re-primed at will rather than being a 60-minute window. It remains undocumented, and docs/deploy-from-the-server.md:113 still tells the operator the body IS in `docker logs api`, which I read and which is false under NODE_ENV=production. Severity stands at blocker: signup→invite-a-colleague is the core onboarding path of a library product and it terminates in a 403 with no self-service exit.

title: Export worker buffers every row of every table in memory and is OOM-killed on any real-sized library
what: readTables() loops the tenant's public tables and runs `const res = await client.query(`SELECT * FROM "${name}"`)` with no LIMIT, no OFFSET and no server-side cursor, pushing the full result set into a JS array (`out.push({ name, columns, rows, numericColumns })`). The MAX_EXPORT_ROWS = 2_000_000 guard (line 26) is evaluated at line 389 — AFTER the table has already been fully materialised — so it protects nothing. For xlsx the rows are then materialised a second time inside ExcelJS (buildWorkbook), and for the `all` scope this repeats per tenant into one zip.
impact: The worker container (`WORKER_MEM_LIMIT: 1g`, infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:269, no --max-old-space-size) is OOM-killed the first time an Institutional-sized library clicks 'Export'. Everything else the worker owns dies with it: the email outbox queue, in-flight CSV/XLSX imports, and all nine cron sweeps. The export job row is left `running` forever because the failure path never executes. And if the box did have the RAM, the 2M-row cap then aborts the export outright — so the largest paying tier can never export its own data (the product sells data export; GDPR Art. 20 portability rests on it).
evidence: RAN, against a tenant DB seeded to the Institutional numbers the pricing sells (400,000 books / 520,000 copies / 100,000 members / 2,000,000 loans / 3,000,000 audit rows, 1479 MB): a faithful replica of readTables() printed `baseline RSS 81 MB` then `audit_log: 3000000 rows in 4409ms — RSS now 1443 MB, cumulative rows 3000000` then `!! MAX_EXPORT_ROWS (2000000) exceeded AFTER buffering — export ABORTS`. Final `heapUsed 1275 MB`. One table alone, on the first iteration, exceeded the 1 GB container limit. Table sizes measured with pg_total_relation_size: audit_log 609 MB, loans 413 MB, books 168 MB.
fix: Stream instead of buffer. Either add `pg-cursor` and read each table in 10k-row chunks straight into the CSV/JSON/XLSX writer (ExcelJS has a streaming workbook writer, `ExcelJS.stream.xlsx.WorkbookWriter`), or use `COPY (SELECT * FROM t) TO STDOUT WITH CSV` via `pg-copy-streams` piped into the archive. Move the row-count check to a cheap `SELECT reltuples` pre-flight so an oversized export is refused before any work, not after 1.4 GB of allocation. Keep the hard cap only as a backstop.
verification: RAN an independent replica of readTables() against libriant_scale (the same 400k/520k/100k/2M/3M seed): `baseline RSS 51 MB` -> `audit_log: 3000000 rows in 4561ms — RSS 1462 MB, heapUsed 1272 MB`. One table alone exceeds the 1 GB worker mem_limit, which I re-read at infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:269 (`mem_limit: ${WORKER_MEM_LIMIT:-1g}`) with no NODE_OPTIONS/--max-old-space-size anywhere in infra or package.json. READ export-processors.ts:384-401 — the MAX_EXPORT_ROWS check is genuinely after `await client.query(`SELECT * FROM "name"`)`, and `out` retains every table for the whole loop, so the cap is cumulative-after-the-fact. READ worker.ts:44-48 — email, scheduled, import, maintenance and export consumers all live in ONE process, so the OOM does take them all down. CORRECTIONS to the original: (1) 'the export job row is left running forever' is FALSE — apps/api/src/jobs/export-cleanup.job.ts:51-68 reaps `status IN ('running','queued')` rows past a timeout and marks them failed; (2) the crash is not an unbounded loop — the queue is added without `attempts`, so BullMQ's stalled checker re-runs it once (maxStalledCount default 1) and then fails it: two OOM kills, not perpetual. Neither correction touches the mechanism or the severity. Severity kept at blocker: a single tenant click destroys the whole background tier for every tenant, and the 2M-row cap means the top-priced plan can never export its own data.

title: Every legal document is offered by an unnamed legal person — no Art. 28 contract, no Art. 13 controller identity, no P.D. 131/2003 provider identification
where: locales/en/legal/terms.md:9; locales/en/legal/privacy.md:26; locales/en/legal/dpa.md:9; locales/en/legal/legal-notice.md:13-20 (and the identical Greek files)
what: The Terms, Privacy Policy, DPA and Legal Notice all name the provider as `[COMPANY LEGAL NAME]` at `[REGISTERED ADDRESS]`, GEMI `[COMPANY REGISTRATION NUMBER / GEMI]`, VAT `[VAT NUMBER]` / `[TAX OFFICE]`, legal representative `[NAME(S)]`, contact `[CONTACT EMAIL]`, DPO `[DPO EMAIL]`. Every rendered page additionally carries a permanent banner reading 'Draft — pending review by qualified legal counsel … not legal advice' (apps/web/app/[locale]/legal/page.tsx:30-32 and [doc]/page.tsx:34-36 render `legal.draftNotice` unconditionally). Separately, apps/site/site.config.json names a DIFFERENT controller — the natural person 'Νικόλαος Πινάτσης', Λάρισα — so libriant.com and app.libriant.com publish two incompatible provider identities.
impact: A GDPR Art. 28(3) processor contract must identify the processor; a privacy notice must identify the controller (Art. 13(1)(a)); Greek P.D. 131/2003 (e-Commerce Directive Art. 5) requires legal name, address, GEMI and VAT on the site. None exist. The clickwrap therefore forms no enforceable contract and no valid Art. 28 agreement, so from the first member record entered, Libriant processes public-library patron data — including children's — with no lawful processor arrangement at all. Every target customer is a public body whose DPO will read /legal/dpa, see the draft banner and the empty party name, and stop the procurement. Both the library and Libriant are exposed to HDPA enforcement under Art. 28 + Art. 83(4)(a).
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/terms.md:9 — 'These Terms of Service ("Terms") are a binding agreement between `[COMPANY LEGAL NAME]`, `[REGISTERED ADDRESS]`, company reg. no. `[COMPANY REGISTRATION NUMBER / GEMI]`'. RAN `grep -o '\[[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9 ,/&.()-]*\]' locales/*/legal/*.md | sort | uniq -c` → 12 uppercase placeholders in privacy.md, 9 in terms.md, 9 in legal-notice.md, 4 in dpa.md, per locale. READ apps/site/site.config.json → "controllerName": "Νικόλαος Πινάτσης".
fix: Register the operating entity, then fill every `[PLACEHOLDER]` in all 14 markdown files (7 slugs x 2 locales), make the site's `identity.controllerName` the same entity, have Greek/EU data-protection counsel review, then delete the `legal.draftNotice` string and the two `<Banner>` blocks and bump LEGAL_VERSION. Do not accept a single signup until this is done.
verification: Re-read every cited line. locales/en/legal/terms.md:9 does read '…between `[COMPANY LEGAL NAME]`, `[REGISTERED ADDRESS]`, company reg. no. `[COMPANY REGISTRATION NUMBER / GEMI]`'; legal-notice.md:13-20 carries seven unfilled identity placeholders under a heading that explicitly cites 'P.D. 131/2003 and Article 13 GDPR'; dpa.md:9-11 names the Processor as `[COMPANY LEGAL NAME]`. Confirmed the conflicting identity: apps/site/site.config.json:4 `"controllerName": "Νικόλαος Πινάτσης"`. Confirmed the render path is unconditional — apps/web/app/[locale]/legal/[doc]/page.tsx:34-36 and legal/page.tsx emit `<Banner>{t('legal.draftNotice')}</Banner>` with no flag, and apps/web/lib/legal.ts passes the markdown to `marked` verbatim, so the file's own '> **Draft — pending review by qualified legal counsel.**' blockquote renders on the page too — the reader sees TWO draft warnings, not one. One correction to the finding's reasoning, which does not change the verdict: the quoted banner wording is the markdown blockquote, not the i18n string (locales/en/legal.json:20 reads 'Draft pending legal review — this document may change before general availability and is not yet legal advice.'), and the assertion that the clickwrap 'forms no enforceable contract' is overstated — a contract with an extrinsically identifiable party is not automatically void. The verdict stands on the parts that are not arguable: no Art. 28(3) processor identification, no P.D. 131/2003 provider identification, and a self-declared draft banner on the page a public-body DPO will read. Severity unchanged.

title: Backups are unencrypted and the off-site copy is never pruned — the DPA's 'encrypted backups' TOM is false and erasure never propagates out of backups
what: backup.sh produces `pg_dumpall`→.sql.gz of the control DB plus every tenant DB, a `tar czf` of the storage volume, and a tar of the Caddy access log. There is no gpg/age/openssl step anywhere — `grep -niE 'gpg|encrypt|age|openssl|crypt' scripts/backup.sh` returns only unrelated matches, and scripts/secrets.ts defines only BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL, BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS, BACKUP_ALLOW_LOCAL_ONLY (no passphrase). Local dailies are pruned at BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS (default 14, scripts/ensure-env.sh:113). The off-site push is `rclone copy --quiet "$dest" "$RCLONE_REMOTE/$day"` (line 188) — `copy`, not `sync`, into a per-day path, with no `--delete`, no lifecycle rule and no prune step anywhere in the repo. Off-site dailies therefore accumulate forever.
impact: Plain-text SQL dumps of every Greek library's complete member registry — fullName, dateOfBirth, home address, phone, email, staffNotes, and the full loan/reservation/fine history of each named person including school-library children — sit on a Hetzner Storage Box readable by anyone who obtains the rclone credentials or the storage-box snapshot. Art. 32(1)(a) explicitly names encryption; the DPA promises it contractually, so the statement in the binding Art. 28 agreement is untrue. Because off-site copies are never deleted, an Art. 17 erasure or a tenant hard-delete never reaches the backups — the Privacy Policy's 'deleted copies age out of backups' is false in the deployed design, not merely in a placeholder.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:88 — '…regular **encrypted** backups with restore testing'. READ locales/en/legal/privacy.md:85 — 'Backups: rotated on a rolling `[14]`-day cycle, after which deleted copies age out of backups.' RAN `grep -niE 'gpg|encrypt|age|openssl|crypt' scripts/backup.sh` → no encryption call. READ scripts/backup.sh:188 `rclone copy --quiet "$dest" "$RCLONE_REMOTE/$day"`; RAN `grep -n 'rclone' scripts/backup.sh` → one call, no delete/prune of the remote.
fix: Encrypt each artefact before it leaves the box (`age -r <recipient>` or `gpg --symmetric` with a key held outside the host, or an `rclone crypt` remote) and record the key-management story in the DPA Annex II. Add a remote-retention step (`rclone delete --min-age ${BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS}d` or a storage-box lifecycle policy) and prove it in scripts/dr-drill.sh. Only then may the DPA say 'encrypted' and the Privacy Policy say copies age out.
verification: RAN `grep -niE 'gpg|encrypt|age -|openssl|crypt' scripts/backup.sh` → one hit, the comment '# ---------- 2. Storage ---' (matches on 'stora**ge**'). No encryption call exists. RAN `grep -n rclone scripts/backup.sh` → the only invocation is :188 `rclone copy --quiet "$dest" "$RCLONE_REMOTE/$day"`, into a per-day path. Widened the search to the whole repo (`grep -rn rclone --include='*.md' --include='*.sh' --include='*.ts'`): docs/deployment-hetzner.md:626-627 sets up a plain `type sftp` remote, and nothing anywhere configures an `rclone crypt` remote or a lifecycle rule — `grep -rniE 'rclone.*crypt|BACKUP_.*(KEY|PASS)'` returns nothing. Local dailies ARE pruned (backup.sh:66-68 `find … -mtime +$BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS -exec rm -rf`); the off-site copy is not, exactly as claimed. Re-read locales/en/legal/dpa.md:88 — 'regular **encrypted** backups with restore testing' — so the Art. 28 document states a measure the code does not implement. One nuance that does not reduce severity: encrypting the artefact on the app host is of limited value against an attacker who already has that host (they have the live DB too). The exposure that justifies blocker is the off-site leg — a plaintext pg_dumpall of every tenant registry on a Hetzner Storage Box, retained forever, reachable with the rclone credentials that sit on the same host — plus the fact that the DPA's statement is untrue either way. Severity unchanged.

title: member-notifications job fails for EVERY tenant on EVERY run (cold Redis client) and reports success
what: `sendMemberNotifications()` constructs a brand-new `RedisService` at line 138 and then immediately enters the per-tenant loop. The first statement of `notifyOneTenant` (line 188) is `await plans.getBool(ctx.id, 'email_notifications_enabled')`, a Redis GET. `RedisService` (apps/api/src/platform/redis.service.ts:27) sets `enableOfflineQueue: false`, so any command issued while the socket is still in `connecting` state rejects synchronously with `Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false`. Because each iteration throws on its very first await, the whole loop drains in microseconds — long before the socket reaches `ready`. Every tenant lands in the `catch` at line 159 (`failed++`, a `logger.warn`), and the job then returns a success-shaped JobResult.
impact: Due-soon reminders, overdue notices and hold-ready pickup emails are never sent for any library, on any hourly tick, forever — while the worker's /healthz reports `{"member-notifications":{"ok":true,"message":"N tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due"}}`. For a launch whose selling point is library member notifications, the feature is 100% dead on arrival and the health surface actively says it is fine. Libraries discover it weeks later when patrons complain they were never told a hold was ready.
evidence:
RAN. Isolated stack (Postgres 16 on :55441, Redis on :6391), three seeded tenants, tenant DBs healthy. Invoking the exact registry handler five times:
```
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=reltwo: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=relthree: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=relfour: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
RUN 0: {"dueSoon":0,"overdue":0,"holdReady":0,"tenantsScanned":3,"tenantsFailed":3} 3 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due
```
5/5 runs, 3/3 tenants, zero successes. Separately confirmed the mechanism directly:
```
status right after construct: connecting
immediate get THREW: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
status after 500ms: ready
later get -> null
```
fix: Await readiness before using a freshly-constructed client: add `async ready(){ if (this.client.status !== 'ready') await new Promise((r,j)=>{this.client.once('ready',r); this.client.once('error',j);}); }` to RedisService and `await redis.ready()` right after line 138 (same for stripe-retry.job.ts:67). Better: pass the worker's long-lived `sharedRedis` into `JobContext` (jobs.types.ts) instead of letting each job mint its own client. Independently, add a regression test that runs the handler against a real Redis without pre-warming.
verification: RE-EXECUTED end to end, not just re-read. (1) Isolated the mechanism: instantiated the real RedisService and issued a GET on the next tick -> `status right after ctor: connecting` / `GET REJECTED -> Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false`, twice in a row. (2) Ran the real handler against the live audit control plane (49 active tenants): every tenant logged `member notifications failed for tenant=<slug>: Stream isn't writeable...` and the function returned `{"message":"49 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due","counts":{"dueSoon":0,"overdue":0,"holdReady":0,"tenantsScanned":49,"tenantsFailed":49}}`. 100% failure, success-shaped message. (3) Checked for a guard elsewhere and found none: EffectivePlanService.readCache (effective-plan.service.ts:275-277) issues the GET with no try/catch, and getEffectivePlan calls it before settings.billingEnabled(), so BILLING_ENABLED=false does not short-circuit the Redis hit. The existing member-notifications.job.spec.ts does not catch this because it supplies a mocked Redis. Severity stands: the feature is 100% dead on every tick.

title: The pnpm pin in all three Dockerfiles is inert — corepack demands pnpm 11.22.0 at runtime, which hard-fails the migrate one-shot and blocks the whole stack from starting
where: apps/api/Dockerfile:28-31,79,97 + scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh:35 + infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:171-181,209-211 (migrate hard-fail); apps/web/Dockerfile:9,64,68 (no COREPACK_HOME, pnpm is PID 1); infra/caddy/Dockerfile:16; vs package.json:6 ("packageManager": "pnpm@11.22.0")
what: Corepack always honours the nearest package.json `packageManager` field; `corepack prepare X --activate` only sets the fallback for projects that declare nothing. So inside every image build, `pnpm install` is pnpm 11.22.0 fetched from https://registry.npmjs.org/pnpm/-/pnpm-11.22.0.tgz at that moment, not the 9.15.4 the Dockerfiles claim to pin. The `packageManager` value carries no `+sha224.<hash>` integrity suffix, so the pin is a version string resolved from the network, and it is the very binary that then executes the allow-listed install scripts during the build. Commit fe0931e bumped `packageManager` to 11.22.0 and removed the `version: 9.15.4` input from pnpm/action-setup in all five CI jobs, but left the three Dockerfile `corepack prepare` lines behind.
impact: The first containerized deploy of this stack does not come up. The `migrate` one-shot exits 1 before touching the database, and api/worker/web are all gated on it completing successfully, so the deploy dies with a corepack cache-permission error that reads nothing like its cause. Independently, the web container fetches its package manager from npmjs.org on every single start, so a registry outage or an egress-restricted host means web never boots. Neither failure is caught by any test — no CI job builds or runs these images.
evidence: RAN with a fresh empty COREPACK_HOME and network disabled, from the repo root: `corepack prepare pnpm@9.15.4 --activate` then `corepack pnpm -v` -> `Network access disabled by the environment; can't reach https://registry.npmjs.org/pnpm/-/pnpm-11.22.0.tgz` — corepack ignored the freshly-prepared 9.15.4 and demanded 11.22.0. Also `/opt/homebrew/bin/pnpm -v` = 9.15.4 but `corepack pnpm -v` = 11.22.0 in this repo, and node_modules/.modules.yaml records `"packageManager": "pnpm@11.22.0"`.
fix: Three one-line changes plus a test. (a) apps/api/Dockerfile:30, apps/web/Dockerfile:9, infra/caddy/Dockerfile:16 -> `corepack prepare pnpm@11.22.0 --activate` so the warmed cache matches what package.json demands. (b) apps/web/Dockerfile: add `ENV COREPACK_HOME=/opt/corepack` before line 9 and `chmod -R a+rX` after, mirroring the api image, so the web container stops downloading pnpm at boot. (c) Add the integrity suffix to package.json:6 (`pnpm@11.22.0+sha224.`) so corepack verifies the tarball. Then add a CI job that actually builds the api image and runs `docker run --rm --user node pnpm --version` — this class of defect is invisible to every check currently in verify.yml.
verification: REFUTATION ATTEMPT FAILED — the finding is real and UNDER-rated; I raised it medium -> blocker after reproducing two distinct container-boot failures. (1) Corepack precedence: RAN `COREPACK_HOME=<fresh> corepack prepare pnpm@9.15.4 --activate` then `corepack pnpm -v` from the repo root -> printed `11.22.0`. The Dockerfile pin is provably inert, exactly as claimed. (2) The migrate one-shot HARD-FAILS, which the original finding only speculated about. apps/api/Dockerfile:79 is `FROM base AS runtime` — NOT from `deps` — so the only thing ever written into /opt/corepack in the shipped image is pnpm 9.15.4 (line 30); the `pnpm install` at line 54 that would have cached 11.22.0 lives in the `deps` layer, which the runtime stage never inherits. Line 31 `chmod -R a+rX` grants read+traverse, NOT write, and the dir is root-owned; line 97 sets `USER node`. compose `migrate` (docker-compose.prod.yml:171-181) runs `sh /app/scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh` as that node user, and prod-bootstrap.sh:35 calls `pnpm db:migrate:deploy` with cwd /app, where /app/package.json declares `packageManager: pnpm@11.22.0`. I reproduced that exact state locally: warmed a COREPACK_HOME with ONLY pnpm/9.15.4, made it non-writable, ran `corepack pnpm --version` from the repo root -> `EXIT=1`, stderr `Failed to create cache directory. Please ensure the user has write access to the target directory (<COREPACK_HOME>/v1)`. No fallback to the activated 9.15.4 — corepack exits 1. prod-bootstrap.sh:35-38 turns that into `FATAL: control-plane migration failed` + exit 1, and api/worker/web all gate on `migrate: condition: service_completed_successfully` (docker-compose.prod.yml:209-211). The stack cannot come up. (3) A SECOND boot path the finding missed: apps/web/Dockerfile sets NO COREPACK_HOME at all (line 9 is a bare `corepack prepare pnpm@9.15.4 --activate` run as root), line 64 is `USER node`, and line 68 is `CMD ["pnpm", "--filter", "@libriant/web", "start"]`. So the web container's PID 1 IS corepack: at EVERY container start it looks in /home/node/.cache/node/corepack (empty — only root's cache was warmed at build), sees packageManager 11.22.0, and downloads https://registry.npmjs.org/pnpm/-/pnpm-11.22.0.tgz live before Next.js starts. That directory IS writable by node, so it does not fail — it makes every web-container start depend on npmjs.org being up and on the host having egress, and executes a freshly-fetched tarball on the boot path. (4) Nothing catches it: `grep -rn 'docker build|docker compose|Dockerfile' .github/workflows/verify.yml` returns NOTHING — no CI job builds or runs these images. Same blind spot that hid the broken DR restore. (5) Corroborated by the repo's own history: commit fe0931e explicitly reasoned about this drift for CI ("CI's pnpm/action-setup still pinned version: 9.15.4, which would now contradict packageManager... Removed from all five jobs") and simply missed the three Dockerfiles.

title: Any unauthenticated caller can lock every Libriant admin out of the control plane, and doing so also kills their already-active sessions
what: `AdminAuthService.recordFailure` increments `adminUser.failedAttempts` and, at `MAX_FAILED_LOGINS` (default 5), sets `lockedUntil = now + LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MS` **and** `status = 'locked'`. The lock is keyed on the account alone — there is no IP component, unlike the tenant side, where login.service.ts:10-16 documents exactly this attack ("A bare-account lock lets ANY attacker lock ANY user out … a trivial, renewable DoS") and fixes it with per-(account+IP) keys. Worse, `AdminAuthGuard.canActivate` rejects on `admin.status !== 'active'`, so flipping status to 'locked' does not merely block new sign-ins: it 403s the admin's **existing, valid session cookie** on the next request. Nothing in the app can clear the lock except a successful login (`recordSuccess` restores `status: 'active'`), which the attacker prevents by re-locking. The only per-IP brake is 20 admin-login attempts / 5 min (admin-auth.controller.ts:54) — and per authn-authz-01 that bucket is itself attacker-controlled.
impact: Five HTTP requests every fifteen minutes, from an unauthenticated attacker who knows or guesses an admin email address, permanently deny the operator access to admin.libriant.com. There is no in-app unlock (no owner-tier unlock endpoint exists) — recovery requires direct database access. The likely moment for this attack is during an incident, when the admin console is exactly what is needed. It also blocks the support-key redemption path, so no engineer can reach a customer's library either.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P4): created an active admin, logged in (`/admin/auth/me` → 200), then sent five wrong-password logins from an unauthenticated client. DB row afterwards: `{"status":"locked","lockedUntil":"2026-08-23T10:02:37.603Z","failedAttempts":5}`. The previously-issued admin cookie then returned **403** `{"message":"Your admin account is no longer active."}`, and a legitimate re-login with the correct password returned **401**. Probe output lines P4.
fix: Key the admin lockout on (adminId, clientIp) in Redis the way LoginService already does, and stop writing `status = 'locked'` — the status column is read by AdminAuthGuard as an account-disabled signal and must not be driven by unauthenticated input. Keep `lockedUntil` as the gate inside `verify()` only. Add an owner-tier unlock endpoint plus a `scripts/` unlock so recovery does not need psql.
verification: Tried hardest to refute this one and could not. READ admin-auth.service.ts:83-96 — `recordFailure` writes `status: 'locked'` alongside `lockedUntil`; admin-auth.guard.ts:46-48 rejects on `admin.status !== 'active'`. RAN end-to-end against the live app: created an active owner-tier admin, logged in (`GET /admin/auth/me` → 200), then sent FIVE unauthenticated wrong-password logins. DB row afterwards `{"status":"locked","lockedUntil":"…","failedAttempts":5}`; the previously-issued, still-unexpired admin cookie then returned **403**, and a legitimate login with the CORRECT password returned **401** `Too many failed sign-in attempts.` Checked for an escape hatch and found none: `recordSuccess` (the only writer of `status:'active'`) is unreachable while `verify()` throws on `lockedUntil`, and grep of the admin route table shows no unlock endpoint at any tier — recovery is psql only. The unauthenticated attacker needs the admin's email address and nothing else. Severity held at high.

title: An impersonating admin can mint permanent tenant credentials, and the audit log the library sees does not show it
what: `RolesGuard.canActivate` begins with `if (req.impersonation) return true;` — the impersonation cookie satisfies every `@Roles(...)` and `@StaffWrite()` annotation in the tenant API without any tenant session. That includes `POST /t/:slug/staff/:id/reset-password`, whose response body contains the new plaintext temporary password, and `DELETE /t/:slug/support/keys/pending`, which lets the impersonator destroy the library's own key-management state. The support-access model's whole premise is a consented, time-boxed, library-revocable 4-hour window; a credential handed out inside that window outlives it indefinitely, because nothing ties `users.passwordHash` to the support session. Meanwhile `SupportAuditInterceptor` writes only `{ method, path, status }` — no request body, no response body, no target — so the row the library reads at `GET /t/:slug/support/sessions/log` says `POST /t/<slug>/staff/<id>/reset-password 200` and gives the library no way to know a working credential was disclosed, or to which account. The interceptor's own comment concedes before/after diffs are "TODO".
impact: A Libriant admin (support tier — `POST /admin/support/redeem` is behind AdminAuthGuard only, with no `@AdminRoles`) who is granted one 4-hour support window walks away with a working staff password for that library, usable from the normal login page forever after the window closes, and can destroy the library's pending-support-key state. The library's audit trail records the request line but not the disclosure or its target, so the library cannot tell from the log which account's credential left the building. (Verification correction: the reset DOES bump `sessionsValidAfter` and re-arm `mustChangeCredentials`, so the affected staff member is locked out and will notice something happened — the disclosure is disruptive rather than silent. It is also bounded: the impersonator cannot create new staff or self-issue a fresh support key, both of which require a real tenant session.) Given the product is sold to Greek public libraries holding member PII, a consented, time-boxed window that yields an unbounded credential defeats the model the feature exists to provide.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P10): with **only** an impersonation cookie for a `support`-role admin and no tenant session at all — `DELETE /t/<slug>/support/keys/pending` → **204**; `GET /t/<slug>/support/sessions/log` → 200; `GET /t/<slug>/staff` → 200; `POST /t/<slug>/staff/<id>/reset-password` → **200, TEMP PASSWORD DISCLOSED**. READ support-audit.interceptor.ts:43-50 — the log row carries only sessionId/method/path/status.
fix: Deny credential-minting and support-key routes under impersonation: replace the blanket `if (req.impersonation) return true` with an allowlist, or add an `@NotUnderImpersonation()` decorator applied to `staff/:id/reset-password`, `staff` create, `staff/:id/role`, `billing/*`, `exports`, and the whole LibrarySupportController. If support genuinely needs a password reset, make it force `mustChangeCredentials` AND set `sessionsValidAfter`, return no plaintext to the admin, and email the credential to the library owner instead. Extend the audit row with target type/id and a redacted body summary so the log is meaningful.
verification: Core claim CONFIRMED by execution, two sub-claims corrected. READ roles.guard.ts:41 (the finding cites :43; the actual line is 41) — `if (req.impersonation) return true;` precedes every role check. RAN with ONLY an impersonation cookie and no tenant session whatsoever: `GET /t/<slug>/staff` → 200; `POST /t/<slug>/staff/<managed-staff-id>/reset-password` → **200 with the plaintext tempPassword in the body**; `DELETE /t/<slug>/support/keys/pending` → **204**. READ support-audit.interceptor.ts:43-50 and confirmed against the live `GET /t/<slug>/support/sessions/log` response, which returned the row `{method:'DELETE', path:'/t/<slug>/support/keys/pending', status:204, targetType:null, …}` — the target columns exist in the schema and are never populated, so the library's log genuinely cannot tell it which account's credential was disclosed. CORRECTIONS that bound the finding: (1) the impersonator CANNOT create a new staff account (`POST /t/:slug/staff` also carries `@UseGuards(EmailVerifiedGuard)`, email-verified.guard.ts:27-32, which 401s with no `req.session`) and CANNOT self-issue a fresh support key to extend the window (`POST /t/:slug/support/keys` takes `@Sess()`, session-context.ts:21-23, which 401s) — I probed for both, since a self-renewing window would have made this a blocker; (2) `staff.service.ts:116-131` DOES set `sessionsValidAfter` and `mustChangeCredentials: true` on the reset, so the affected staff member is locked out of their own account and will notice — the finding's 'indistinguishable from a real staff sign-in / not detectable' overstates the stealth. What survives, and holds the high, is that a 4-hour consented window yields a permanent working tenant credential plus destruction of the library's key-management state, with a role guard that is bypassed wholesale rather than by allowlist.

title: Stripe Checkout's success and cancel URLs 404 — every library that pays lands on "This page could not be found"
what: startCheckout builds successUrl/cancelUrl as `${BILLING_RETURN_URL}/t/<slug>/billing?checkout=success`. The web app has exactly one billing route, `/[locale]/t/[slug]/billing` (4 path segments, locale mandatory). `/t/<slug>/billing` is 3 segments, there is no root-level catch-all (apps/web/app contains only `[locale]`, `api`, page.tsx, not-found.tsx), no Next middleware, and next.config.mjs rewrites only `/_assets/*`, `/lbr-api/*` and `/admin/*`. Neither web caller ever supplies `returnPath` (PlanGrid.tsx:109-115 and ChoosePlanScreen.tsx:62-68 send only planSlug + interval), so the locale-less fallback on line 302 is always what Stripe receives.
impact: A library that has just paid lands on "This page could not be found" instead of a confirmation, and the Customer Portal return_url (billing.service.ts:335-340) has the identical defect. The subscription is real and correctly provisioned by the webhook, so the damage is confidence and support load rather than money — but it is the first thing a paying customer sees.
evidence:
EXECUTED. Booted the existing production build (`next start -p 3999`) and requested both paths:
  /t/demo/billing?checkout=success -> 404   (body contains "could not be found")
  /el/t/demo/billing               -> 307   (redirect to login, i.e. the route exists)
Route table confirms it: `grep -o '"/[^"]*billing[^"]*"' apps/web/.next/types/routes.d.ts` yields exactly one entry, "/[locale]/t/[slug]/billing".
fix: Prefix the locale in the return path: resolve the caller's locale (pass it from the client, or default to `el`) and build `${base}/${locale}/t/${slug}/billing?checkout=success`. Apply the same fix to openCustomerPortal's return_url (billing.service.ts:335-340), which has the identical defect. Add an assertion in the checkout spec that the generated successUrl matches a real Next route.
verification: CONFIRMED the mechanism, DOWNGRADED the severity. Verified independently of the original probe: `grep -o '"/[^"]*billing[^"]*"' apps/web/.next/types/routes.d.ts` yields exactly one route, "/[locale]/t/[slug]/billing". Hunted for the rewrite that would rescue the locale-less path and found none — apps/web/app contains only [locale]/, api/, layout.tsx, page.tsx, not-found.tsx; there is no middleware file anywhere under apps/web; next.config.mjs rewrites only /_assets/*, /lbr-api/* and /admin/*; and the Caddyfile has no /t/* handler (its app-host block is handle_path /lbr-api/*, handle /webhooks/*, then a catch-all reverse_proxy to web:3000). Confirmed neither caller passes returnPath: PlanGrid.tsx:111-116 and ChoosePlanScreen.tsx:61-68 both send only {planSlug, interval}. Downgraded blocker -> high because the stated harm does not fully follow: the charge and the webhook-driven provisioning both succeed, and the librarian recovers by navigating back into the app. It is an alarming 404 at the worst possible moment and a fifteen-minute fix, but the money and the data are correct — the double-subscription harm belongs to billing-03, not to this.

title: A webhook that fails during a database outage is lost permanently — 200 is returned to Stripe and no durable row exists for the sweep to rescue
what: The durable `stripe_webhook_events` insert is best-effort: its `.catch()` on line 83 logs a warning and continues. The handler then dispatches; on failure it logs, attempts an update of the row that was never written (swallowed by `.catch(() => undefined)`), deletes the Redis lock, and returns `{ received: true }` with HTTP 200 (the @HttpCode(200) on line 48 applies to every non-throwing return). Stripe treats 200 as final and never redelivers. The retry sweep can only find rows in stripe_webhook_events (stripe-retry.job.ts:52). The comment on line 118 — 'Drop the Redis lock so a Stripe retry can re-attempt' — describes a retry that cannot happen, because we already told Stripe the event was received.
impact: The one failure mode both recovery mechanisms are built for — a Postgres blip — is the exact case where both are unavailable, because the insert and the dispatch fail together. Subscription state silently diverges from Stripe: a cancellation never applied, a payment failure never recorded, a paid upgrade never provisioned, with no error row, no alert, and no way to know which events were lost.
evidence: READ, stripe-webhook.controller.ts:73-123. The upsert's failure path is a warn-and-continue; the dispatch catch block ends in `return { received: true }` at line 123 with no rethrow and no status change. Cross-checked against the sweep's query (stripe-retry.job.ts:52-60), which selects only from stripe_webhook_events.
fix: If the durable insert fails, do not proceed — rethrow so Nest returns a 5xx and Stripe retries. Likewise, on a dispatch failure where the error row could not be written, return non-2xx. A 200 must mean 'this event is durably ours'.
verification: READ-verified the exact control flow and looked hard for the recovery path the comments promise. stripe-webhook.controller.ts:73-85 — the durable upsert's `.catch()` logs a warning and falls through; :101-121 — dispatch failure logs, attempts an update of the row that was never written (swallowed by `.catch(() => undefined)`), drops the Redis key, and :123 returns `{received:true}` under `@HttpCode(200)` at :48. Checked the sweep as the candidate guard and it does not cover this: stripe-retry.job.ts:52-60 selects exclusively FROM stripe_webhook_events, so a row that was never inserted is invisible to it forever. Note the window is wider than 'Postgres is down' — a single transient failure on that one upsert is enough, because the dispatch that follows will fail the same way and the 200 is unconditional. Kept at high: silent, unbounded divergence from Stripe with no error row and no alert.

title: The founding-offer procedure the go-live doc mandates cannot be carried out, and the term it creates expires silently
where: docs/billing-go-live.md ('Founding-offer libraries must be on billingMode = manual with paidUntil twelve months out')
what: billingMode is never settable on its own: every write derives it from the chosen plan (billing.service.ts:241 selectPlan, :415 applyAdminPlanChange, :618 syncStripeSubscription, auth/signup.service.ts:181). The only plan with billingMode='manual' is `on-prem-enterprise`. applyManualPayment refuses unless billingMode is already 'manual' (line 452). So making one of the five launch libraries 'manual' means moving them to on-prem-enterprise, which (a) grants 1,000,000,000 on every quota rather than the tier they were promised, and (b) has monthlyPriceCents = 0, which getDesktopAccess reads as a free plan and blocks — `if (sub.plan.monthlyPriceCents <= 0) return { allowed:false, reason:'free-plan' }` (billing.service.ts:186-188). Separately, nothing anywhere watches paidUntil: `grep -rn paidUntil apps/api/src` shows it read only by the effective-plan SQL and written only by applyManualPayment; there is no job, no email, no admin list of upcoming expiries.
impact: The twelve-months-free cohort — the entire Greek go-to-market — cannot be configured as documented. If they are put on on-prem-enterprise they lose the desktop app the offer includes. Whatever is done, on the day paidUntil passes the effective-plan join drops (effective-plan.service.ts:180) and all five libraries fall to Starter caps mid-morning with no warning to them and no notification to the operator.
evidence: EXECUTED: the plans table shows on-prem-enterprise as the only manual plan, monthlyPriceCents=0, and its plan_feature_values are 1000000000 across every integer feature with every boolean true. READ: desktop-access.spec.ts covers free/paid/trialing/past_due/canceled/paused but has no manual-plan case (`grep -n 'it(' apps/api/src/desktop/desktop-access.spec.ts`).
fix: Base the desktop entitlement on billingMode/plan tier rather than `monthlyPriceCents > 0`. Allow billingMode to be set per-subscription independently of the plan (an admin flag), so a library can sit on Municipal with manual billing. Add a scheduled job that warns the operator — and the library — 30 and 7 days before paidUntil lapses, and an admin view listing expiring manual terms.
verification: EXECUTED against the audit control plane plus targeted reads. `SELECT slug, billingMode, monthlyPriceCents, isPublic FROM plans` returns on-prem-enterprise as the ONLY billingMode='manual' row, with monthlyPriceCents=0 and isPublic=false. Verified each link in the chain rather than trusting it: billingMode is derived from the plan at every write (selectPlan :241, applyAdminPlanChange :415, syncStripeSubscription :618, signup.service.ts:181) — there is no independent setter; applyManualPayment refuses unless billingMode is already 'manual' (:453-457); getDesktopAccess returns {allowed:false, reason:'free-plan'} for monthlyPriceCents <= 0 (:186-188), which on-prem-enterprise is. Re-ran the paidUntil grep myself: it is read only by effective-plan.service.ts:180/226-229 and written only by applyManualPayment — no job, no email, no admin expiry list.
