(1) Serializer: `pino-std-serializers@7.1.0 .res()` on a fake response returns `{"statusCode":null,"headers":{"set-cookie":[...],...}}` — set-cookie is in the serialised object. (2) Live API: POST /auth/logout, then read the API's own log file. The pino-http INFO line contains `"res":{"statusCode":204,"headers":{...,"set-cookie":"libriant_session=; Path=/; ..."}}`. The logout cookie is empty by construction, but it proves the response Set-Cookie header is emitted verbatim into stdout, so a login/signup response logs the live JWT. Verified the cited guard does NOT cover it: app.module.ts:48 `redact: ['req.headers.authorization','req.headers.cookie']` — request headers only, no res path. Severity stands (note: this is a credential-exposure finding sitting in the reliability set; dedupe against authn-authz if it also appears there).

title: No alert is ever delivered to a human — Alertmanager is commented out and the monitoring stack is not part of any deploy
what: prometheus.yml's `alerting:`/`alertmanagers:` block is commented out, and alerts.yml's own header states the rules are only "visible in the Prometheus + Grafana 'Alerts' views" until one is wired. There is no Alertmanager service in infra/monitoring/docker-compose.monitoring.yml's scrape/alert path and no email/Slack/ntfy receiver anywhere in the repo. The monitoring stack is a separate manual `docker compose -f infra/monitoring/docker-compose.monitoring.yml up -d` (docs/deployment-hetzner.md:790) that no deploy step, script, or workflow runs.
impact: `LibriantApiDown`, `HostDiskCritical`, `LibriantPgConnectionsCritical` — none of them reach a person. Nobody wakes up at 3am because nothing wakes them. Compounding this, Compose's `restart: unless-stopped` does not act on healthcheck failures, so a container that is up-but-permanently-unhealthy (the Redis-outage state in reliability-02, a wedged queue consumer) is neither restarted nor reported. On Monday the detection path for a total outage is 'a librarian emails support'.
evidence: READ. `grep -n alertmanagers infra/monitoring/prometheus.yml` → line 19, inside a comment block. alerts.yml lines 5-7: "Wire an Alertmanager (email / Slack / ntfy) in prometheus.yml to actually deliver these; until then they're visible in the Prometheus + Grafana 'Alerts' views." `grep -rn 'docker-compose.monitoring' .github/ scripts/` → no matches (only two doc mentions).
fix: Before launch: add an Alertmanager container to the monitoring compose file with one receiver the founder actually reads (email to the ops mailbox, or ntfy/Pushover on a phone), uncomment the `alerting:` block, and add the monitoring stack to the deploy runbook's mandatory steps. Also add an external, off-box uptime check (healthchecks.io / UptimeRobot) hitting the public origin, so a dead host — which also kills Prometheus — is still detected.
verification: Re-derived from the files. prometheus.yml:17-21 — the whole `alerting:`/`alertmanagers:` block is commented out; the only live directive is `rule_files: - /etc/prometheus/alerts.yml`. alerts.yml:5-7 states delivery is not wired. `grep -rni alertmanager` over the repo returns only comments in those two files plus server-handbook.md:389 which admits it. alerts.yml defines 10 rules (TargetDown, LibriantApiDown, HostDiskCritical, LibriantPgConnectionsCritical, ...) with no delivery path for any of them. `grep -rn docker-compose.monitoring` finds only its own header comment and two doc lines — no script or workflow starts it. Also verified the compounding claim: docker compose `restart: unless-stopped` does not act on healthcheck state, so an up-but-unhealthy container is neither restarted nor reported. Severity stands: this is the finding that makes several others undetectable.

title: restore.sh untars tenant uploads into the in-container path on the host — a default restore silently recovers zero files and reports success
what: `STORAGE_DIR="${STORAGE_DIR:-/srv/libriant/storage}"`. That is the IN-CONTAINER mount target (docker-compose.prod.yml:168,228 `storage:/srv/libriant/storage`); on the host, uploads live in the `libriant_storage` docker volume. backup.sh went to considerable lengths to fix exactly this asymmetry — it resolves the real mountpoint via `docker volume inspect ... --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'` (backup.sh:54-63) and its own comment states the in-container path "does NOT exist on the host, so defaulting to it silently skipped every upload". restore.sh never got the same treatment. With the default, restore.sh does `mkdir -p /srv/libriant/storage`, untars every tenant's covers/branding/exports into that freshly-created host directory, logs `storage restored`, and finishes with `restore complete`. No container ever mounts it.
impact: During a real recovery — the one time this script is ever run, under pressure — every tenant upload appears to be restored and none of it is. The operator gets a clean exit and a green tenant-count check (which only counts databases), puts the cluster back into service, and the libraries find their cover images, logos and generated exports gone. The correct invocation exists only in prose (docs/server-handbook.md:449, docs/deployment-hetzner.md:661 pass `STORAGE_DIR=/mnt/libriant/storage`); nothing in the script enforces it, and deployment-hetzner.md:620 tells the operator that for backup "no STORAGE_DIR is needed", which primes them to omit it for restore too.
evidence: READ. `scripts/restore.sh:30` `STORAGE_DIR="${STORAGE_DIR:-/srv/libriant/storage}"` versus `scripts/backup.sh:54-63` which resolves `docker volume inspect "${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME}_storage" --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'` with fallbacks and then hard-aborts if the directory is missing. The DR drill does not exercise storage at all (see reliability-08), so nothing catches the divergence.
fix: Copy backup.sh's resolution block into restore.sh verbatim (volume inspect → conventional volume path → bind path) and make an unresolvable/nonexistent STORAGE_DIR a hard `die`, not a silent `mkdir -p`. After untarring, assert a non-zero file count and print the resolved path. Add a storage round-trip leg to dr-drill.sh.
verification: Re-derived, and I closed the one gap the original evidence left open — whether /srv/libriant/storage happens to be a host path after all. It is not: docker-compose.prod.yml:401-407 declares `storage:` as a NAMED VOLUME (the file's own header says 'The single bind mount is the storage box' but the volumes block lists storage among pg_data/redis_data/caddy_*), so the host path is /var/lib/docker/volumes/<project>_storage/_data and /srv/libriant/storage exists only inside the containers. restore.sh:30 defaults to the in-container path and restore.sh:145-161 does `mkdir -p "$STORAGE_DIR"` then `tar -C "$STORAGE_DIR" -xzf` and logs `storage restored` — no existence check, no post-untar file-count assertion. backup.sh:50-56 does resolve the real mountpoint via `docker volume inspect` with two fallbacks, and backup.sh:139-147 HARD ABORTS on a missing dir; restore.sh has neither. Confirmed the doc asymmetry that primes the mistake: deployment-hetzner.md:620 'no STORAGE_DIR needed' for backup vs :661 and server-handbook.md:449 which pass STORAGE_DIR for restore. Severity stands — this is a silent total-loss-of-uploads path on the one run that matters.

title: Scheduled jobs report success while every tenant fails — tenantsFailed is discarded by the runner
what: Each multi-tenant sweep catches per-tenant errors, increments a local `failed` counter, emits a `logger.warn`, and then builds its `JobResult` with a message that never mentions failures and a `counts.tenantsFailed` field. The runner (line 92) stores only `{ at, message: result.message, ok: true }` in `lastResults` — `result.counts` is dropped entirely. jobs.types.ts documents counts as something that "get bumped on `libriant_worker_jobs_total{job=...}` later"; that metric does not exist — the worker's /metrics (worker.ts:110-135) exposes only uptime and in-flight gauges.
impact: The one health surface an operator would look at — the worker's /healthz `scheduledLastResults` — actively lies. A tenant whose fine accrual, reservation-pickup expiry, storage cleanup or member notifications throw on every tick shows up as `"ok": true, "message": "3 tenant(s) scanned; no fines to accrue"`. The only trace is a warn line in a rolling Docker log that nothing alerts on (see reliability-04). Fines silently stop accruing, holds silently stop expiring, and the failure is discovered by a librarian, months later, as a data-integrity complaint.
evidence:
RAN. Pointed one tenant's `dbUrl` at an unreachable host and invoked the handlers directly:
```
WARN [FineAccrualSweeper] accrual failed for tenant=reltwo: 
FINE-ACCRUAL RESULT: {"message":"1 tenant(s) scanned; no fines to accrue","counts":{"fines":0,"tenantsScanned":1,"tenantsFailed":1}}
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=reltwo: ...
MEMBER-NOTIFICATIONS RESULT: {"message":"1 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due","counts":{...,"tenantsScanned":1,"tenantsFailed":1}}
```
100% of tenants failed; both messages read as clean successes. Note also that the fine-accrual warn line carried an EMPTY reason (`... for tenant=reltwo: ` with nothing after the colon), so even the log line does not say what went wrong.
fix: In scheduled-jobs.runner.ts store the whole `JobResult` (message + counts) and set `ok: false` when `counts.tenantsFailed > 0`. Append the failure count to every sweep's message (`… ; N tenant(s) FAILED`). Export `libriant_worker_job_last_ok{job=...}` and `libriant_worker_job_tenants_failed{job=...}` from worker.ts /metrics and add a Prometheus rule on them. Log the full error object, not `(err as Error).message`, so an empty-message Prisma init error still says something.
verification: Confirmed by reading the runner and by my own execution of reliability-01. scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:88-99 stores `{ at, message: result.message, ok: true }` — `result.counts` is never read, so tenantsFailed cannot reach lastResults(), which is what /healthz surfaces. My live run of sendMemberNotifications() produced `tenantsFailed: 49` alongside the message '49 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due', so the health surface would show ok:true with that text. Verified the missing metric claim: `grep -rn 'requests_total|http_request|_duration_seconds' apps/api/src` returns nothing, and a live /metrics scrape returned only uptime, build_info, tenants_total, storage_used_bytes, pg_connections(+max), pg_cache_hit_ratio and redis_used_memory_bytes — no per-job gauge exists. One correction to the finding's framing: fine-accrual.job.ts does not touch Redis at all (`grep -rn 'new RedisService()' apps/api/src` -> worker.ts:161, stripe-retry.job.ts:67, member-notifications.job.ts:138 only), so its failure mode is a genuinely independent one (tenant-DB unreachable) rather than a second instance of reliability-01. The masking defect is the same in both. Severity stands: this is the mechanism that hid reliability-01.

title: A backup that never runs, or aborts every night, is undetectable — the dead-man's switch is optional and unset
what: backup.sh aborts (exit 1) on six distinct conditions: control-DB query failure, an off-host tenant, a <1 KiB dump, a failed gzip integrity check on either archive, and a missing storage dir. All of them write to stdout, which the documented cron redirects to `/var/log/libriant/backup.log`. The only active notification is `BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL`, which is (a) optional, (b) pinged only on SUCCESS at the very end, and (c) not written by ensure-env.sh, not present in .env.prod.example, and not mentioned in the cron line in either doc. Nothing installs the crontab either — it exists only as a comment in backup.sh:21 and a snippet in docs/deployment-hetzner.md:646 and docs/server-handbook.md:427.
impact: On a host where the operator forgot the crontab line, or where the cron silently aborts (a relocated tenant, a full disk truncating the gzip, a wrong STORAGE_DIR), there is simply no backup and no signal. Given reliability-04 (nothing alerts at all), the first time anyone learns the backups stopped is when a restore is needed. For a product holding other organisations' catalogues and member records, that is the top-of-list 3am scenario.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn 'BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL' .` matches only scripts/backup.sh:208-209 — no .env.prod.example entry, no ensure-env.sh write, no doc reference. `grep -rn 'crontab' scripts/ .github/` → no matches; the cron is prose only. backup.sh:208 gates the ping on `[ -n "${BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL:-}" ]`, so unset means silence.
fix: Make the heartbeat mandatory in production: have ensure-env.sh provision `BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL` and have backup.sh refuse to run without it (or log a loud WARN and set a non-zero exit) when NODE_ENV/production markers are present. Ping a `/start` endpoint at the top and `/fail` from an `ERR` trap so aborts are reported, not just successes. Ship the crontab as a file (`infra/cron/libriant-backup`) installed by the deploy script rather than a snippet to copy by hand.
verification: Substance confirmed, one piece of the evidence corrected. backup.sh:206-212: the heartbeat is gated on `[ -n "${BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL:-}" ]` and sits in section '6. Success heartbeat' at the very end, after the rclone push — so it fires only on success, never on any of the aborts. CORRECTION: the finding says grep matches only backup.sh; it also matches scripts/secrets.ts:292-304, where BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL IS catalogued — but with `requirement: 'optional'` and `gen: { kind: 'none' }`, so nothing provisions or demands it. Everything else holds: it is absent from .env.prod.example (which has RCLONE_REMOTE= empty at :101 but no heartbeat line), absent from ensure-env.sh, and `grep -rn 'crontab|cron.d' scripts/ .github/` returns a single hit — a comment at backup.sh:20. deploy-on-host.sh checks docker, data dirs, cert and admin email but never that the backup cron exists. Combined with reliability-04 (no alert delivery at all), a backup that never runs is genuinely undetectable. Severity stands — for a product holding other organisations' member records this is the top-of-list 3am scenario.

title: Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned by a mutable tag, and those tags hold the production SSH key, the GHCR push token and the code-signing secrets
where: .github/workflows/deploy.yml:195 (webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0), deploy.yml:91,93,100,112,127 (docker/setup-buildx-action@v4, docker/login-action@v4, docker/build-push-action@v7 x3), verify.yml:23,75,137,229 and desktop-release.yml:110 (pnpm/action-setup@v6)
what: `uses:` references resolve a git ref at run time. `v7`, `v6`, `v4`, and `v0.10.0` are all mutable tags in repositories Libriant does not control; the action owner (or anyone who compromises that account or repo) can repoint them at any commit and the next workflow run executes it. There is not one `@<40-hex-sha>` pin in the repository (`grep -rn '@sha256:\|uses: .*@[0-9a-f]\{40\}' .github/` returns nothing). The blast radius is not uniform: `webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0` is handed `secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` — the key that opens a root-equivalent shell on every production host — and the docker/* actions run in a job with `permissions: packages: write` and the GHCR credential the fleet pulls images from.
impact: A single upstream tag repoint (the tj-actions/changed-files pattern, March 2025) yields either the production SSH private key or the ability to push a poisoned `libriant-api:latest` to GHCR that every host pulls on the next deploy. That is total compromise of customer library data, with no signal in the repo.
evidence: READ .github/workflows/deploy.yml:195 `uses: webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0` with `ssh-private-key: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}` at :197. RAN `grep -n "uses:" .github/workflows/*.yml` — 27 occurrences, every external one a tag, zero SHAs. Commit fe0931e ("every GitHub Action to its latest major", 2026-08-22) moved checkout v4->v7, setup-node v4->v7, action-setup v4->v6, build-push v5->v7, login v3->v4, buildx v3->v4, ssh-agent v0.9->v0.10 — i.e. the update pass re-pinned to tags rather than SHAs.
fix: Pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment, e.g. `uses: webfactory/ssh-agent@a6f90b1f127823b31d4d4a8d96047790581349bd # v0.9.0`. Do this at minimum for webfactory/ssh-agent and the three docker/* actions before deploy.yml is ever dispatched. Add a Dependabot `github-actions` ecosystem entry so SHA bumps arrive as reviewable PRs.
verification: Tried to refute on three axes; all three failed. (a) RAN `grep -rn 'uses:' .github/workflows/` — 27 hits, every external one a floating tag, zero 40-hex SHAs; `grep -rn '@sha256:' .github/` returns nothing. deploy.yml:195-197 does hand `secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` to `webfactory/ssh-agent@v0.10.0`. (b) Looked for a compensating guard: none exists — no .github/dependabot.yml, no CODEOWNERS, no allowlist of actions. Host-key pinning (deploy.yml:199-221) constrains WHERE the deploy connects, not what code runs on the runner holding the key. (c) The one genuine mitigation the finding omits: deploy.yml:25-31 is `workflow_dispatch` ONLY (the push trigger was deliberately removed 2026-08-22), so the ssh-agent action executes only on a deliberate operator dispatch, not on every push. That narrows the window but not the blast radius, and the first dispatch against 195.201.13.95 is imminent. ONE CORRECTION to the finding's wording: the GHCR credential at deploy.yml:97 is `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` — an ephemeral, job-scoped token, not the long-lived credential the fleet pulls with. The push-a-poisoned-`:latest` path is still real (the job carries `permissions: packages: write`, deploy.yml:37-39), but 'the GHCR credential the fleet pulls images from' overstates it. Severity unchanged: root-equivalent SSH key handed to a mutable third-party tag is the tj-actions scenario verbatim.

title: GET /admin/tenants/:id returns every tenant's plaintext Postgres superuser URL to any authenticated platform admin, including the support tier
what: The `@Get(':id')` handler carries no `@AdminRoles(...)` decorator. AdminRolesGuard short-circuits with `if (!required || required.length === 0) return true;` (admin-roles.guard.ts:36), so the route is reachable by any admin session, and the selected columns include `dbUrl` — the full connection string with the plaintext Postgres password (see tenant-isolation-02). The class docstring at :29-36 asserts the opposite: "Read endpoints are metadata only — admin must redeem a support key (Step 18a) to see a tenant's actual library data." Retrieving the credential creates no SupportSession and no SupportActionLog row, so the consented-impersonation control is bypassed with no trace.
impact: A support-tier Libriant staff account — the lowest platform privilege, and the one intended to require a library-issued support key before seeing any patron data — can read and write every library's members, loans, fines and photos directly in Postgres, unlogged and unconsented. Independently of the role question, the credential is emitted in a plain HTTP response body, so it reaches browser memory, any response logging, and any XSS on the admin origin.
evidence:
RAN (throwaway spec apps/api/test/integration/zzz-verify-tenantiso.spec.ts against the live audit env, since deleted). Created an AdminUser with role='support', logged in at POST /admin/auth/login (Host: admin.localhost):
  V-F01 support login status = 200
  V-F01 GET /admin/tenants/:id status = 200
  V-F01 keys = ["id","slug","name","defaultLocale","status","primaryEmail","customSubdomain","cellId","dbUrl","storageUrl","createdAt","updatedAt","subscription","billingAccount"]
  V-F01 dbUrl = postgresql://libriant:auditpw@127.0.0.1:55440/tenant_cmt5n4wv7ed6d7f79e762aa19ae
  V-F01 supportSessions for A = 0
READ admin-roles.guard.ts:36 and admin-tenants.controller.ts:113-143.
verification: Reproduced end to end; the mechanism is exactly as claimed. Two corrections to the original entry. (a) EVIDENCE ERROR: the original claimed "/admin/tenants status=200 n=23; dbUrl exposed for 5/5 sampled tenants". The LIST endpoint does not select dbUrl — I re-ran it as the same support admin and got keys ["id","slug","name","defaultLocale","status","primaryEmail","createdAt","cellId","plan","billingStatus","billingMode"] (admin-tenants.controller.ts:74-91). Only the detail route leaks. (b) SEVERITY: downgraded blocker→high. The precondition is a platform admin session, and at launch there is one admin — scripts/bootstrap-admin.ts:73 creates a single account, and no endpoint creates further admins (grep `adminUser.create` finds only that script and three test files). That operator already holds PG_SUPERUSER_URL, so on Monday nobody new gains anything. ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED also defaults to true outside development (env.ts:311) and admin-auth.guard.ts:65 forces enrollment, so the session is not password-only in production. It is a real, one-line-fixable privilege-boundary and audit-trail defect that must land before a second (support) admin ever exists — but it cannot cause the stated harm this week.
fix: Drop `dbUrl` and `storageUrl` from the `@Get(':id')` select (nothing renders them — apps/web/app/[locale]/admin/(authed)/tenants/[id]/page.tsx:24 declares dbUrl in its type and never displays it), and add `@AdminRoles('owner')` to the handler.

title: Logout clears the cookie but does not revoke the JWT; the only revocation path is a password reset, and there is no "sign out everywhere"
what: `POST /auth/logout` only calls `cookies.clearSession(res)`. It does not bump `users.sessionsValidAfter`, does not touch Redis, and the JWT carries no `jti` — there is no server-side session record of any kind. The only revocation primitive in the system is the account-wide `sessionsValidAfter` epoch, which is written solely by a password reset, an admin-forced reset, `completeSetup` with a new password, and deactivation. Consequently a session token that was captured before logout stays valid for its full TTL: 7 days by default, 30 days for a "remember me" login (`SESSION_REMEMBER_TTL_SEC` default 30d, env.ts:292), and sliding re-issue on every GET past half-life (session.middleware.ts:52-70) keeps refreshing it up to the 90-day absolute cap. There is no "sign out of all devices" endpoint and no session list.
impact: On the exact machines this product targets — the shared circulation desk that cookie.service.ts:22-27 explicitly designs for — clicking "Sign out" gives the user a false guarantee. Anyone who captured the cookie (shared browser profile, XSS-free but disk-resident cookie jar, backup, stolen laptop, malware) retains full library access for weeks, and the librarian has no action available that stops it short of performing a password reset they have no reason to think they need. A signup issues `remember: true` unconditionally (signup.service.ts:230), so owners are always on the 30-day token.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P1): `POST /auth/logout` with the owner cookie returned 204; re-presenting the same cookie to `GET /auth/me` returned **200** with the full user + tenant payload. Probe output: `P1 /auth/me after logout -> 200`.
fix: Give the token a `jti` and, on logout, write a Redis denylist entry `session:revoked:<jti>` with a TTL equal to the token's remaining lifetime, checked in AuthGuard and TenantGuard alongside the existing `sessionsValidAfter` check. Add `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all` that bumps `sessionsValidAfter` and calls `AuthGuard.invalidateAuthCache`, and surface it in the UI as "Sign out everywhere".
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED by execution: `POST /auth/logout` with a live owner cookie returned 204 and re-presenting the same cookie to `GET /auth/me` returned 200 (probe line `V02 me-before= 200 logout= 204 me-after= 200`). READ auth.controller.ts:198-202 — the handler body is only `this.cookies.clearSession(res)`; jwt-session.service.ts has no `jti`. BUT the title's second clause — 'there is no way to terminate a session at all' — is FALSE and is why the severity is cut. READ auth.guard.ts:24-31 and tenant.guard.ts:86-89: every request, cache hit or miss, rejects a token whose session start predates `users.sessionsValidAfter`; that column IS written by password reset (password-reset.service.ts), admin-forced reset (staff.service.ts:128, verified live — `resetPassword` sets `sessionsValidAfter: new Date()`), `completeSetup` with a password, and deactivation. So a working revocation path exists and is enforced on both guards; what is missing is logout being one of them, plus a self-service 'sign out everywhere'. Exploitation also requires the attacker to already hold the cookie (HttpOnly, Secure in prod, SameSite=Lax), and for a non-`remember` login the cookie is a browser-session cookie (cookie.service.ts:34) that dies on browser close — verified in the live Set-Cookie: the staff login carried no `Expires`, only the signup owner cookie did. Real defect, false-reassurance UX, but not a high: high→medium.

title: Disabling a Libriant admin does not end their live impersonation session — they keep full write access to a customer's library
what: ImpersonationMiddleware validates the `supportSession` row (endedAt, expiresAt, tenantId, adminId) but never reads `adminUser` — it does not check `status`, `disabledAt`, or `sessionsValidAfter`. TenantGuard then short-circuits to `return true` on `req.impersonation` before any account check, and RolesGuard returns true unconditionally for impersonation. The admin session cookie is a separate credential with its own 1-hour TTL; the impersonation cookie is signed with `IMPERSONATION_SECRET` and lives for `SUPPORT_SESSION_TTL_SEC` (default 4 hours). So the only thing that ends impersonation is the support-session row itself, which nothing updates when an admin is offboarded. AdminAuthGuard's careful `disabledAt`/`status`/`sessionsValidAfter` re-read on every `/admin/*` request has no counterpart on the impersonation path.
impact: Offboarding a support engineer — the moment when revocation matters most — leaves them with up to four hours of unrestricted read and write access to a live customer library: member PII, loans, catalogue, staff credentials. The library's own "end support access" control still works, but the library has no reason to use it and no signal that the admin was terminated. Same hole applies to a compromised admin account: locking or deleting the adminUser row does nothing to an already-open session.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P7): opened a supportSession for an active admin, minted the impersonation cookie, confirmed `GET /t/<slug>/members` → 200. Then set the adminUser to `status:'disabled', disabledAt: now`. With the same cookie: `GET /t/<slug>/members` → **200**, and `POST /t/<slug>/members` (a write) → **201**. Probe output lines P7.
fix: In ImpersonationMiddleware, join the adminUser in the same query (`supportSession.findUnique({ include: { admin: { select: { status, disabledAt, sessionsValidAfter } } } })`) and refuse to attach `req.impersonation` when the admin is not active or the JWT `iat` predates `sessionsValidAfter`. Additionally, have the admin disable/lock path call `SupportSessionService.end(..., 'admin_ended')` for every open session held by that admin.
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED by execution. READ impersonation.middleware.ts:49-63 — the `supportSession.findUnique` selects only `id, endedAt, expiresAt, tenantId, adminId`; the `adminUser` row is never read. RAN: opened a supportSession row for an ACTIVE support-tier admin, minted the impersonation cookie with `IMPERSONATION_SECRET`, confirmed `GET /t/<slug>/members` → 200; then set the adminUser to `status:'disabled', disabledAt: now()`. With the SAME cookie: `GET /t/<slug>/members` → **200** and `POST /t/<slug>/members` (a real write, valid CreateMemberDto) → **201**. So the revocation asymmetry against AdminAuthGuard is real and gives live write access to customer data. Severity cut because the harm is doubly conditional in a way the original write-up glossed: it requires (a) the tenant to have consented and an impersonation session to be OPEN at the exact moment of the disable, and (b) the blast radius is capped at the remaining `SUPPORT_SESSION_TTL_SEC` (4h default), during which the LIBRARY still holds a working kill switch (`DELETE /t/:slug/support/sessions/active`, library-support.controller.ts:108) and the platform can end the row directly. A revocation gap bounded to ≤4h behind a consent gate is a medium, not a high: high→medium.

title: Three mutating tenant surfaces carry no role guard — the read-only `volunteer` role can upload and delete member photos, book covers and arbitrary files
what: `roles.decorator.ts:31-38` defines the policy explicitly: `StaffWrite()` is "the role set allowed to CREATE/EDIT/ARCHIVE core library data … Excludes `volunteer` — a deliberately limited role that may READ everything but must not mutate. Apply to every mutating handler." Three controllers with mutating handlers are annotated `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` only, with no RolesGuard and no `@Roles`/`@StaffWrite`: MemberPhotosController (`POST` and `DELETE /t/:slug/members/:id/photo`), CoversController (`POST` and `DELETE /t/:slug/catalog/books/:id/cover`), and StorageDemoController's `POST /t/:slug/storage/:resourceType` (arbitrary upload, up to `STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, default 25 MB). Note the same file gets it right for `DELETE .../storage/:resourceType/:filename` and `POST .../storage-admin/recompute`, which do carry `@Roles('owner','admin')` — so the omission is an oversight, not a decision. The delete paths call `storage.delete(...)`, which removes the underlying file, not just the reference.
impact: Any volunteer account — the role a library hands to a helper it does not fully trust — can permanently destroy every member photograph and every book cover in the library (irreversibly; the files are deleted, not soft-deleted), replace a member's photo with arbitrary content, and burn the tenant's storage quota with 25 MB uploads. Member photographs are personal data of library members, many of them minors in a school-library deployment; their deletion or substitution by a limited-rights account is both a data-integrity and a GDPR-accountability failure.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P3): created a `volunteer` staff account. Control: `POST /t/<slug>/members` (a `@StaffWrite()` route) → **403**, confirming the role is correctly limited elsewhere. Same volunteer cookie: `POST /t/<slug>/members/<id>/photo` → **201** `{"photoAssetRef":"members/…png"}`; `DELETE /t/<slug>/members/<id>/photo` → **200**. Probe output lines P3.
fix: Add `RolesGuard` and `@StaffWrite()` to the `@Post`/`@Delete` handlers in members/photos.controller.ts and catalog/covers.controller.ts, and to `POST /t/:slug/storage/:resourceType` in storage-demo.controller.ts. Then add a lint/CI check that fails any `@Post|@Put|@Patch|@Delete` handler on a `t/:slug/*` controller which resolves to no `@Roles`/`@StaffWrite` metadata — the enumeration above shows spot-checking is what let three slip through.
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED by execution. READ members/photos.controller.ts:29-30, catalog/covers.controller.ts:10-11 and storage/storage-demo.controller.ts:21-22 — all three mutating handlers carry `@UseGuards(TenantGuard)` with no RolesGuard, while storage-demo.controller.ts:66-68 gets it right for `DELETE …/storage/:resourceType/:filename` (`@Roles('owner','admin')`), so it is an omission, not a policy. RAN with a real `volunteer` staff cookie: control `POST /t/<slug>/members` → **403** (the role IS correctly limited on `@StaffWrite()` routes); same cookie `POST /t/<slug>/members/<id>/photo` → **201** `{photoAssetRef:'members/…png'}`, `DELETE /t/<slug>/members/<id>/photo` → **200**, `POST /t/<slug>/storage/covers` → **201**. Severity cut because the impact does not carry a high: the actor is an authenticated staff account the library itself provisioned, there is NO confidentiality gain (volunteers already read every member and catalogue record by design — reads carry no `@Roles`), no cross-tenant reach, and the harm is integrity/availability against display assets recoverable from the nightly backup. A documented intra-tenant role-boundary violation by a provisioned insider is a medium: high→medium. The fix remains exactly as written and is three decorators.

title: The forced first-login credential change is bypassable with an empty request body, leaving the admin-known temporary password valid forever
what: `CompleteSetupDto` makes both `fullName` and `newPassword` optional, and `LoginService.completeSetup` sets `mustChangeCredentials: false` unconditionally — the flag is cleared whether or not a password was supplied (`const data = { mustChangeCredentials: false }`, then `if (input.newPassword) { … }`). `POST /auth/complete-setup` requires only a live session, which the staff member already has from signing in with the temp password. So a single `POST /auth/complete-setup {}` clears the gate. The docstring calls this deliberate ("Either field may be omitted (\"keep the same\")"), but the effect is that the credential the creating admin generated, saw in plaintext (`staff.service.ts` returns `tempPassword`), and typed into a chat message is the account's permanent password, and `sessionsValidAfter` is never bumped, so nothing about the account changes.
impact: Every admin-created staff account can end up permanently authenticated by a 12-character password that at least one other person knows verbatim and that was very likely transmitted over WhatsApp/email. The library believes the forced-change screen guaranteed otherwise — the UI shows the prompt once and never again. An admin who is later demoted or leaves retains working credentials for every staff account they ever created.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P2): created a librarian, signed in with the temp password (`mustChangeCredentials: true` in the login response), then `POST /auth/complete-setup` with body `{}` → **200 {"ok":true}`. DB afterwards: `mustChangeCredentials = false`, `sessionsValidAfter = null`. Signing in again with the **original** temp password → **200**. Probe output lines P2.
fix: Make `newPassword` required in `CompleteSetupDto` when the user's `mustChangeCredentials` is true (or simply require it always on this endpoint — it exists only for the forced-change flow), and only clear the flag in the branch that actually wrote a new hash. Keep bumping `sessionsValidAfter` there, as the code already does.
verification: CONFIRMED by execution, and the DTO/service reading is exact. READ login.dto.ts:39-52 — both `fullName` and `newPassword` are `@IsOptional()`; login.service.ts:177-191 — `const data = { mustChangeCredentials: false }` is unconditional and only the `if (input.newPassword)` branch writes a hash and `sessionsValidAfter`. RAN: owner created a librarian (`tempPassword: 'S6VBZ8KSDFZC'` returned in the 201 body), signed in with it (200, `mustChangeCredentials: true`), then `POST /auth/complete-setup` with body `{}` → **200 {ok:true}**; DB afterwards `{"mustChangeCredentials":false,"sessionsValidAfter":null}`; signing in AGAIN with the original temp password → **200**. Checked whether the web client forces a password (which would have made this cosmetic) — the gate is server-side only and the endpoint is directly callable. Medium held: the harm is a shared-over-chat credential becoming permanent, not an immediate compromise.

title: Account email can be changed with no password step-up, no notice to the old address, and no session invalidation
what: `POST /auth/change-email` is behind `AuthGuard` alone. It takes only `{ newEmail }` — no current password, no TOTP, no re-authentication of any kind — and stages a change confirmed by a link sent **only to the new address**. `requestEmailChange` sends nothing to the old address. When the token is redeemed, `verify()` runs `updateMany({ where: { id, tenantId }, data: { email: p.email, emailVerifiedAt: new Date() } })`: it does not check that the account's email is still the one that was current when the change was staged, and it does not bump `sessionsValidAfter`. The account's password is unchanged, so the legitimate owner is not logged out and gets no signal at all.
impact: Chained with authn-authz-02 (a session cookie is never revocable by logout), a stolen or borrowed session on a shared circulation-desk browser converts into permanent account ownership: the attacker points the email at an address they control, confirms it from their own inbox, and then uses `POST /auth/password-reset/request` to obtain a password and lock the real owner out. For a tenant `owner` account that is the whole library — billing, staff, export of all member data. The victim's only notification is the reset email that arrives at an address they no longer control.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P5): `POST /auth/change-email` with the owner's session cookie and body `{"newEmail":"attacker-…@evil.test"}` and no password → **202 {"ok":true}`. READ email-verification.service.ts:197-228 — no credential check, no message to `user.email`; :144-158 — the apply step does not re-validate the prior address nor touch `sessionsValidAfter`.
fix: Require the current password (and TOTP once tenant MFA exists) in `ChangeEmailDto` and verify it in `requestEmailChange`. Send a plain-text security notice to the OLD address at staging time with a revoke link. Record the prior email in the token payload and refuse to apply the change if `user.email` no longer matches. Bump `sessionsValidAfter` when the change lands.
verification: CONFIRMED. RAN: `POST /auth/change-email` with only the owner's session cookie and body `{newEmail:'attacker-…@evil.test'}` → **202 {ok:true}** with no password, no TOTP, no re-auth. READ email-verification.service.ts:197-228 — `requestEmailChange` reads `user.email` only to reject a no-op change and sends exclusively to the NEW address (`send({ email: newEmail, mode: 'change' })`); nothing is sent to the old one. READ :144-152 — the apply step is `updateMany({ where: { id, tenantId }, data: { email: p.email, emailVerifiedAt: now } })`, which (unlike the `signup` branch three lines below it, which DOES pin `email: p.email` in the where-clause) neither re-validates the prior address nor bumps `sessionsValidAfter`. Medium held: the takeover chain is real but every step needs an already-stolen live session.

title: An already-enrolled admin's second factor can be silently replaced with no step-up — a stolen admin cookie is enough
what: `POST /admin/mfa/setup` and `POST /admin/mfa/verify` are behind `AdminAuthGuard` only. Neither checks whether the admin is already enrolled, and neither requires the current password or a code from the currently-registered authenticator. `verify` overwrites `mfaSecretCipher`/`mfaNonce`/`mfaKeyId` and sets `mfaEnabled: true` for whatever secret the caller just enrolled. There is no re-authentication gate anywhere on the admin surface: `AdminSessionService` mints a 1-hour cookie at login and nothing ever asks for credentials again inside that window. The controller docblock also advertises a `POST /admin/mfa/disable` route "exposed for completeness" that does not exist in the file — the documentation and the code disagree about the MFA surface.
impact: MFA is the control that stops a stolen admin password from yielding the control plane (admin-auth.controller.ts:87 — "a password alone must not yield the control plane") and is a hard precondition for redeeming support keys into customer libraries (admin-support.controller.ts:101). An attacker who obtains an admin session cookie for one hour — XSS on the admin origin, an unlocked laptop, a cookie exported from a browser profile — re-points the second factor to their own authenticator and converts a transient session into durable, MFA-blessed control-plane access, including impersonation into any customer library that issues a support key. The real admin discovers it only when their own code stops working.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P6): created an admin, logged in, set `mfaEnabled: true` on the row to simulate an enrolled admin, then called `POST /admin/mfa/setup` with only the session cookie → **200, NEW SECRET ISSUED**. Probe output line P6.
fix: Gate `/admin/mfa/setup` and `/admin/mfa/verify` behind a re-authentication step when `mfaEnabled` is already true: require the current password and a valid code from the existing secret (via `MfaService.verifyTokenOnce`) before issuing or persisting a replacement. Bump `adminUser.sessionsValidAfter` on any MFA change and email the admin. Delete the stale `disable` line from the docblock or implement it with the same step-up.
verification: CONFIRMED by execution. READ mfa.controller.ts:64-107 — `setup` and `verify` sit behind `@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard)` at the class level (line 37) and neither reads `mfaEnabled` nor asks for the current password or a code from the existing authenticator; `verify` overwrites `mfaSecretCipher`/`mfaNonce`/`mfaKeyId` unconditionally. RAN: created an admin, logged in, flipped `mfaEnabled: true` on the row to model an enrolled admin, then `POST /admin/mfa/setup` with only the session cookie → **200 with a fresh secret issued**. Also verified the docblock/route mismatch at mfa.controller.ts:29 — it advertises `POST /admin/mfa/disable`, which does not exist in the file. Medium held rather than raised: obtaining the cookie in the first place requires defeating an MFA-gated login (admin-auth.controller.ts only calls `recordSuccess` after the TOTP check), HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Strict, and a 1-hour TTL.

title: Tenant login lockout exists only in Redis and fails open; the documented database backstop is never written
what: `isLockedOut()` reads a Redis key and `catch { return false }` — a Redis error means not locked. `recordFailure()` wraps the whole lock write in `try/catch {}` — a Redis error means no lock is recorded. `RateLimitService.hit` fails open for every non-`signup:` bucket, and its comment justifies that with "Per-account lockout (LoginService) is the backstop". That backstop does not exist: `users.lockedUntil` is `select`-ed at login.service.ts:102 and never read, and the only writes to it anywhere in the codebase set it to `null` (login.service.ts:134, password-reset.service.ts:140, staff.service.ts:126). Nothing in the tenant auth path ever sets a non-null `lockedUntil`. So a Redis outage removes 100% of brute-force protection from `/auth/login` simultaneously at both layers, and a Redis restart/flush instantly clears every in-flight lock.
impact: During any Redis incident — the same Redis that also backs the rate limiter, the reset tokens and the auth revalidation cache — every library account on the platform is open to unlimited password guessing at bcrypt-cost-12 speed, with no counter anywhere and no log line indicating the protection is off. The failure is silent: the login endpoint keeps returning ordinary 401s. Reading the code, an operator would reasonably believe `users.lockedUntil` still holds the line.
evidence: RAN (integration probe P9): six wrong logins for one account from one IP → Redis lock key present = true, DB row `{"failedLogins":5,"lockedUntil":null,"status":"active"}`. Deleting the two Redis keys (equivalent to a flush/restart) and immediately logging in with the correct password → **200**. READ: `grep -n lockedUntil apps/api/src/auth/*.ts apps/api/src/staff/*.ts` returns only `lockedUntil: true` (a select) and three `lockedUntil: null` writes — no write ever sets a time.
fix: Persist the lockout: in `recordFailure`, atomically increment `failedLogins` and set `lockedUntil` in the same `user.update` once the threshold is reached, and have `login()` check the DB `lockedUntil` in addition to the Redis key. Keep Redis as the fast path. Either delete the false "backstop" claim from rate-limit.service.ts:38-42 or make it true.
verification: CONFIRMED by execution and by exhaustive grep. `grep -rn lockedUntil apps/api/src packages/db-control/prisma` returns exactly eight hits: two `select`s (login.service.ts:102, admin-auth.service.ts:41), one admin read (admin-auth.service.ts:53), ONE non-null write which is admin-only (admin-auth.service.ts:93), three tenant-side writes that all set `lockedUntil: null` (login.service.ts:134, password-reset.service.ts:140, staff.service.ts:126) and the schema columns. No tenant-side code path ever sets a non-null `lockedUntil`, so the 'backstop' rate-limit.service.ts:38-42 names does not exist. READ login.service.ts:197-203 (`catch { return false }`) and :217-231 (whole lock write in `try{}catch{}`). RAN: six wrong logins from one IP → Redis key present, DB row `{"failedLogins":5,"lockedUntil":null}`; a correct-password login from the locked bucket → 401; then deleted the two Redis keys (a flush/restart) and immediately logged in correctly from the SAME previously-locked IP → **200**. Medium held: the exposure is real but gated on a Redis incident, and bcrypt cost 12 caps the guessing rate at the API tier.

title: A subscription whose first payment never succeeded (`incomplete`) is granted the full paid plan for 7 days, repeatably
what: The status map sends Stripe's `incomplete` to our `past_due` (line 567). `incomplete` is the state of a subscription whose INITIAL invoice has not been paid — the customer abandoned 3-D Secure, or the first charge was declined. Because localStatus is past_due, the write on line 630 arms `graceUntil = now + BILLING_GRACE_PERIOD_DAYS` (default 7), and the effective-plan resolver deliberately keeps full feature access for past_due inside its grace window (effective-plan.service.ts:175). The grace window is meant to protect an established payer whose card lapsed; it is applied here to someone who has never paid at all. Nothing prevents the same tenant starting checkout again once the incomplete subscription expires.
impact: A subscription that has never had a settled invoice is granted full paid-tier entitlement while it sits in Stripe's `incomplete` state — in practice up to the ~23 hours before Stripe expires it, not the 7 days the code arms. Lost revenue is small; the real risk is a tenant that bulk-imports against the elevated cap and is left over quota when the window closes.
evidence:
EXECUTED with BILLING_ENABLED forced on through PlatformSettingsService, against the audit control plane:
  BEFORE  plan= starter        max_books= 5000    api_access= false
  row after incomplete: institutional past_due grace= 2026-08-30T09:54:32.915Z
  AFTER   plan= institutional  max_books= 400000  api_access= true
  => paid entitlement granted with ZERO payment for 7.0 days
fix: Map `incomplete` to a status that grants nothing (add an `incomplete` value to SubscriptionStatus, or map it to `canceled`) and arm graceUntil only when transitioning from a previously-paid state. A grace window should require evidence of at least one settled invoice.
verification:
CONFIRMED the mechanism, REFUTED most of the impact. Executed over HTTP against the audit control plane: a signed `customer.subscription.created` with status='incomplete' on the institutional price gave
  B05 -> institutional past_due graceUntil 2026-08-30T10:13:58.748Z
so the 7-day grace window is really armed for a subscription that has never paid. But I then sent the event Stripe actually follows it with:
  B05 after incomplete_expired -> institutional canceled graceUntil null
The mapStatus entry `incomplete_expired: 'canceled'` (billing.service.ts:568) drives localStatus to canceled, and the graceUntil ternary at :627-635 writes null on any non-past_due status, so the window collapses the moment Stripe expires the incomplete subscription — which Stripe does automatically after ~23 hours. On top of that, Stripe Checkout in subscription mode does not create a subscription at all when the customer abandons the card step, so 'anyone who reaches Checkout and abandons gets a week of the top tier, renewably' does not hold; reaching `incomplete` needs a delayed-notification payment method or an API/dashboard-created subscription. Real defect (grace should require a settled invoice), bounded exposure — high -> medium.

title: The stale-replay guard is inert for exactly the events that matter — a replayed mid-cycle plan change silently reverts the plan
what: The STRIPE-RETRY-STALE-REPLAY guard rejects a payload only when `nextPeriodStart < existing.currentPeriodStart` — strictly earlier. A mid-cycle plan change does not move the billing period: Stripe keeps `current_period_start` and prorates. So both the old and the new `customer.subscription.updated` carry the same period start, the guard's condition is false, and whichever event is applied last wins. The retry sweep (jobs/stripe-retry.job.ts:52-60) re-dispatches stored payloads ordered by receivedAt, and Stripe itself does not guarantee delivery order; nothing else compares `event.created` (the webhook envelope's timestamp is not persisted or consulted anywhere).
impact: A library upgrades to Municipal, an older Community event is redelivered or swept, and their plan quietly reverts to Community while Stripe bills Municipal. The reverse is equally possible after a downgrade. The event is logged as processed with no error, so the only symptom is a librarian hitting a 402 on a plan they paid to leave.
evidence:
EXECUTED. Same subscription id, same current_period_start throughout:
  after annual community sub_A               plan=community  status=active  stripeSub=sub_A
  after upgrade to municipal (same period)   plan=municipal   status=active  stripeSub=sub_A
  after stale replay of the community event  plan=community   status=active  stripeSub=sub_A
No 'ignoring stale subscription event' warning was emitted — the guard did not fire.
fix: Persist the event envelope's `created` timestamp (and/or Stripe's `Subscription.metadata`-free monotonic proxy) on the subscriptions row and reject any event older than the last one applied for the same subscription id, instead of comparing period starts.
verification:
CONFIRMED the mechanism by re-executing it, then narrowed the reachability. Over HTTP, three signed events on the same subscription id with an identical current_period_start:
  B06 after community: community
  B06 after municipal : municipal
  B06 after stale replay of community: community
The guard at :600-612 never fired — its predicate needs nextPeriodStart STRICTLY earlier than the persisted one, and a mid-cycle plan change does not move the period. So last-write-wins is real. Downgraded because the finding's headline replay path is largely blocked by two guards it does not credit: the controller's Redis SETNX dedupe key (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:90-99) holds for 30 days per event id, and the sweep only selects rows with `processedAt: null` (stripe-retry.job.ts:52-55). An already-applied event therefore cannot simply be replayed. Two live paths survive: Stripe does not guarantee delivery order between two subscription.updated events, and an event whose first dispatch errored is re-dispatched by the sweep later, after a newer one has already been applied. Both are plausible; neither is routine. high -> medium.

title: A webhook payload with a null `customer` rewrites an arbitrary tenant's subscription (Prisma turns null into IS NULL)
what: `controlDb.billingAccount.findFirst({ where: { stripeCustomerId: payload.customer } })` is called with no validation that `payload.customer` is a non-empty string. Prisma renders a null filter value as `stripeCustomerId IS NULL`, which matches every tenant that has never been through Checkout — i.e. essentially the entire tenant base, since signup creates a billing_accounts row with a null customer id. findFirst then returns whichever row the planner emits first and the handler rewrites that tenant's plan, billingMode and stripeSubscriptionId. handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted (line 652) has the identical lookup, and its own stale-delete guard passes trivially for a victim whose stripeSubscriptionId is null, so a null-customer delete downgrades an arbitrary tenant to starter/canceled.
impact: Given the ability to forge a webhook (billing-02), an attacker needs no identifier at all — a null customer picks a victim for them, and handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted's stale-delete guard (:658-666) passes trivially for any tenant with a null stripeSubscriptionId, so the same trick downgrades an arbitrary library to starter/canceled. Without billing-02 it is a robustness hole with no known trigger.
evidence:
EXECUTED. `findFirst({where:{stripeCustomerId:null}})` returned tenant cmt5mhy41dd101750da0616e3d7 (owner@aud-072bfa.test), an unrelated library. Feeding syncStripeSubscription a payload with `customer: null`:
  victim before: starter active
  victim after : institutional active sub_nullcustomer
fix: Guard at the top of syncStripeSubscription, handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted and tenantForSubscriptionInvoice: `if (typeof payload.customer !== 'string' || !payload.customer) { log; return; }`. Prefer resolving the tenant from `client_reference_id` (already set on every Checkout session, stripe-real.driver.ts:74) with the customer id as a fallback.
verification:
CONFIRMED the mechanism twice, DOWNGRADED because it is not independently reachable. (1) Prisma probe against the audit control plane: 46 billing_accounts rows, 44 with a NULL stripeCustomerId (signup.service.ts:195 creates every one of them that way), and `findFirst({where:{stripeCustomerId: null}})` returned cmt5mhy41dd101750da0616e3d7 — an unrelated tenant. (2) Over HTTP, a signed event with `customer: null`:
  B07 victim before: institutional active
  B07 POST status: 200
  B07 victim after : institutional active sub_nullcustomer
— the write landed on a tenant the payload never named. But every route into this code requires a payload that passes verifyWebhookSignature, and Stripe never emits a subscription event with a null customer, so the only actor who can trigger it is one who can already forge webhooks (billing-02) or who holds the real whsec. The sweep cannot manufacture it either: it re-dispatches stored Stripe payloads, which always carry a customer. This is a billing-02 amplifier and a missing input guard, not an independent high.

title: ensureStripeCustomer races itself — a duplicate Stripe customer means the library is charged while staying on the free plan
what: Read-then-create with a network call in between and no lock, no transaction and no Stripe Idempotency-Key: findUnique (line 747) → stripe.customers.create (line 754) → update/create (lines 761-777). Two concurrent requests — a double-clicked Subscribe button, or the chooser and the billing page in two tabs — both see no customer, both create one, and the second write wins. The user completes Checkout against whichever customer their session used; if that is the loser, every subsequent webhook for it fails the `findFirst({stripeCustomerId})` lookup at line 534 and returns after logging 'Webhook: no BillingAccount for customer …'. `client_reference_id` carries the tenantId on every session (stripe-real.driver.ts:74) and would resolve this, but nothing reads it — the controller treats checkout.session.completed as a deliberate no-op (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:144-147).
impact: The library's card is charged every month by a live Stripe subscription that our database has never heard of. They stay on the free plan, hit Starter quotas, and see 'no active paid subscription to cancel' if they try to stop it. Recovery requires someone to notice a warn-level log line and repair the customer id by hand. There is no reconciliation job that would ever catch it.
evidence: READ, billing.service.ts:746-780 — no transaction, no unique constraint on the create path, no idempotency key on any Stripe write in stripe-real.driver.ts (`grep -n idempotency apps/api/src` returns nothing).
fix: Pass a stable Stripe Idempotency-Key (`customer:<tenantId>`) to customers.create, and make the local write an upsert inside a transaction so a losing racer adopts the winner's id. Additionally, handle checkout.session.completed by reconciling `client_reference_id` → `customer`, which repairs the mismatch even when it happens.
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED, framing corrected, severity reduced. billing.service.ts:746-777 is read-then-create with an unguarded network call in between: no transaction, no advisory lock, and `grep -rn -i 'idempotency' apps/api/src` shows keys on loans, email and the interceptor but NOTHING in either Stripe driver. One correction to the finding: the `create` branch at :766 is effectively dead, because signup.service.ts:195 already inserts a billing_accounts row for every tenant, so both racers take the `update` branch at :761 and the second simply overwrites the first — there is no unique-constraint error to make the race visible. Downgraded to medium: the mechanism is real and the consequence is severe, but it needs two genuinely concurrent checkout starts for the same tenant, and PlanGrid disables its own button while busy (PlanGrid.tsx:106, 243), leaving the two-tab case as the realistic trigger.

title: Nothing reconciles the local price catalogue with Stripe, and the go-live verification step passes on the seeded placeholders
what: PATCH /admin/plans/:slug writes stripePriceId and stripeAnnualPriceId as bare optional strings (UpdatePlanDto lines 34-49). There is no format check (`price_` prefix), no rejection of the `price_seed_*` placeholders, no call to Stripe to confirm the Price exists, no check that its currency and unit_amount match the plan's `currency`/`monthlyPriceCents`/`annualPriceCents`, no check that the Price's recurring interval matches the column it is being stored in, and no guard against putting the SAME id in both columns. Separately, `hasStripePrice`/`hasStripeAnnualPrice` are computed as `!!p.stripePriceId` (billing.service.ts:116-117), and the seed ships non-null placeholders for every paid plan — so the verification command docs/billing-go-live.md ends with, which asks the operator to confirm `hasStripeAnnualPrice: true`, returns true on a completely unconfigured database.
impact: The document's single mechanical safeguard is vacuous: it reports success on the seed data it was written to catch. A monthly id pasted into the annual column bills €39/month to a library that clicked '390 € a year'; a bad id 500s at Checkout; a mismatched amount means the advertised price and the charged price differ with nothing to detect it. All of these survive every check the product performs.
evidence:
EXECUTED. Fresh seeded control plane:
  starter|stripe|0|(null)|price_seed_starter|(null)|EUR
  community|stripe|3900|39000|price_seed_community|price_seed_community_annual|EUR
  … all five paid plans carry non-null placeholders, so hasStripePrice and hasStripeAnnualPrice are both true for every one of them.
Also EXECUTED: `UPDATE plans SET "stripePriceId"='price_dup', "stripeAnnualPriceId"='price_dup' WHERE slug='community'` → UPDATE 1, both unique indexes satisfied, no error.
fix: In the PATCH handler, call `stripe.prices.retrieve(id)` and reject unless it is active, its currency equals plan.currency, its unit_amount equals the matching *PriceCents, and its recurring.interval matches the column. Reject any id equal to another column's on the same plan and any id matching /^price_seed_/. Change hasStripePrice to mean 'verified against Stripe' rather than 'non-null', so the go-live check has something to fail on.
verification: Both halves CONFIRMED by execution, severity reduced for a guard the finding overlooks. Against the audit control plane: all five paid plans carry price_seed_* placeholders (starter/price_seed_starter, community/price_seed_community + _annual, and so on), so hasStripePrice and hasStripeAnnualPrice — computed as `!!p.stripePriceId` at billing.service.ts:116-117 — are true on a completely unconfigured database, and the doc's Verify step passes on seed data. Also executed `UPDATE plans SET "stripePriceId"='price_dup_x', "stripeAnnualPriceId"='price_dup_x' WHERE slug='community'` -> ACCEPTED, both unique indexes satisfied. Read UpdatePlanDto and confirmed no format check and no Stripe round-trip. Downgraded high -> medium because docs/billing-go-live.md does carry a compensating manual check the finding does not credit: its closing instruction is to 'Take one plan all the way through Stripe test mode and confirm the amount on the Checkout page matches the card that sent you there', which catches exactly the swapped-column and wrong-amount cases. The defect is that nothing in the software enforces it.

title: The billing page's downgrade-to-free button sends the library to Stripe Checkout, and Starter's placeholder price can never be removed
what: PlanGrid's button chain is isCurrent → isManual → !hasStripePrice → upgrade(). It has no free-plan branch: unlike ChoosePlanScreen (ChoosePlanScreen.tsx:55-59, which routes monthlyPriceCents===0 to POST /billing/select), PlanGrid calls POST /billing/checkout for Starter too. Server-side, startCheckout only rejects a missing priceId (billing.service.ts:276) — and Starter's is not missing, because the CHECK constraint `plans_stripe_price_matches_mode` (migrations/20260822140000_repricing/migration.sql:35-41) requires every billingMode='stripe' plan to carry a non-null stripePriceId, and the seed makes Starter stripe-billed with `price_seed_starter`. docs/billing-go-live.md line 'Starter is free and gets no Price' plus 'every one of them must be replaced' is therefore not executable.
impact: One button on the billing page is broken: 'Switch to Starter' posts to /billing/checkout with price_seed_starter, which Stripe rejects, so the librarian gets a 500 on a plausible action. The supported route back to free — Cancel, then the subscription.deleted webhook — still works. Secondary: the free plan permanently carries a fabricated Stripe price id that no audit of the plans table can distinguish from a real one, which is what makes billing-10's check vacuous for Starter.
evidence: EXECUTED: `UPDATE plans SET "stripePriceId"=NULL WHERE slug='starter';` → ERROR: new row for relation "plans" violates check constraint "plans_stripe_price_matches_mode". READ: PlanGrid.tsx:236-249 has no `isFree` branch in the action chain, while ChoosePlanScreen.tsx:55-59 does.
fix: Give PlanGrid the same free-plan branch as ChoosePlanScreen (POST /billing/select), and have selectPlan cancel any live Stripe subscription first. Reject planSlug values whose monthlyPriceCents is 0 in startCheckout. Relax the CHECK to allow a stripe-billed plan with monthlyPriceCents=0 to hold a null price id, so Starter can be honest about having none.
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED, impact REFUTED in part. Executed `UPDATE plans SET "stripePriceId"=NULL WHERE slug='starter'` -> ERROR 23514, violates plans_stripe_price_matches_mode (migrations/20260822140000_repricing/migration.sql:35-41), so Starter is structurally forced to carry a fake price id — confirmed. Read PlanGrid.tsx:224-250 and confirmed the action chain is isCurrent -> isManual -> !hasStripePrice -> upgrade(), with no free-plan branch, while ChoosePlanScreen.tsx:55-59 does route monthlyPriceCents===0 to /billing/select; Starter is isPublic=true so it renders in the grid with a live 'Switch to Starter' button. But the finding's central impact claim — 'There is no working way to move from a paid plan back to the free tier' — is FALSE. billing/page.tsx:127-135 renders BillingActions for every stripe-mode tenant, which offers cancel-at-period-end; the resulting customer.subscription.deleted is handled at billing.service.ts:645-695 and downgrades the tenant to starter. The real defect is one dead button, not a dead-end. high -> medium.

title: Admin 'set plan' onto the manual plan leaves the Stripe subscription live and simultaneously removes the tenant's ability to cancel it
what: applyAdminPlanChange writes planId, billingMode (taken from the target plan) and status='active', and deliberately leaves stripeSubscriptionId untouched — the comment on lines 417-418 says Stripe remains the source of truth for that subscription's lifecycle, but no code ever cancels it. Once billingMode is 'manual', cancelAtPeriodEnd throws 'Your library is billed manually' (line 363) and openCustomerPortal throws 'there is no self-serve portal to open' (line 329), and the web UI hides BillingActions entirely for manual mode (billing/page.tsx:120-129).
impact: Moving a paying library onto a contract or on-prem arrangement — the normal reason an operator touches this endpoint — leaves the card being charged every month with the self-serve stop button removed from the product. The only remedy is someone remembering to cancel it in the Stripe dashboard by hand; nothing in the app, the audit log or the doc prompts them to.
evidence: READ, billing.service.ts:410-419 versus 359-367 and 322-331. There is no call to cancelSubscriptionAtPeriodEnd on the admin path, and the StripeDriver interface offers no other way to stop a subscription.
fix: When applyAdminPlanChange moves a tenant with a live stripeSubscriptionId onto a manual plan, cancel that subscription through the driver (immediately or at period end, as a parameter) and null the id; refuse the change if the cancel call fails, so it cannot half-apply.
verification: CONFIRMED by reading all three sites together and looking for the missing cancel. applyAdminPlanChange (:395-425) writes planId, billingMode from the target plan and status='active', and its own comment at :417-418 says stripeSubscriptionId is left alone; there is no call to cancelSubscriptionAtPeriodEnd on that path and the driver interface offers no other stop (stripe-driver.ts:93-110). Verified the two exits then close: cancelAtPeriodEnd throws for billingMode!=='stripe' (:361-365) and openCustomerPortal likewise (:327-331); billing/page.tsx:118-135 renders a static notice instead of BillingActions when billingMode is 'manual'. Downgraded to medium: the trigger is a deliberate operator action on an admin-only endpoint that is written to the admin audit log (recordAdminAudit at :427), and the money is recoverable from the Stripe dashboard in one click. It is a sharp footgun, not an autonomous failure.

title: `stripeReady` is computed for the admin UI and no UI ever reads it — the only signal that production is running the fake driver is a log line
what: subscriptionsStatus() returns `stripeReady` with the comment 'the admin UI can warn that checkout won't really charge', and setBillingEnabled logs a warning in the same situation (lines 60-66). Neither reaches a human: `grep -rn stripeReady apps/web` returns nothing, and SubscriptionsToggle.tsx renders only billingEnabled, source and awaitingChoice (its warning banner at line 102 is about the plan chooser). Nothing refuses the flip.
impact: An operator who enables subscriptions from the admin panel — which docs/billing-go-live.md explicitly instructs them to do, and which requires no .env change — while STRIPE_DRIVER is still fake sees a completely normal screen. Libraries then click Subscribe, are redirected to their own billing page with `?checkout=success` appended by the fake driver (stripe-fake.driver.ts:54), and are never charged. Revenue is zero and the UI says everything worked.
evidence: EXECUTED: `grep -rn 'stripeReady' apps/web apps/api/src` returns four hits, all inside platform-settings.service.ts. READ: SubscriptionsToggle.tsx:95-105.
fix: Render stripeReady as a blocking banner on the Subscriptions page and disable the enable-toggle while it is false, or make setBillingEnabled throw outside development when the driver is not real (see billing-02).
verification: EXECUTED the grep myself: `grep -rn 'stripeReady' apps/web apps/api/src` returns four hits, all inside platform-settings.service.ts (lines 58, 71, 86, 102) — no consumer anywhere in apps/web. Read setBillingEnabled (:60-66): it logs at warn level and returns `enabled`; nothing throws, nothing blocks. Severity left at medium rather than raised, because the operator-visible consequence (checkout that does not charge) is loud on the first real attempt, and because the deeper defect is billing-02.

title: Default tenant connection budget is 2.5x Postgres max_connections — the pool config and the DB config in the same repo contradict each other
what: TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE defaults to 50 (env.ts:288) and is not set in compose. Each cached tenant client is built by makeTenantPrismaClient with no maxPoolSize override (apps/api/src/tenancy/tenant-prisma.service.ts:72), so it falls back to DEFAULT_TENANT_POOL_MAX = 5 (TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX is never set in compose either). That is 50 x 5 = 250 direct Postgres backends per process, and both `api` and `worker` run this code — up to 500. Tenant URLs are built by swapping the DB name on PG_SUPERUSER_URL (tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-108), i.e. `postgres:5432` DIRECTLY, bypassing pgbouncer entirely; only the control plane goes through the pooler. Meanwhile the Postgres service is started with `-c max_connections=200`.
impact: At sustained concurrency across roughly 35+ simultaneously-busy tenant databases (api + worker combined) new tenant pool connections get 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already' on the SHARED Postgres, so the control plane and every other library fail at the same moment, not just the tenant that tripped it. Not reachable at the five-library launch scale; it arrives silently as the customer count and per-library concurrency grow, and nothing asserts the budget anywhere.
evidence: READ. env.ts:288 `tenantClientCacheSize: num('TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE', 50, ...)`; packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:21 `const DEFAULT_TENANT_POOL_MAX = 5;`; tenant-prisma.service.ts:38 `max: env.tenantClientCacheSize`, :72 `makeTenantPrismaClient({ databaseUrl: ctx.dbUrl })` with no maxPoolSize; docker-compose.prod.yml:320-325 `command: [postgres, -c, shared_preload_libraries=..., -c, max_connections=200]`. Cross-check of every process.env read in apps/api + packages against the compose x-app-env block confirms TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE and TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX are never injected, so the defaults are what production runs.
fix: Set explicit, arithmetically-consistent values in docker-compose.prod.yml x-app-env: e.g. TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE=12 and TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX=3 (12x3x2 processes = 72, leaving headroom under 200 for pgbouncer, the migrate one-shot and psql), or route tenant DBs through pgbouncer too. Additionally assert the budget at boot: fail if tenantClientCacheSize * poolMax * 2 exceeds a configured PG_MAX_CONNECTIONS.
verification: Mechanism confirmed by reading AND measured; impact arithmetic and trigger corrected, so severity drops high -> medium. Verified reads: env.ts:288 `tenantClientCacheSize: num('TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE', 50, ...)`; packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:21 `const DEFAULT_TENANT_POOL_MAX = 5;` and :56 `new PrismaPg({connectionString, max: resolveMaxPoolSize(...)})`; tenant-prisma.service.ts:72 passes no maxPoolSize; `grep -n TENANT_ infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` returns ONLY line 46 TENANT_PATH_PREFIX, so both defaults do ship; compose:324 `-c max_connections=200`; provisioning path is apps/api/src/provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-108 (the original 'where' cited apps/api/src/tenancy/..., which does not exist) and it does swap the DB name on PG_SUPERUSER_URL, which compose:87 points at `postgres:5432` directly, bypassing pgbouncer. EXECUTED a pool probe against the audit Postgres (10 clients from makeTenantPrismaClient, 5 concurrent queries each, backend count read from pg_stat_activity): 'after constructing 10 clients (no query): 0' / 'right after 10x5 concurrent burst: 50' / '2s later: 50' / '15s later (idle): 0'. So connections are opened lazily and node-postgres reaps them after ~10s idle. CORRECTION to the finding: the ceiling is driven by PEAK CONCURRENCY, not by how many libraries are cached — an idle cached client holds zero backends. Exhaustion needs ~35 tenants (200 minus pgbouncer's DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE=20 and superuser reserve, divided by 5) each with 5 in-flight queries at the same instant, across api+worker. The launch posture is five pilot libraries, so this cannot fire on Monday; it is a growth-time cliff, not a release blocker. The 250-vs-200 contradiction between two files in one repo is real and worth fixing before the fleet grows.

title: ensure-env.sh writes EMAIL_DRIVER=console on every deploy, permanently defeating the compose fail-fast that was deliberately added to prevent exactly that
what: docker-compose.prod.yml deliberately passes EMAIL_DRIVER through unset (`EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}`) with a comment (REL-06) explaining that a `:-console` default was removed because it 'silently DISABLED the fail-fast env.ts builds in for production', and that 'an operator who forgets gets the loud env.ts boot-time failure rather than silent, PII-logging email'. But scripts/ensure-env.sh:101 does `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console`, and ensure-env.sh --auto runs on EVERY deploy (deploy-on-host.sh:97, .github/workflows/deploy.yml:281) before compose reads the file. So .env.prod always contains EMAIL_DRIVER=console and the loud failure the compose file promises is unreachable — including for an operator who deliberately deletes the line to get it.
impact: No email is ever delivered in production and nothing at boot says so. Password reset, email verification, support-key delivery and announcement mail all silently no-op; the outbox row is marked sent with a fabricated `console-<hex>` providerId, so even the admin view says delivered. A librarian who forgets her password has no self-service recovery path and no error to report. Two files in the same deploy path assert opposite policies, which means whichever one a future operator reads, they will be wrong.
evidence: EXECUTED + READ. Executed: booting with EMAIL_DRIVER set to empty (the exact value compose injects) under NODE_ENV=production exits 1 with `Error: EMAIL_DRIVER=smtp requires SMTP_URL (e.g. smtp://user:pass@host:587).` at smtp-driver.ts:27 — i.e. the compose fail-fast works, and is the only thing standing between a fresh host and a crash-loop. Read: ensure-env.sh:62 `ensure_default() { ... [ -n "$(getv ...)" ] || setv ... }` and :101 `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console`; deploy-on-host.sh:97 `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto "$ENV_FILE"`. console-driver.ts:31-36 confirms the non-dev branch only logs 'NOT delivering ... (body withheld)' at warn level.
fix: Delete the `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console` line so the compose contract holds, and instead have ensure-env.sh prompt for (or require) a real driver. If a console-only launch is genuinely intended, make it explicit and loud: log an ERROR-level line at boot naming every feature that is disabled, and surface a persistent banner in the admin panel.
verification: Contradiction confirmed; impact partly overstated and partly restates the brief's known state, so severity drops high -> medium. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:69-77 carries the REL-06 comment and `EMAIL_DRIVER: ${EMAIL_DRIVER:-}` (pass-through unset, deliberately no `:-console`); scripts/ensure-env.sh:62 `ensure_default() { ... [ -n "$(getv "${k}")" ] || setv ... }` and :101 `ensure_default EMAIL_DRIVER console`; scripts/deploy-on-host.sh:97 and .github/workflows/deploy.yml:281 both run `bash scripts/ensure-env.sh --auto` before compose. So the loud boot failure the compose comment promises is indeed unreachable on any host these scripts touch, and an operator who deletes the line gets it re-added on the next deploy. Two files in one deploy path do assert opposite policies. CORRECTION: 'nothing says so' is only true of BOOT — console-driver.ts:30-35 logs a per-send WARN in every non-dev environment ("NOT delivering \"<subject>\" to <to> (body withheld). Configure EMAIL_DRIVER=resend|smtp to actually send."), so the condition is observable in the logs on every attempted send, and the same code path means reset TOKENS are NOT written to prod logs (contrary to the audit brief's own known-state note). The remaining harm — outbox rows marked sent with a fabricated `console-<hex>` providerId (console-driver.ts:24,37) so the admin view reads as delivered, and no self-service password recovery — is real but is also the deliberate, known launch posture rather than an accident.

title: The web container's healthcheck cannot fail while the API is down, and the deploy gate trusts it
what: The web service healthcheck is `wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/api/healthz`. That route returns a constant `{status:'ok'}` and, by its own comment, 'Doesn't touch the API or any other dependency'. A `/api/readyz` route already exists that fetches the API's /readyz over the docker network — it is not used by any probe. deploy-on-host.sh:181 gates the deploy on `web=healthy`, and web's own `depends_on: api: condition: service_healthy` only covers the initial start ordering, not steady state.
impact: A wrong API_INTERNAL_URL or a broken `app` network is invisible: web reports healthy, all four deploy-gate signals go green, and every page a librarian opens renders an error. In steady state the web container can never transition to unhealthy however badly the API is behaving, so the container-health dashboard is permanently green for the web tier. (A fully dead api container IS caught at deploy time by the `api=healthy` check — that half of the original impact does not hold.)
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:259-264 (`test: ['CMD','wget','-qO-','http://localhost:3000/api/healthz']`); apps/web/app/api/healthz/route.ts:3-14; apps/web/app/api/readyz/route.ts:22 (`await fetch(\`${apiBase}/readyz\`)`); deploy-on-host.sh:181 (`[ "$web" = "healthy" ]`).
fix: Point the web healthcheck at /api/readyz (keeping /api/healthz for a pure liveness probe), and make the deploy gate additionally curl one real page through Caddy rather than only asserting container health.
verification: Confirmed, with the impact tightened. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:259-264 `test: ['CMD','wget','-qO-','http://localhost:3000/api/healthz']`; apps/web/app/api/healthz/route.ts:13-15 returns a constant `{status:'ok', bootedAt}` and its comment says "Doesn't touch the API or any other dependency"; apps/web/app/api/readyz/route.ts:12-45 already fetches `${API_INTERNAL_URL}/readyz` with a 3s AbortController and returns 503 — and `grep` shows no probe anywhere references it. CORRECTION to the finding's impact: the deploy gate is NOT blind to a dead API — deploy-on-host.sh:181 requires `api=healthy`, and the api healthcheck (compose:223) is the deep `/readyz`. The real residual is narrower but still real: the gate's four signals are `edge` (Caddy's own static `respond "ok" 200` at infra/caddy/Caddyfile:136-140 — proves nothing about any app), `site` (the marketing-site vhost), `api=healthy`, and `web=healthy` (the constant). Not one of them ever renders a real panel page or crosses the web->api hop, so a wrong API_INTERNAL_URL or a broken `app` network passes the gate with everything green, and in steady state web can never go unhealthy no matter what happens behind it. Medium upheld.

title: `books.isbn13` has no unique constraint, yet the import treats it as the natural key for skip/update
what: The import's dedupe is `findFirst({ where: { isbn13, archivedAt: null } })` with nothing behind it — the only ISBN objects in the schema are a non-unique btree index and the `books_isbn13_shape` digits CHECK. `BooksService.create` performs no ISBN lookup at all.
