evidence: READ: schema.prisma:21 and :563 promise the job; `ls apps/api/src/jobs/` and registry.ts:23-80 show it absent; `grep -rn 'retention' apps packages scripts --include=*.ts` returns only definitions and the apps/site/src/plans.ts:232 admission. RAN: on the scale DB `pg_total_relation_size` gives audit_log 609 MB (289 MB heap + 319 MB indexes) at 3M rows — the largest object in the tenant database, larger than loans.
fix: Add an `audit-retention` cron that, per tenant, resolves `audit_log_retention_days` from EffectivePlanService and runs a chunked `DELETE FROM audit_log WHERE "occurredAt" < $cutoff LIMIT 10000` loop (or partitions audit_log by month and drops partitions). Add equivalent sweeps for email_outbox (delete `sent`/`failed` rows older than N days), announcement_deliveries, stripe_webhook_events and support_redemption_attempts. Until a sweep exists, remove `audit_log_retention_days` from the published plan table.
verification: Growth claim CONFIRMED: `grep -rn retention apps packages scripts` returns only feature definitions, plan seeds and the plans.ts comment — no pruning code; registry.ts:23-80 lists the nine jobs and none prunes a data table; the only `deleteMany` calls in apps/api/src are bookAuthor link replacement (books.service.ts:365, import-engine.ts:340) and importRowIssue cleanup (import-worker.ts:68). audit_log measured at 609 MB / 3M rows, the largest object in the tenant DB. EmailOutbox confirmed unpruned (email-worker.ts only updates status, never deletes) and member-notifications.job.ts:275-278 keys the overdue reminder on `dayKey(now)`, so it really does write one full-body row per overdue loan per day into the shared control DB. TWO CLAIMS REFUTED. (1) 'Customers were sold a retention figure ... so the plan feature is also a false claim' is false: apps/site/src/plans.ts:220-235 deliberately omits audit_log_retention_days from the published pricing table, naming this exact reason ('nothing prunes audit rows, so a printed retention figure would be an unenforced restriction'), and `grep audit_log_retention_days apps/web apps/api/src` returns nothing — the figure is never shown to a customer. (2) 'none of them prunes anything' overstates: export-file-cleanup (registry.ts:45-49) does prune export artifacts and reaps stale job rows. Also worth recording for whoever writes the fix: EmailOutbox.idempotencyKey is `@unique` and IS the dedup mechanism (schema.prisma:754), so deleting sent rows re-arms duplicate sends and needs a separate dedup ledger. Unbounded disk growth on a shared volume, no false customer claim — medium.

title: Hourly overdue sweeps scan the whole loans table, buffer every row, then do N+1 round trips per row
what: `accrueOneTenant` runs an unbounded `client.loan.findMany({ where: { status: 'active', dueAt: { lt: now } } })` and then, for each row, issues `loan.findUnique` + `fine.findFirst` and usually a `fine.updateMany` — three sequential round trips per loan, on a pool the code believes has one connection (see performance-06). `sendMemberNotifications` (apps/api/src/jobs/member-notifications.job.ts:244) runs the identical unbounded scan hourly and then calls `emails.enqueue()` serially per row; when the message already exists, `enqueue` costs a failed INSERT (P2002) plus a `findUniqueOrThrow` against the control DB (apps/api/src/email/email.service.ts:96-120). Neither sweep has a `take`; both jobs iterate every active tenant sequentially in one tick.
impact: For each Institutional tenant, every hour: a 32,845-page seq scan of loans, ~15,000 rows buffered in Node, ~45,000 sequential queries against the tenant DB (fine accrual) and ~30,000 against the shared control DB (notifications, of which ~29,000 are dedup misses that produce nothing). Because the amount changes at every day boundary, the fine `updateMany` fires for every overdue loan once a day. Tenants are processed sequentially, so the hourly tick's duration grows linearly with tenant count and with each library's overdue backlog — and reservation-pickup-expiry, announcement-publish and support-session-expiry are trying to run on 60-second ticks in the same worker.
evidence: RAN against the scale DB. `fine-accrual: overdue findMany -> 15000 rows in 233ms`; sampled the per-row work: `500 loans x 2 reads = 152ms (0.30 ms/loan)` -> `extrapolated for 15000 overdue loans (read-only, no writes) = 4.6s` on a loopback socket, before any writes. `member-notifications overdue: 15000 rows in 309ms (all buffered in memory)`. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS)` of the shared predicate: `Parallel Seq Scan on loans ... Rows Removed by Filter: 661667`, 32,757 buffers, 75.978 ms.
fix: Add the partial index from performance-02 so the sweep seeks instead of scanning. Page the sweep (`take: 500` + keyset cursor) instead of buffering. Collapse the per-row N+1 into set operations: one `fine.findMany({ where: { loanId: { in: batchIds }, status: 'outstanding' } })` per batch, then `createMany`/bulk `UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...)`. In the notification job, pre-filter with a single `emailOutbox.findMany({ where: { idempotencyKey: { in: keys } } })` so duplicates never reach the failed-insert path, and process tenants with bounded concurrency rather than strictly sequentially.
verification: READ fine-accrual.job.ts:95-98 — `client.loan.findMany({where:{status:'active',dueAt:{lt:now}}})` with no `take`, then lines 100-140 do `loan.findUnique` + `fine.findFirst` + `fine.updateMany`/`create` per row. member-notifications.job.ts:244-256 is the same unbounded findMany plus a serial `emails.enqueue()` per row. Predicate cost re-measured: `Parallel Seq Scan on loans`, 32,845 buffers, 58.8 ms warm for the overdue filter (see performance-02). Both sweeps iterate every active tenant sequentially in one tick (fine-accrual.job.ts:61). ONE NARROWING, which is why this stays medium and not high: both are gated on tenant settings that default OFF — schema.prisma:135 `overdueFinesEnabled @default(false)`, :159/:162/:163 `notifyDueSoon/notifyOverdue/notifyHoldReady @default(false)` — and fine-accrual returns at line 89 before the scan when fines are off. The cost only appears for libraries that switch these on, which any real library eventually will. Medium.

title: Dashboard tiles derive counts from list page sizes, buying two full table scans for numbers that are wrong
what: `safeCount` calls a list endpoint and returns `res.items.length` — the page size, not a total. The tiles request `loans?status=active&limit=100`, `loans?overdue=1&limit=100` and `reservations?status=queued&limit=100`, and the service clamps limit to 100 anyway. So the dashboard pays for two full seq scans of the loans table (performance-02) and a full sort of the hold queue (performance-10) on every render, to display a number that saturates at 100.
impact: The most-visited page in the app is also the most expensive query it can issue, and the answer it renders is wrong for any library with more than 100 active loans. Server-rendered, so it re-runs on every navigation to the tenant home, per user.
evidence: READ page.tsx:28-53 (`return { count: res.items.length, error: false }` with the comment 'Cursor-paged endpoints don't return a total; render the page-1 size ... a totals endpoint can replace this later'), and the `Math.min(100, ...)` clamps in loans.service.ts:793 / reservations.service.ts:424. RAN: the two loans queries measured at 106.8 ms and 74.8 ms, 32,845 buffers each (performance-02).
fix: Add one `/t/:slug/summary` endpoint returning real counts from indexed aggregates (`SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='active'), count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='active' AND "dueAt" < now()) FROM loans` backed by the partial index from performance-02), cache it in Redis for 30-60 s, and have the dashboard call that once instead of five list endpoints.
verification: READ apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/page.tsx:28-54 and confirmed verbatim: `safeCount` returns `res.items.length`, and the six parallel calls include `loans?status=active&limit=100`, `loans?overdue=1&limit=100` and `reservations?status=queued&limit=100`. Both loans calls were measured as 32,845-buffer parallel seq scans (363 ms and 59 ms, see performance-02), so every server-rendered visit to the tenant home costs two full scans of a 256 MB table. ADDITIONAL, worse than the finding says: the books and members tiles use `limit=1`, so a 400,000-title catalogue renders its tile as the page-1 size of 1. The number is not merely capped at 100, it is 1. Medium.

title: A one- or two-character search term seq-scans the whole catalogue; nothing enforces a minimum length server-side
what: `if (opts.q) where.searchText = { contains: normalizeText(opts.q) }` renders as `searchText LIKE '%q%'`. The `books_search_trgm` / `members_search_trgm` GIN indexes accelerate that only when the pattern yields at least one full trigram, i.e. from three characters. For one or two characters the planner falls back to a full sequential scan. No minimum is enforced in the DTO or the service (the Combobox has a client-side `minQueryChars`, but the catalog and members search boxes go through DataTable's URL-driven search, which does not).
impact: Typing two letters into the catalogue search and pressing enter costs a 400,000-row seq scan; on the members screen it costs 100,000 rows. In Greek this is a realistic query (single-word stems, and users searching by initials), and it is trivially repeatable — an authenticated staff user can hold the shared Postgres at 100% CPU with a search box.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL AND "searchText" LIKE '%ab%' ORDER BY "sortTitle", id LIMIT 26`: `Parallel Seq Scan on books (actual time=112.111..112.111 rows=0 loops=3)`, `Buffers: shared hit=1199 read=8858`. The 16-character control query on the same column used `Bitmap Index Scan on books_search_trgm`, 1371 buffers, 14 ms.
fix: Reject or ignore `q` shorter than three characters in the DTO for books, members and collection records (return an empty page with a 'keep typing' hint), and enforce the same `minQueryChars` in DataTable's search box so the request is never made.
verification: REPRODUCED precisely on libriant_scale. `... WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL AND "searchText" LIKE '%ab%' ORDER BY "sortTitle", id LIMIT 26` -> `Parallel Seq Scan on books`, `Buffers: shared hit=4950 read=5107` (10,057 buffers). The same query with a three-character term -> `Bitmap Heap Scan on books` via books_search_trgm, `Buffers: shared hit=4 read=3` (7 buffers). A 1,400x difference at the two/three-character boundary, exactly as claimed. No server-side floor exists: books.controller.ts:44,53 passes `q` straight through whenever `q.length` is non-zero, and books.dto.ts has no query DTO with a `@Length` on it. Rate limiting does not cover this — `RateLimitService` is wired only into auth.controller.ts, admin-auth.controller.ts, password-reset.service.ts, email-verification.service.ts and applications.service.ts; no list or search route touches it, and infra/caddy/Caddyfile has no rate_limit directive. Medium.

title: A platform owner-admin can export any library's entire database with no support key, no notice to the library and no audit entry
what: `POST /admin/exports` with `{scope:'tenant', tenantId}` (or `scope:'all'`) is gated only by `AdminAuthGuard` + `@AdminRoles('owner')`. `createForAdmin` inserts an `export_jobs` row and enqueues the job; it writes no `controlDb.auditEvent`, writes nothing to the target tenant's own audit_log, and sends no notification. This sits beside a carefully built consent model for the OTHER access path: support impersonation requires the TENANT to generate a `SupportKey` (schema.prisma:845-876), which is bcrypt-hashed, single-use, expiring, and every action is written to `support_action_log`. The export path bypasses all of it and yields strictly more data — the full members, loans, reservations and fines tables in one file.
impact: Under DPA §3.1 Libriant may process Controller Personal Data only on the library's documented instructions; taking a complete copy of a library's member registry on a Libriant employee's own initiative is not an instruction, and Art. 28(3)(a)/28(10) make that the processor's liability. The library has no way to detect it: the export leaves no trace in the only log the library can see. DPA §9 promises 'the information necessary to demonstrate compliance with Article 28' — for this operation there is none to give.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/export/admin-export.controller.ts:31-34 (`@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard, AdminRolesGuard)`) and :52-53 (`@Post() @AdminRoles('owner')`). READ apps/api/src/export/export.service.ts:77-106 — the method body creates the exportJob row and enqueues; RAN `grep -rn 'audit' apps/api/src/export/*.ts` → no matches outside specs, and the only global interceptor is SupportAuditInterceptor (apps/api/src/app.module.ts:82-83), which keys on an active support session.
fix: Write a control-plane AuditEvent (`tenant.exported`, actorType admin) AND a tenant-side audit row for every scope='tenant'/'all' export, e-mail the library's owner when their tenant is exported, and require an active tenant-issued SupportKey session for scope='tenant'. Then describe the residual capability in DPA Annex I.
verification: The mechanism holds: admin-export.controller.ts:52-62 gates `POST /admin/exports` on `@AdminRoles('owner')` only, and export.service.ts:77-105 `createForAdmin` creates the exportJob row and enqueues — RAN `grep -rn audit apps/api/src/export/` → zero hits, so no control AuditEvent and no tenant-side row is written, and no notification is sent. But the stated impact is partly refuted. The finding says 'The library has no way to detect it: the export leaves no trace in the only log the library can see.' It does leave one: an admin export with scope='tenant' sets `targetTenantId` to that tenant (export.service.ts:88-93), and `listForTenant` (export.service.ts:107-113) selects `where: { targetTenantId: tenantId, scope: 'tenant' }` with NO filter on requestedByKind — so the job appears in the library's own `GET /t/:slug/exports` list (tenant-export.controller.ts:38-41) and the library can even download it. The detection channel is unattributed (publicExportJob at export.service.ts:8-24 omits requestedByKind/requestedById) and scope='all' is genuinely invisible, but 'no way to detect' is false. Downgraded to medium for a second reason the finding does not weigh: a platform owner-admin already holds the control-plane and tenant DB credentials. The export endpoint is a convenience over `psql`, not a privilege they otherwise lack, so the defect is a missing audit trail and consent gate around an inherently privileged role — a governance gap, not an access-control breach.

title: The Art. 30(2) record of processing activities does not exist
what: Art. 30(2) obliges every processor to maintain a written record of all categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller — controller identities, categories of processing, third-country transfers, and a general description of the Art. 32 measures. Nothing of the kind exists in the repository. `grep -rniE 'dpia|record of processing|article 30|ropa|data protection impact' docs locales apps` returns only the two DPA sentences that PROMISE Art. 35 assistance, plus unrelated hits. The Art. 30(5) small-organisation exemption does not apply here on any of its three limbs: the processing is not occasional, it is large-scale relative to the entity, and it includes data of children.
impact: The record is the first document the Hellenic DPA asks for in any inspection or breach follow-up, and a public-body customer's DPO will request it during onboarding due diligence — public authorities are required to document their processors. Not having one is an independent Art. 83(4)(a) infringement and, practically, an immediate procurement blocker for exactly the δημοτικές and school libraries the launch campaign targets.
evidence: RAN `grep -rniE "dpia|record of processing|article 30|art\. 30|ropa|data protection impact" docs locales apps --include="*.md" --include="*.ts"` → hits are docs/brand/name-clearance (EUIPO), the 2026-06 audit findings, and locales/{el,en}/legal/dpa.md:59/67 ('assist … with your obligations under Articles 32–36 … DPIAs'). No Art. 30 record, no DPIA material, in any language.
fix: Write `docs/legal/ropa.md` covering, per controller category: categories of data subjects (members incl. minors, staff/volunteers), categories of data (identity, contact, dateOfBirth, address, photo, borrowing/reservation/fine history, custom fields, staffNotes), purposes, sub-processors and their locations, transfer safeguards, retention, and a summary of the Art. 32 measures that are actually implemented. Keep it versioned with the code and publish it on request.
verification: Absence verified. RAN `grep -rniE 'record of processing|article 30|art\. 30|ropa|data protection impact|dpia' docs locales apps --include='*.md' --include='*.ts' --include='*.json'` and, discounting the audit's own findings files, the only substantive hits are dpa.md's promises of Art. 32-36 assistance. `ls docs/legal` → the directory does not exist; `ls locales/en/legal` → the seven published slugs, none of which is a processor record. The Art. 30(2) obligation and the inapplicability of the 30(5) exemption (children's data) are correctly stated. Downgraded from high to medium. It is a document that does not exist, not a defect that harms anyone: no data subject is worse off, no data is exposed, and nothing in the running system behaves incorrectly. It is also blocked on privacy-legal-01 — a record of processing has to name the processor, and the processing entity is not registered yet — so it cannot be written first and is fully subsumed by 'the legal layer is unfinished'. Rating it high displaces attention from the four items that touch live data.

title: Acceptance is recorded but not evidenced: one global version string, written once, never read, with no archived copy of the accepted text and no re-acceptance flow
what: `LEGAL_VERSION = '2026-06-22'` is a single string covering all seven documents; editing any one of them without bumping it silently invalidates every stored acceptance. Signup writes `legalAcceptedVersion` / `legalAcceptedAt` on Tenant and User and `legalAcceptedIp` on User — and `grep -rn 'legalAccepted' apps/api/src apps/web` shows those are the ONLY five occurrences in the codebase: nothing ever reads them. There is no re-acceptance prompt (the README calls it 'a future flow'), no admin screen showing who accepted what, and no version archive: apps/web/lib/legal.ts loads `locales/<locale>/legal/<slug>.md` from disk, so /legal/terms always renders whatever is at HEAD. Only the owner ever accepts; staff invited later are never asked and their `legalAcceptedVersion` stays NULL.
impact: Art. 5(2) and Art. 7(1) require the controller to be able to DEMONSTRATE what a person agreed to. Here the record is a bare date string pointing at a mutable file. The five launch libraries will accept documents that are, by their own banner, drafts about to be rewritten by counsel — and once rewritten, nothing prompts them to re-accept and nothing preserves what they saw. In a dispute, or in an HDPA file, Libriant cannot produce the accepted text. Combined with privacy-legal-01, the acceptance evidences agreement to an unnamed party's draft.
evidence: READ packages/shared/src/legal.ts:18 `export const LEGAL_VERSION = '2026-06-22';` and :33 `export const SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS: readonly LegalDocSlug[] = ['terms', 'privacy'];`. RAN `grep -rn "legalAccepted" apps/api/src apps/web --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` → five hits, all in signup.service.ts:148-174; no reader. READ locales/legal-README.md — 'A future "please re-accept the updated terms" flow can compare a user's stored version against LEGAL_VERSION.'
fix: Snapshot the accepted text: store a content hash per document at acceptance (or commit the rendered documents to an immutable, version-addressed path and record the path). Give each document its own version. Add the gate that compares `user.legalAcceptedVersion` to `LEGAL_VERSION` on login and blocks until re-accepted, and an admin view of the acceptance record. Have the launch libraries re-accept the counsel-reviewed version explicitly.
verification: Verified: packages/shared/src/legal.ts:18 is a single `LEGAL_VERSION = '2026-06-22'` covering all seven slugs listed at :21-29. RAN `grep -rn legalAccepted apps/api/src apps/web packages --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' --include='*.prisma'` → five writes (signup.service.ts:148-149 on Tenant, :172-174 on User) plus three schema declarations and one comment. No reader, no login-time comparison, no admin view. apps/web/lib/legal.ts reads `locales/<locale>/legal/<slug>.md` from LOCALES_ROOT at request time and memoises it, so /legal/terms always renders HEAD — there is no archived copy of what anyone accepted. One sub-claim refuted: 'staff invited later are never asked and their legalAcceptedVersion stays NULL' is not a defect. There is no invite flow at all — `inviteToken` (schema.prisma:384) is declared and never used; staff.service.ts:96-108 creates staff users directly with a temp password and `mustChangeCredentials: true`. The contracting party is the library, bound by the owner's acceptance; an employee does not separately accept their employer's SaaS terms, so a NULL on a staff row is correct. Downgraded to medium: this is an accountability/evidence gap affecting contract disputes, not data subjects, and its practical bite comes entirely from privacy-legal-01 (the accepted text is a draft that will be rewritten). Fix -01 and this becomes 'bump the version and re-prompt', which is what the fix already says.

title: The whole contract with a public body rests on one checkbox self-certifying authority, and the liability cap is EUR 0 for every launch customer
what: Signup requires `acceptLegal === true` and nothing else; Terms §2.1 relies on 'If you are accepting on behalf of an organisation, you confirm you are authorised to bind it'. The customers are Greek public and municipal libraries and school libraries — public bodies whose capacity to contract and to appoint a processor is statutory, exercised by a named representative, not by whichever librarian fills in the form. Separately, Terms §10.3 caps aggregate liability at 'the fees you paid or owed in the 12 months before the event … (or `[EUR amount]` where no fees were paid)'. The launch offer is twelve months free for the first five libraries, so for every launch customer the first limb evaluates to zero and the fallback is an unfilled placeholder.
impact: If the librarian could not bind the municipality, there is no Art. 28 contract and no Terms — Libriant is processing a public authority's patron registry with no legal instrument, and the authority is in breach of Art. 28(1) for using a processor it never appointed. On the liability side, the library is asked to hand over a children-inclusive member registry to a counterparty whose stated maximum liability during the entire free period is nothing at all (and a GDPR Art. 82 claim is not capped by a private contract in any case, which the clause does not carve out beyond §10.1). Any competent public-sector legal review rejects both points.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/terms.md:129-132 — 'each party's total aggregate liability … is capped at the **fees you paid or owed in the 12 months** before the event giving rise to the claim (or `[EUR amount]` where no fees were paid).' READ apps/api/src/auth/dto/signup.dto.ts:115-118 — the only gate is `@Equals(true) acceptLegal`. Cross-referenced with the launch campaign's twelve-months-free offer for the first five libraries.
fix: For public-body customers use a counter-signed order form / DPA (a PDF signed by the library's legal representative) rather than clickwrap, and record the signed instrument against the tenant. Fill `[EUR amount]` with a real figure proportionate to the risk (not zero) and add an express carve-out that the cap does not limit liability under GDPR Art. 82.
verification: Both facts verified. locales/en/legal/terms.md:129-132 caps aggregate liability at 'the **fees you paid or owed in the 12 months** before the event … (or `[EUR amount]` where no fees were paid)' — with the launch offer of twelve months free, the first limb is zero and the fallback is unfilled. apps/api/src/auth/dto/signup.dto.ts:117-120 is a bare `@Equals(true) acceptLegal`, and SignupForm.tsx:363-382 renders one checkbox; terms.md:17-18 carries the 'you confirm you are authorised to bind it' self-certification. Downgraded from high to medium and narrowed. Two of the three limbs do not survive scrutiny as findings: (a) `[EUR amount]` is one of the placeholders already counted in privacy-legal-01, so rating it separately double-counts; (b) 'a librarian cannot bind a municipality, therefore there is no contract' is a contested commercial-legal position — apparent-authority clickwrap is what essentially every SaaS vendor selling to European public bodies relies on, and calling it a defect is an opinion, not a falsifiable finding. What genuinely survives is narrow and worth fixing: for every launch customer the cap resolves to EUR 0, and §10.1/§10.3 contain no carve-out for GDPR Art. 82 claims, which no private contract can cap anyway.

title: Support impersonation — Libriant staff acting inside a library's member data — is disclosed nowhere in the DPA or Privacy Policy
what: The product implements a tenant-consented impersonation flow: a tenant user generates a SupportKey, a platform admin redeems it, and for the session's lifetime that admin acts as a tenant user with full access to members, loans and fines, with every request written to `support_action_log` including `beforeJson`/`afterJson` snapshots of the touched records. The mechanism is well built. It is also invisible in the legal layer: `grep -ni 'support|impersonat' locales/en/legal/{dpa,terms,privacy}.md` finds only a Privacy row for 'Support communications', Terms §6 'Support is provided [via email…]' and a passing 'provide and support the Service'. DPA Annex I (§2) does not list it among the nature/purpose of processing, Annex II (§6) does not mention it as a control, and Privacy §10 'Sharing your data' does not mention it.
impact: The controller cannot describe in its own member-facing privacy notice a category of access that actually exists, and cannot assess it in a DPIA. Because the DPA defines the documented instructions as 'these Terms, this DPA, your configuration, and your use of the Service's features' (§3.1), a support session is only weakly inside instructions — the tenant-issued key is the saving grace, but nothing in writing says what a Libriant admin may do with the access or for how long. It also causes member record snapshots to be copied into the control plane (see privacy-legal-04) with no disclosure and no retention.
evidence: RAN `grep -ni "support|impersonat|access your data|our staff" locales/en/legal/dpa.md locales/en/legal/terms.md locales/en/legal/privacy.md` → 5 hits, none describing impersonation. READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:901-921 (`SupportActionLog … beforeJson Json? // Pre-mutation state captured by Prisma middleware`).
fix: Add a DPA section describing support access: that it requires a key the library itself issues, its maximum duration, what is logged, where the log lives (control plane), and its retention. Mirror it in Privacy §10 and give libraries wording they can paste into their own member notice.
verification: RAN `grep -niE 'support|impersonat|our staff|access your data' locales/en/legal/{dpa,privacy,terms}.md` → five hits and not one describes staff access to tenant data: privacy.md:46 is a processing-purpose table row 'Support communications | Respond to your requests'; privacy.md:99 is about assisting the library with data-subject requests; terms.md:54 'solely to provide and support the Service'; terms.md:85/91 are the availability-and-support section. DPA Annex I (§2 nature/purpose) and Annex II (§6 controls) do not mention it. Confirmed the mechanism exists and is substantial: schema.prisma:845-876 SupportKey (bcrypt codeHash, prefix-narrowed lookup, expiring, single-use) and :924-931 SupportRedemptionAttempt with ipAddress, plus SupportActionLog with beforeJson/afterJson. Also checked subprocessors.md — it lists third parties, so it is not the place this would be disclosed either. The finding is accurate and correctly rated: a real, well-built capability that the legal layer does not describe. Severity unchanged.

title: The documented 'prove the restore works' drill still uses the pre-fix, unfiltered pipeline — aimed at the live cluster
what: Under the heading "Before you need it: prove the restore works", the guide instructs: `rclone copy "$BACKUP_REMOTE:$(date -d yesterday +%Y%m%d)" .` then `gunzip -c *.sql.gz | psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U libriant -d postgres`. That is precisely the pipeline the 2026-08-22 fix exists to replace: no `pg_restore_preamble`, no `pg_restore_filter` (scripts/_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh), and it targets 127.0.0.1 — the production cluster — despite the surrounding prose claiming it restores "into a throwaway database". `$BACKUP_REMOTE` is also not a variable this repo defines (backup.sh uses `RCLONE_REMOTE`), so the copy step fails and the operator improvises.
impact: An operator following the guide's own pre-launch checklist pipes a `pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists` script — which begins with `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS` for every database — straight into the live cluster. Without `ON_ERROR_STOP` it does not abort cleanly; it grinds through partial drops, failed creates against still-connected databases, and duplicate-key errors re-importing over live tables. The single documented step called 'prove the restore works' is itself a production-destroying command. It also teaches the wrong pipeline, so the operator will reach for it again during an actual incident.
evidence: READ. docs/deployment-hetzner.md:874-882 quoted above. Contrast scripts/restore.sh:127-131, which wraps the same stream as `{ pg_restore_preamble "$PG_ROLE"; gunzip -c ... | pg_restore_filter "$PG_ROLE"; } | psql ... -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, and scripts/_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh:9-18 which records that the unfiltered form "destroys everything and restores nothing. Reproduced: psql exit 3, zero databases left." The correct procedure does exist two hundred lines earlier in the same file (deployment-hetzner.md:650-662, which calls restore.sh) — this second copy was never updated.
fix: Delete the raw-psql snippet and replace it with `bash scripts/dr-drill.sh` (against a throwaway cluster) plus `STORAGE_DIR=... BACKUP_ROOT=... scripts/restore.sh <YYYYMMDD> --yes` on a rebuilt host. Grep the whole docs/ tree for any other `gunzip -c *.sql.gz | psql` occurrence and remove it.
verification: The snippet is exactly as quoted (deployment-hetzner.md:872-882: `rclone copy "$BACKUP_REMOTE:..."` then `gunzip -c *.sql.gz | psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U libriant -d postgres`), and $BACKUP_REMOTE is indeed undefined anywhere in the repo — `grep -rn 'BACKUP_REMOTE\|RCLONE_REMOTE' scripts/ docs/` shows backup.sh:41 uses RCLONE_REMOTE. But the stated impact does NOT follow. I checked whether that psql can reach production: it cannot. In docker-compose.prod.yml the ONLY service with a `ports:` mapping is caddy (lines 135-138, 80/443); postgres (305-334) and pgbouncer (336-360) are on the internal `data` network with no published port, and the file's own network comment at 389-391 says the data tier 'CANNOT publish'. `psql -h 127.0.0.1` on the host gets connection refused — there is no live cluster on the host loopback to destroy. The rclone step also fails first on the undefined variable. So the real defect is narrower: the documented pre-launch 'prove the restore works' procedure is broken and teaches the unfiltered pipeline that scripts/_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh exists to prevent, leaving the operator with no working drill and a dangerous pattern to improvise from (it WOULD destroy if they reached for `dc exec -T postgres psql` when 127.0.0.1 refused). Downgraded high -> medium: documentation defect with a plausible but indirect path to harm, not a production-destroying command as written.

title: The DR drill passes, but it covers only Postgres — storage, backup.sh, restore.sh and the off-site copy are all untested
what: I re-ran the drill and it is sound (see evidence). What it does not cover: (a) the storage tarball — backup.sh's `tar -C "$STORAGE_DIR"` and restore.sh's untar are never exercised, which is exactly why reliability-05 survived; (b) backup.sh itself — the drill re-implements only `pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists | gzip -9`, so the off-host-tenant guard, the volume-mountpoint resolution, the prune, the manifest and the rclone push are untested; (c) restore.sh itself — the drill imports `_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh` but never invokes restore.sh, so the container stop/start ordering, the `trap restart_apps EXIT`, the archive validation and the tenant-count assertion are untested; (d) the off-site leg — nothing ever pulls a backup back from `RCLONE_REMOTE`; (e) realism — the fixture is 502 rows and a 5 KB dump, so nothing about restore duration or RTO is known; (f) restoring an OLD dump against NEWER code, i.e. Prisma migration drift after a rollback.
impact: The repo's stated guarantee — "scripts/dr-drill.sh now proves it" — is narrower than it reads. A green drill is compatible with a recovery that loses every uploaded file (reliability-05), with a backup that never ran (reliability-09), and with an off-site copy nobody can actually retrieve. The one leg that is proven is the one that was already fixed.
evidence: RAN. On a purpose-built isolated Postgres 16 cluster (`initdb --auth-host=scram-sha-256`, port 55441): `30 checks passed, 0 failed / DR DRILL PASSED — backup → restore round trip is sound` in 3.4 s, including the negative control `✓ password auth is enforced`, `✓ self-role drift undone`, `✓ role can still authenticate`, row censuses, extension sets, sequence values and byte-identical schema diffs for all three fixture databases. Coverage gaps confirmed by reading: `grep -n 'storage\|restore.sh\|backup.sh' scripts/dr-drill.sh` matches only comments and the re-implemented `pg_dumpall` line at 210.
fix: Extend the drill: create a fixture storage tree, run the real `backup.sh` (with COMPOSE overrides pointed at the fixture) and the real `restore.sh --yes` against the throwaway target, then diff the storage tree and assert file count/checksums. Add an `rclone` round-trip leg against a local `rclone` remote. Record and print elapsed restore time so RTO is a measured number.
verification: Coverage claim CONFIRMED by grep: `grep -n 'storage|restore.sh|backup.sh|rclone' scripts/dr-drill.sh` matches only header comments plus line 209-210, which re-implements `pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists | gzip -9` inline. The script sources _lib/pg-restore-filter.sh but never invokes backup.sh or restore.sh, and there is no storage tarball leg and no rclone leg. Worth adding: the CI step that runs it (.github/workflows/verify.yml:338-341) describes itself as exercising 'the real backup.sh -> restore.sh pipeline', which is the same overstatement. Downgraded high -> medium because the harm is entirely derivative: the concrete defects the gap allows through are reliability-05 (storage restore) and reliability-09 (unmonitored backup), both reported separately at high. On its own, a narrow drill causes no failure — it only fails to catch one. Rating it high alongside its own consequences double-counts the same 3am event.

title: Abandoned ('dead') outbox emails have no surface anywhere — password resets can be dropped silently
what: After `maxAttempts` the worker writes `status: 'dead', abandonedAt: now, lastError: reason` and gives up. Repo-wide, the only other reads of `'dead'` are the skip check at line 175 — there is no admin endpoint, no metric, no /healthz field, no scheduled sweep and no alert that counts dead rows. The single trace is one `console.error` per failure in a rolling Docker log.
impact: When the provider is misconfigured, rate-limits, or a domain gets blocked, password-reset links, email-verification links and hold-ready notices are permanently abandoned with no operator-visible signal. Users experience 'the reset email never arrives' and support has no way to see it happened, let alone re-drive it. This becomes live the moment EMAIL_DRIVER stops being `console`.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn "'dead'" apps/api/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v spec` → exactly two hits, both in email-worker.ts (175, 215). `grep -rn 'emailOutbox' apps/api/src | grep -v email-worker\|email.service` → one hit, an unrelated read in support-session-expiry.job.ts:71. No admin route, no metric.
fix: Expose `libriant_email_outbox_rows{status=...}` from the worker's /metrics and add a Prometheus rule on `dead > 0` and on `pending` older than N minutes. Add an admin panel view of the outbox with a re-drive action (set back to `pending`, reset attempts), so a provider outage is recoverable rather than a permanent data loss of user-facing mail.
verification: Mechanism confirmed: `grep -rn "'dead'" apps/api/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v spec` returns exactly two hits, email-worker.ts:175 (skip) and :215 (write). Files touching emailOutbox at all: email-worker.ts, email.service.ts, support-session-expiry.job.ts — no admin route, no metric, no healthz field. Downgraded high -> medium after reading the surrounding code: the failure is not actually silent at the point it happens. email-worker.ts:219 re-throws after marking the row, so BullMQ records the failure and the worker's failed handler logs it; the row itself is durable and carries `lastError`, `failedAt` and `abandonedAt`, so a dead letter is recoverable by SQL rather than lost; and the triggering condition (a misconfigured or blocked provider) fails EVERY message, which is loud in logs. What is genuinely missing is an operator surface and a re-drive action, which is an observability gap of the same family as reliability-04/17 rather than an independent high. Note the finding is correct that this is dormant only while EMAIL_DRIVER=console.

title: /readyz's dependency breakdown never reaches the caller — the global filter re-skins the 503 into a generic envelope
what: The readiness handler deliberately builds `{status:'not_ready', dependencies:{redis, controlDb}}` and throws it inside a `ServiceUnavailableException`. `HttpExceptionFilter` treats any status >= 500 — 503 included — as a server bug: it discards the declared body, mints a support code, logs the whole thing, and returns the generic "Sorry — something went wrong on our end… code: XXXXXXXX" envelope.
impact: The one endpoint designed to tell an operator WHICH dependency is down tells them nothing. `docker inspect` shows `unhealthy` with a useless body, a `wget -qO- /readyz` gives a support code instead of `{"redis":true,"controlDb":false}`, and diagnosis requires grepping the API log for that code. It also means every failed readiness probe (every 15 s per the compose healthcheck) writes a full stack trace, so a DB outage floods the log with 4 stack traces a minute.
evidence:
RAN. With Postgres stopped and Redis up:
```
readyz: {"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end. We've logged it. Please try again, or send us this code if it keeps happening: 784L88W5","supportCode":"784L88W5"} [503]
```
The designed body `{"status":"not_ready","dependencies":{...}}` is nowhere in the response.
fix: Either exempt 503 from the re-skin (`if (status < 500 || status === HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE) { res.status(status).json(body); return; }`), or have the readiness handler write the response directly with `@Res()` instead of throwing. Also drop the readiness probe's log level from `error`+stack to a single warn line so a DB outage does not bury the real errors.
verification: RE-EXECUTED against the live API. Stopped Postgres with Redis up (so the readiness handler itself ran) and got: `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end... code: 4FWVPCBI","supportCode":"4FWVPCBI"}` with HTTP 503. The designed body `{"status":"not_ready","dependencies":{"redis":...,"controlDb":...}}` from health.controller.ts:41-47 is nowhere in the response. Cause re-read and confirmed: http-exception.filter.ts:44-49 passes through only `status < 500`, so 503 falls into handle5xx (lines 76-105), which discards `declaredBody`, mints a support code and logs a full stack. The log-flood sub-claim also holds — the compose healthcheck polls /readyz every 15 s (docker-compose.prod.yml:223-228), so a DB outage writes four stack traces a minute. Severity stands.

title: The stripe-retry sweep has the same cold-Redis defect, and it only bites when there is something to retry
what: Identical shape to reliability-01: `const redis = new RedisService()` at line 67, then the first thing the loop does is `await redis.client.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', ..., 'NX')` at line 88 on a socket that is still `connecting`, which rejects under `enableOfflineQueue:false`. Unlike member-notifications, that throw is not caught per-row — it escapes the whole handler, so the sweep aborts having retried nothing. The job returns early (`if (failed.length === 0) return`) whenever there is nothing to do, so the bug is invisible on a healthy system and fires exactly when failed Stripe webhook events exist.
impact: Currently dormant (BILLING_ENABLED=false, STRIPE_DRIVER=fake). The moment billing is switched on, the safety net for failed Stripe webhooks — the thing that stops a missed `customer.subscription.updated` from leaving a library on the wrong plan or wrongly suspended — fails on its first event every 5 minutes. At least this one is loud: BullMQ marks the job failed and the runner records `ok:false`.
evidence: READ, mechanism proven by execution elsewhere. Same construct-then-immediately-command pattern as member-notifications.job.ts:138/188, whose failure I reproduced 5/5 times (reliability-01). stripe-retry.job.ts:67 `const redis = new RedisService();`, line 88 `const claimed = await redis.client.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', SWEEP_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS, 'NX');` with no intervening await that yields long enough for the socket to reach `ready`.
fix: Same as reliability-01 — `await redis.ready()` after construction, or take the shared client from JobContext. Fix both call sites together; `grep -rn 'new RedisService()' apps/api/src` finds all three (worker.ts:161 is the correct, long-lived one).
verification: UPGRADED FROM read-only TO EXECUTED. I inserted a failed webhook row into the live control plane (`stripeWebhookEvent { id: 'evt_audit_rel16', type: 'customer.subscription.updated', error: 'previous failure' }`) and invoked sweepFailedStripeWebhooks() directly. Result: `SWEEP THREW: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false` — the whole handler aborts on the first row, retrying nothing, exactly as predicted. Re-read confirms the cited lines: stripe-retry.job.ts:67 `const redis = new RedisService()` and :88 `await redis.client.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', SWEEP_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS, 'NX')`, with the early return at :61 hiding it whenever there is nothing to retry. Severity stands at medium: dormant while BILLING_ENABLED=false, and unlike reliability-01 it is loud when it fires (the throw escapes, BullMQ marks the job failed, the runner records ok:false).

title: The API exports no request, error or latency metrics — a 5xx storm is unalertable
what: `/metrics` emits `libriant_api_uptime_seconds`, `libriant_api_build_info`, tenant counts by status, summed storage bytes, Postgres connection count/max, Postgres cache-hit ratio and Redis used_memory. There is no HTTP request counter, no status-code breakdown, no latency histogram, and no per-tenant error counter. The worker's /metrics is similarly limited to uptime plus in-flight gauges. Consequently infra/monitoring/alerts.yml has no rule that could reference an error rate.
impact: There is no signal for 'the app is up but broken'. A regression that 500s one route, a tenant whose every request errors, a latency cliff after a bad migration — all invisible to Prometheus and Grafana. The only availability signal is `up{job="libriant-api"}`, which requires /metrics itself to fail. Reliability-02 happens to trip that (Redis down 500s /metrics too), but a narrower breakage will not.
evidence: READ, and RAN. Full scrape of a live API returned only the gauges listed above. `grep -n 'requests_total\|http_request\|_duration_seconds' apps/api/src` → no matches. infra/monitoring/alerts.yml contains no rule mentioning an error or request metric.
fix: Add a tiny counter/histogram in the pino-http `onResponse` hook or a global interceptor: `libriant_api_requests_total{method,route,status}` and `libriant_api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route}`. Then add alert rules for sustained 5xx ratio and p95 latency. Route labels must be the Nest route pattern, not the raw URL, so tenant slugs and ids do not explode cardinality.
verification: RE-EXECUTED. Full scrape of the live API's /metrics returned exactly eight gauges and nothing else: libriant_api_uptime_seconds, libriant_api_build_info, libriant_tenants_total{status}, libriant_storage_used_bytes, libriant_pg_connections, libriant_pg_connections_max, libriant_pg_cache_hit_ratio, libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes. `grep -rn 'requests_total|http_request|_duration_seconds' apps/api/src` -> no matches. Cross-checked the consequence: `grep -n 'alert:' infra/monitoring/alerts.yml` lists 10 rules (TargetDown, LibriantApiDown, HostLowMemory, HostSwapping, HostDiskFilling, HostDiskCritical, HostHighCPU, LibriantPgConnectionsHigh, LibriantPgConnectionsCritical, LibriantPgCacheHitLow) — every one is a liveness or host/DB-capacity rule; none can express an error rate or latency. The 'up but broken' state is genuinely unobservable. Severity stands.

title: Desktop code-signing identity and the auto-update publish token are exposed to a job that executes third-party install scripts and downloads network artifacts
where: .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml:97-208 (job `release`), specifically :118 `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, :123 `pnpm rebuild electron`, :156-191 `electron-builder --publish always`, env block :193-208
what: One job holds, simultaneously: `CSC_LINK` + `CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` (the Apple Developer ID .p12 and its password), `APPLE_API_KEY_P8` (App Store Connect notarization key), the full Azure Trusted Signing service principal (`AZURE_TENANT_ID`/`CLIENT_ID`/`CLIENT_SECRET`), and `GH_TOKEN` with workflow-level `permissions: contents: write` (desktop-release.yml:54-55) on the very repository whose Releases are the electron-updater feed. In that same job it runs `pnpm install`, which executes the install scripts of `@prisma/engines`, `prisma`, `esbuild` and `electron-winstaller` (all allow-listed in pnpm-workspace.yaml:27-40), then `pnpm rebuild electron`, then electron-builder, which downloads the Electron dist archive and (on Windows) 7-Zip from the network at package time. Any one of those packages, or any of the 611 packages installed, running arbitrary Node at install time, can read the signing material out of the environment and can also overwrite the release assets.
impact: Compromise of any package in the install closure -> theft of the Apple Developer ID certificate and the Azure code-signing credential (identity theft that outlives the repo, and cannot be revoked without invalidating every shipped installer), plus the ability to publish a signed installer that every desktop client auto-installs. Fleet-wide RCE on library staff machines from one npm account takeover.
evidence: READ desktop-release.yml:54-55 (`permissions: contents: write`), :117-123 (Install + `pnpm rebuild electron`), :193-208 (all seven signing secrets in one `env:`). RAN an enumeration of every package in node_modules/.pnpm with a preinstall/install/postinstall hook: `@prisma/engines@7.9.1 postinstall=node scripts/postinstall.js`, `prisma@7.9.1 preinstall=node scripts/preinstall-entry.js`, `esbuild@0.28.2 postinstall=node install.js`, `electron-winstaller@5.4.0 install=node ./script/select-7z-arch.js` — four arbitrary-code hooks that run in this job.
fix: Split the pipeline: build unsigned artifacts in a job with no secrets and `permissions: contents: read`, upload them as workflow artifacts, and sign+publish in a separate minimal job that runs no `pnpm install` (download the artifact, run only the signing tool). Gate the publish job behind an `environment:` with required reviewers. Until then, do not populate MAC_CSC_LINK / AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET.
verification: The mechanism is exactly as described and I could not refute it: desktop-release.yml:54-55 is `permissions: contents: write`; the `release` job env block at :193-208 carries all seven signing secrets; :118 runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` in that same job; and I RE-RAN the install-hook enumeration over node_modules/.pnpm and got precisely the four arbitrary-code hooks claimed (`@prisma/engines@7.9.1 postinstall`, `prisma@7.9.1 preinstall`, `esbuild@0.28.2 postinstall`, `electron-winstaller@5.4.0 install`). But the stated impact does not follow TODAY, which is what the severity has to reflect. Every one of those signing secrets is unset: the workflow's own branches prove it — :138 `if [ -z "${CSC_LINK:-}" ]` and :172 `if [ -n "${AZURE_CLIENT_ID:-}" ]` are what select the unsigned paths that actually run, and commit 7d71e7e ('ad-hoc sign unsigned macOS builds') exists precisely because there is no Developer ID cert. An unset GitHub secret interpolates to the empty string; there is no Apple certificate and no Azure service principal in that environment to steal. So 'theft of the Apple Developer ID certificate... identity theft that outlives the repo' cannot happen on Monday. What genuinely remains is a package in the install closure reading GITHUB_TOKEN with contents:write and rewriting release assets — real, but the same distribution channel supply-chain-11 covers, and one that already requires the attacker to own an npm package in the tree. Medium: a correct latent design defect that MUST be fixed before signing secrets are ever populated, not a live exposure.

title: The production API image ships the entire dev and web dependency tree — 611 packages, 880 MB, including eslint, vitest, turbo, typescript, Next.js and Prisma Studio
where: apps/api/Dockerfile:54 (`RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, no --prod) and apps/api/Dockerfile:92 (`COPY --from=build /app /app`); same pattern at apps/web/Dockerfile:24,61
what: The deps stage installs the whole workspace with dev dependencies, and the runtime stage copies /app wholesale. Nothing prunes. The image therefore contains every root devDependency (eslint 10.9.0, typescript-eslint, prettier, turbo, tsx, typescript 6.0.3), the API's own devDependencies (vitest 4.1.11, supertest), the complete Next.js 16 tree (198 MB) including the SWC and lightningcss native binaries, sharp + libvips, and — via the Prisma optional peer (see supply-chain-04) — the Prisma CLI (42 MB), @prisma/studio-core (42 MB, a database-browsing web UI), @prisma/dev, @electric-sql/pglite (23 MB, an embedded WASM Postgres) and mysql2. Only apps/api/src actually runs.
impact: Three concrete harms. (1) Attack surface: a foothold in the API container lands in a ready-made toolkit — a TypeScript compiler, a bundler, a MySQL client and an embedded Postgres, all executable by the `node` user, on a container that already holds CONTROL_DATABASE_URL and every tenant credential. (2) CVE surface: every future advisory in eslint/vitest/turbo/Next.js becomes a production advisory that has to be triaged and shipped, permanently. (3) Cost: ~880 MB of node_modules pulled to each host on every deploy, on a pipeline that already prunes images at deploy.yml:294 to avoid ENOSPC.
evidence: RAN a faithful replay of the API Dockerfile deps stage in a scratch directory (copied exactly the manifests apps/api/Dockerfile:40-50 copies, then `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`): result `Packages: +611`, `du -sh node_modules` = **880M**. Largest entries: next@16.3.2 198.3 MB, @next/swc 84.8 MB, @prisma/client 74.9 MB, @prisma/studio-core 42.2 MB, prisma 41.9 MB, @turbo/darwin-arm64 34.9 MB, typescript 23.6 MB, @electric-sql/pglite 23.2 MB, prettier 9.6 MB. A `--prod` install of only the API-relevant workspaces gives 444 packages / 459 MB — so 167 packages and 421 MB are pure dev tooling that has no business on a production host.
fix: Use `pnpm deploy --filter @libriant/api --prod --legacy /app/out` (or `pnpm install --prod` after the Prisma generate step) in the build stage and copy only the pruned output into the runtime stage. Drop apps/web/package.json from the API Dockerfile's COPY set (apps/api/Dockerfile:42) — the API never imports the web app. Verify with `docker image inspect` that eslint/vitest/turbo/next are gone.
verification: Reproduced the measurement exactly rather than trusting it. RAN a byte-faithful replay of apps/api/Dockerfile:40-50 in a scratch dir (same eight manifests, same lockfile) then `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`: `Packages: +611`, `du -sh node_modules` = **880M**, and `ls node_modules/.pnpm/` confirms next@16.3.2, eslint@10.9.0, vitest@4.1.11, turbo@2.10.11, typescript@6.0.3, prisma@7.9.1, @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0, @electric-sql/pglite@0.4.3, mysql2@3.15.3 are all present. The Dockerfile facts hold: line 54 has no `--prod`, line 92 is `COPY --from=build /app /app`, and line 42 pulls apps/web/package.json into a stage whose source is never copied — so the entire Next.js tree is installed into the API image and never used. Downgraded high -> medium because no failure scenario follows from the mechanism alone. 'Attack surface' and 'future CVE triage' are not defects with a victim; they amplify other defects. The one harm with a real precedent is disk: deploy.yml:288-292 records that unpruned images 'has broken a deploy at the seed step with ENOSPC' — but that is already mitigated by the `docker image prune -af --filter until=72h` at :294. ALSO: the finding's own fix is wrong as written. `tsx` is a devDependency of apps/api (apps/api/package.json devDependencies: tsx, typescript, vitest, supertest) and the runtime CMD at Dockerfile:105 is `./apps/api/node_modules/.bin/tsx apps/api/src/main.ts`. A plain `pnpm install --prod` would delete the container's own entrypoint. The pruning must keep tsx (promote it to a dependency, or precompile) — do not apply the suggested fix verbatim.

title: Nothing pinned by digest: base images, the third-party pgbouncer image, and the package manager itself are all resolved from live registries at build/deploy time
what: `grep -rn '@sha256:' infra/ .github/ apps/*/Dockerfile` returns nothing. Every base image is a floating tag. `node:26-alpine`, `caddy:2-alpine`, `postgres:16-alpine` and `redis:8-alpine` all move whenever upstream republishes; `edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.25.2-p0` is a community image (not an official/verified publisher) that sits in the credential path with POSTGRES_PASSWORD in its environment, and its tag is equally mutable. On the host, deploy.yml:296 runs `docker compose pull`, so whatever the tag points to that minute becomes production.
impact: The deployed stack is not reproducible and not verifiable: two deploys of the same IMAGE_TAG can run different Postgres, Redis, Caddy and pgbouncer binaries. A compromised or hijacked upstream tag (edoburu/pgbouncer is the softest target — a single-maintainer community image handling the database password) lands straight in production with no signal. Compounding it, deploy.yml:294 runs `docker image prune -af --filter until=72h` BEFORE the pull, so the previous base image is gone and a rollback re-pulls the same floating tag rather than restoring what was running.
evidence: RAN `grep -rn "@sha256:" infra/ .github/ apps/*/Dockerfile` — no output. READ the six image lines above. READ deploy.yml:294-296 (prune, then pull).
fix: Pin each base image as `image: postgres:16-alpine@sha256:<digest>` (tag retained for readability) in the Dockerfiles and in docker-compose.prod.yml, and bump digests deliberately. For pgbouncer, either pin the digest or switch to building a thin image from the official Alpine pgbouncer package so the supply chain is one you control.
verification: Core claim verified: RAN `grep -rn '@sha256:' infra/ .github/ apps/api/Dockerfile apps/web/Dockerfile` -> no output (exit 1), and `grep -rnE '^\s*(FROM|image:)'` confirms node:26-alpine (x3), caddy:2-alpine, postgres:16-alpine, redis:8-alpine and edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.25.2-p0 are all floating tags, with `docker compose pull` at deploy.yml:296 resolving them at deploy time. edoburu/pgbouncer is indeed a community image and does sit in the credential path. ONE SUB-CLAIM REFUTED — strike it from the evidence. The finding says the prune at deploy.yml:294 means 'the previous base image is gone and a rollback re-pulls the same floating tag rather than restoring what was running.' That is false on two counts, both readable at deploy.yml:288-294: `docker image prune -a` never removes an image that a container is using, and postgres/redis/pgbouncer are running containers; and the `until=72h` filter protects everything newer than three days, which the comment says explicitly ('in-use images are protected regardless of age, so the running stack and recent tags (for fast rollback) survive'). The rollback path also pulls app images by immutable 12-hex SHA tag (deploy.yml:236-238), not by a floating tag. Severity held at medium: non-reproducible infrastructure is a genuine defect, but the exposure is concentrated in one single-maintainer community image, not in the Docker Official Images.

title: Every tenant database is opened with the same Postgres superuser role, and the per-tenant credential model is dead code
what: `urlForDb()` builds every tenant's connection string from `PG_SUPERUSER_URL` by swapping only the database name (`const u = new URL(this.env.pgSuperuserUrl); u.pathname = '/'+dbName;`). That string, password included, is persisted verbatim to `tenants.dbUrl` and is what TenantPrismaService connects with on every request. The `TenantDbCredential` model (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:331-346 — "Sensitive per-tenant DB role secret … Postgres role name owning this tenant's DB") is never read or written anywhere in apps/, scripts/ or packages/. There is no per-tenant role, no GRANT, no REVOKE CONNECT and no RLS.
impact: The separation between libraries is a physically separate database enforced only by which connection string the application picks. Any single leak of one connection string, or any future SQL-injection or SSRF into the data tier, yields read/write on all libraries at once and — because the role is superuser — COPY FROM PROGRAM on the Postgres container. It also turns tenant-isolation-01 and -03 from metadata leaks into fleet-wide credential leaks, and puts every tenant's password in plaintext in every pg_dumpall backup (scripts/backup.sh:116).
evidence: READ tenant-provisioning.service.ts:105-109. RAN `psql "$CONTROL_DATABASE_URL" -c 'select id,slug,status,left("dbUrl",60) from tenants order by "createdAt" desc limit 6'` — all rows are `postgresql://libriant:auditpw@127.0.0.1:55440/tenant_…`, identical but for the dbname. RAN a signup and dumped the resolver cache: same superuser URL (see tenant-isolation-03 evidence). GREP `customSubdomain`-style search for `tenantDbCredential` / `tenant_db_credentials` across apps, scripts and packages: zero hits outside the schema and the generated migration.
verification: Mechanism re-verified by reading and by querying the live control DB — accurate as written. Severity downgraded high→medium on two grounds. (1) The stated amplifier "one SQL injection" has no surface today: `grep -rn 'queryRawUnsafe|executeRawUnsafe'` finds exactly two non-test call sites, effective-plan.service.ts:144 (fully parameterised, `s."tenantId" = $1`) and maintenance-processors.ts:149 (`SELECT 1`); every other query goes through Prisma's parameterised client. (2) A physically separate database per tenant is a real boundary, and the harm described is entirely amplification of other defects rather than a defect that fires on its own. Rating it high would put a per-tenant-role migration on the Monday critical path and displace attention from the cheap fixes. Recording it at medium with the Monday-sized half called out.
fix: Monday-sized half: stop persisting the password in `tenants.dbUrl` — store host/port/dbname only and inject the password from `PG_SUPERUSER_URL` at connect time, so reading a control row (or a control-DB backup) is no longer reading a credential. Full fix: in `provision()`, CREATE ROLE tenant_<id> with a random password, GRANT ALL ON DATABASE to it, REVOKE CONNECT … FROM PUBLIC, store the encrypted secret in the already-modelled `TenantDbCredential`, and keep PG_SUPERUSER_URL for provisioning and migrations only.

title: The tenant resolver caches each tenant's plaintext DB superuser URL in Redis, and the production Redis has no password
what: `resolveCached()` JSON-serialises the whole `TenantContext` — `dbUrl` and `storageUrl` included — into `lbr:tenant:slug:<slug>` (keyPrefix `lbr:` from redis.service.ts:30 + `tenant:slug:` from tenant-resolver.service.ts:16) with a `TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC` (default 300s) TTL, on every cache miss. Nothing in the request path needs `dbUrl` to be shared across processes. The production Redis runs `redis-server --appendonly yes --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:372) with `REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379` (line 37) — no `requirepass`, no TLS — so the credential also lands in the `redis_data` AOF on disk.
impact: Anything that reaches Redis on the `data` network, or reads the `redis_data` volume, gets the superuser password for every tenant database with no Postgres authentication involved. Redis being unauthenticated means any future service or sidecar attached to that network is implicitly trusted with the fleet's database credentials.
verification: The cached blob is exactly as claimed — dumped verbatim from the live Redis. Downgraded high→medium because the marginal disclosure is much smaller than stated. The same superuser password is already (a) in the api/worker container environment as PG_SUPERUSER_URL, (b) in `tenants.dbUrl` in the control DB, and therefore (c) in every backup — scripts/backup.sh:116 runs `pg_dumpall` over the control DB plus every tenant DB, and does not touch Redis at all (grep of backup.sh: no redis). So the original's headline scenarios ("reads the volume or an unencrypted host backup") are already true via Postgres without Redis, and the only process class that can reach Redis (`networks: [data]`, `internal: true`, no published ports) is the same api/worker that already holds the env var. What genuinely remains: an unauthenticated Redis on a shared network, and one more at-rest copy in the AOF. That is a hardening gap, not an independent compromise path — and the root cause is tenant-isolation-02, which this duplicates one channel of.
fix: Cache only `{id, slug, name, defaultLocale, status, customSubdomain, tags}` and resolve `dbUrl`/`storageUrl` from a process-local map keyed by tenant id. Separately set `--requirepass` on the prod Redis and put the password in `REDIS_URL` — `redactUrl` in redis.service.ts:62 already handles a password being present in the logged URL.

title: Password-reset and email-verification tokens are stored in Redis in plaintext, keyed by the token itself
what: `const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')` is used verbatim as the Redis key (`pwreset:<token>`, `emailverify:<token>`) with the user/tenant ids as the value. The bearer secret is therefore stored at rest exactly as it appears in the email link. Redis in the production compose (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:362) runs `redis:8-alpine` with no `requirepass`, on the internal Docker network; anything that can `docker exec` into the box, read a Redis dump, or reach 6379 from another container can `KEYS pwreset:*` and mint a password reset for any account. The 60-minute TTL bounds the exposure window but the tokens are continuously present in a busy deployment.
impact: Any read of Redis state — an operator, a compromised sidecar, a backup archive, a monitoring exporter — yields directly usable account-takeover tokens for every library that has requested a reset in the last hour, including tenant owners. This turns a read-only foothold into full tenant compromise with no further work.
evidence: READ password-reset.service.ts:70-77 (`const key = \`pwreset:${token}\`; await this.redis.client.set(key, JSON.stringify({uid, tid}), 'EX', 3600)`) and email-verification.service.ts:76-88 (same pattern). READ infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:362 — `image: redis:8-alpine`, no `requirepass` in the command.
fix: Store `sha256(token)` as the key and keep the plaintext only in the email — `getdel('pwreset:' + sha256(submitted))` preserves the existing atomic single-use claim with a one-line change. Also set `requirepass` on the production Redis.
verification: CONFIRMED read-only, exactly as described. READ password-reset.service.ts:70-77 — `const token = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); const key = \`pwreset:${token}\`; redis.set(key, JSON.stringify({uid, tid}), 'EX', 3600)`; email-verification.service.ts:76-88 is the same shape with `emailverify:${token}`. Verified the deployment claim rather than taking it: infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:361-375 runs `image: redis:8-alpine` with `command: ['redis-server','--appendonly','yes','--maxmemory-policy','allkeys-lru']` — no `requirepass` — on the internal `data` network, with `--appendonly yes` meaning the tokens are also written to disk in the `redis_data` volume (and therefore into any volume-level backup), which the original finding did not note. Low held: it needs a pre-existing read foothold on the box or on a backup.

title: Mandatory admin-MFA is bypassed by any request path that merely contains `/mfa/` or `/auth/` as a substring
what: `isMfaEnrollmentPath(path)` returns `path.includes('/mfa/') || path.includes('/auth/')`. It is a substring test on the whole request path, not an allowlist of the enrollment routes. Today only `/admin/mfa/*` and `/admin/auth/*` match, so the gate holds — but any future admin route whose path contains those segments anywhere (`/admin/tenants/:id/auth/...`, `/admin/settings/mfa/policy`, or a `:param` whose value is `auth`) silently escapes `ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED` with no test to catch it. The guard is the only thing enforcing AUTH-06.
impact: A latent bypass of mandatory admin MFA that will be introduced by an ordinary, innocuous-looking route addition, with nothing in CI to notice. Not exploitable against the current route table.
evidence: READ admin-auth.guard.ts:76-78 — `return path.includes('/mfa/') || path.includes('/auth/');`. Enumerated the admin route table (`grep -n '@Controller|@Post|@Patch|@Put|@Delete' apps/api/src/**/*controller.ts`): no current route other than `admin/mfa/*` and `admin/auth/*` matches, so this is latent rather than live.
fix: Replace the substring test with an explicit set of exempt route paths (`/admin/mfa/status`, `/admin/mfa/setup`, `/admin/mfa/verify`, `/admin/auth/me`, `/admin/auth/logout`), or better, mark them with an `@MfaExempt()` decorator the guard reads via Reflector so exemption is opt-in at the handler.
verification: CONFIRMED, with the auditor's own supporting evidence corrected in a way that makes it slightly worse but still latent. READ admin-auth.guard.ts:76-78 — `return path.includes('/mfa/') || path.includes('/auth/');`, a substring test on the full request path. The finding claims 'no current route other than /admin/mfa/* and /admin/auth/* matches'; that is WRONG — `grep -n "@Controller(" apps/api/src | grep -i admin` shows three parameterised admin controllers whose paths can be made to contain the magic segments by choosing the parameter value: `admin/tenants/:tenantId/overrides`, `admin/tenants/:tenantId/tags` and `admin/billing/tenants/:tenantId` (e.g. `GET /admin/tenants/auth/overrides` contains `/auth/`). It stays latent rather than live only because no tenant row has the id `auth` or `mfa`, so every such request resolves to a 404 before doing anything. Also note the ceiling on the impact: the guard's MFA check enforces ENROLMENT, not authentication — an admin who is enrolled must still pass TOTP at login (admin-auth.service.ts:63-71 defers `recordSuccess` to the controller's post-TOTP path), and support-key redemption independently requires `mfaEnabled`. Low held.

title: The applicant-PII CSV export is behind AdminRolesGuard but carries no @AdminRoles, so any admin tier can pull it
what: `GET /admin/applications.csv` is annotated `@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard, AdminRolesGuard)` with no `@AdminRoles(...)`. `AdminRolesGuard.canActivate` returns `true` immediately when no roles metadata is present (admin-roles.guard.ts:36), so the guard is a no-op here and the route is open to every authenticated admin including `support` tier. Every other owner-sensitive admin route in the tree (`admin/tenants/:id/delete`, `admin/exports`, `admin/plans/*`, `admin/system-mode/*`, `admin/subscriptions`, `admin/announcements/*`, `admin/library-requests/*/approve`) does carry `@AdminRoles('owner')`; the sibling admin export controller (`export/admin-export.controller.ts:64-65`) gates its download at owner. The CSV contains `contact_name`, `contact_email`, `phone`, `library_name`, `city` and free-text `message` for every prospect that used the public application form.
impact: Whole prospect list, with names, emails and phone numbers, exportable by the lowest admin tier. Minor at current headcount but it is a full personal-data export with no owner gate and no audit row, which is exactly the kind of thing a GDPR access review flags.
evidence: READ applications.controller.ts:117-118 (guards present, no `@AdminRoles`) plus admin-roles.guard.ts:36 (`if (!required || required.length === 0) return true;`). Cross-checked against the full route enumeration: every other mutating or PII-exporting admin route in the codebase names `@AdminRoles('owner')`.
fix: Add `@AdminRoles('owner')` to `exportCsv`, matching `admin-export.controller.ts`. Consider making `AdminRolesGuard` fail closed on `/admin/*` routes that lack metadata, so the default is restrictive rather than open.
verification: CONFIRMED by execution. READ applications.controller.ts:117-118 — `@Get('admin/applications.csv') @UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard, AdminRolesGuard)` with no `@AdminRoles(...)`, and admin-roles.guard.ts:36 `if (!required || required.length === 0) return true;` makes the second guard a no-op. RAN: created a `support`-tier admin, logged in, `GET /admin/applications.csv` → **200** returning 1,970 bytes of CSV containing `contact_name`, `contact_email`, `phone`, `city` and free-text `message` for every prospect. (Incidental, same request set: `GET /admin/exports` also returns 200 to support tier — only the download in admin-export.controller.ts:64-65 is owner-gated. Reported here as context, not as a separate finding.) Low held: real personal-data exposure, but only to an already-authenticated Libriant admin.

title: The go-live doc's webhook step can be completed successfully while nothing is actually wired: the one event a reader would naturally subscribe to is a deliberate no-op
what: Step 3 says: point the endpoint at /webhooks/stripe, 'Send a test event and confirm a 200'. It never lists which events the endpoint must be subscribed to. The controller acts on customer.subscription.created/updated/deleted and invoice.payment_succeeded/failed, and explicitly ignores checkout.session.completed — the event whose name most obviously matches 'someone subscribed'. Every unlisted type falls to the default branch and is logged at debug. The doc also never mentions saving a Customer Portal configuration in the Stripe dashboard, without which billingPortal.sessions.create fails for every tenant that clicks 'Open portal'.
impact: An operator who subscribes the endpoint to checkout.session.completed alone gets a 200 on the test event, sees a green tick in Stripe, and ships. Libraries then pay and nothing provisions: no plan change, no status, no grace handling — and the failure is silent because the ignored event is logged at debug level. The portal button 500s on first use for everyone.
evidence: READ. docs/billing-go-live.md step 3 in full: 'Stripe → Developers → Webhooks → https://app.libriant.com/webhooks/stripe. Send a test event and confirm a 200 in dc logs api.' No event list, no portal configuration step. stripe-webhook.controller.ts:144-147 returns immediately for checkout.session.completed; :148-149 logs unknown types at debug.
fix: List the five required event types verbatim in the doc and add a startup/health check that reports which of them have been seen at least once. Add the Customer Portal configuration step. Consider handling checkout.session.completed properly rather than relying on ordering (it also fixes billing-09).
verification: CONFIRMED as written, downgraded to low. docs/billing-go-live.md step 3 reads in full 'Stripe -> Developers -> Webhooks -> https://app.libriant.com/webhooks/stripe. Send a test event and confirm a 200 in dc logs api.' — no event list, no portal configuration step; and stripe-webhook.controller.ts:144-147 does return immediately for checkout.session.completed while :148-149 logs unknown types at debug. Downgraded because the harm requires a specific operator mistake the doc does not induce, and the doc's own Verify section ends by taking one plan all the way through Stripe test mode, which would expose an endpoint subscribed to the wrong events. The load-bearing half is the omission the finding mentions almost in passing: Stripe's billingPortal.sessions.create fails in live mode until a portal configuration is saved in the dashboard, and nothing in the doc says to save one.

title: The doc's own pre-flight check — 'check no existing tenant is already over its cap' — cannot be performed in production
what: The doc tells the operator to verify no tenant is over its cap before enabling enforcement, and in the very next bullet concedes that GET /t/:slug/plan/usage sits behind NonProductionOnlyGuard. That guard is the first in the chain (plan-demo.controller.ts:72), so the endpoint 404s in production. There is no admin-side equivalent — `grep -rn 'plan/usage' apps` finds only that controller — and no bulk query, so the doc asks for a check the product does not offer and supplies no SQL to do it by hand.
impact: Enforcement is switched on blind. Every tenant that grew past a Starter cap during the free period discovers it as a 402 in the middle of a task on Monday morning, with no usage screen to explain why (the same guard hides that from them too).
evidence: READ. plan-demo.controller.ts:68-72 — 'NonProductionOnlyGuard MUST run first so prod requests 404 before TenantGuard' — followed by @Get('plan/usage') at line 86. No other route serves usage counters.
fix: Add an admin endpoint that lists every tenant whose current counters exceed the caps of the plan they would be enforced against, and reference it from the doc as the pre-flight command. Open the tenant-facing usage endpoint in production so a librarian who is refused can see why.
verification: CONFIRMED the facts, downgraded the severity. plan-demo.controller.ts:72 is `@UseGuards(NonProductionOnlyGuard, TenantGuard, RolesGuard, PlanGuard)` with the comment at :68-69 saying NonProductionOnlyGuard must run first, and `@Get('plan/usage')` at :86 is the only usage route in the repo — `grep -rn "plan/usage|'usage'" apps/api/src` finds nothing else. So the pre-flight check the doc asks for genuinely cannot be run through the product in production. Downgraded because the doc itself discloses the limitation in the very next bullet rather than concealing it, nothing is broken, and the consequence it describes — 402s on Monday morning — is the plan-enforcement dimension's harm, not a billing defect. This is a missing operator tool.

title: The payment-failure banner is hardcoded English on a Greek-first product
what: The past_due banner's title is translated (t('billing.errors.paymentFailed')) but its body is a literal template string: `Your plan stays active until ${fmtDate(snapshot.graceUntil)}.` Every other string on the page goes through the catalog.
impact: The one sentence that tells a Greek librarian how long they have to fix a failed card — the highest-stakes message in the billing screen — appears in English regardless of locale, so the deadline may simply not be read.
evidence: READ, billing/page.tsx:59-61.
fix: Move it to the catalog as billing.errors.paymentFailedGrace with a {date} parameter, in both el and en.
verification: READ-verified at the exact lines. billing/page.tsx:56-62 renders `<Banner title={t('billing.errors.paymentFailed')}>{snapshot.graceUntil ? `Your plan stays active until ${fmtDate(snapshot.graceUntil)}.` : null}</Banner>` — the title goes through the catalog, the body is a bare template literal. Checked for an el override and found none. Low is correct.

title: NODE_ENV is cast, never validated — a typo silently un-gates the dev-only smoke-test controller, honours RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED, and collapses STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET into SESSION_SECRET
what: `const nodeEnv = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') as AppEnv['nodeEnv'];` — a bare cast with no allow-list. Four separate protections key on the string being EXACTLY 'production': main.ts:15 (refuse to boot with RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true), platform/rate-limit.service.ts:67 (ignore the flag), plans/plan-demo.controller.ts:45 (NonProductionOnlyGuard), env.ts:344 (require STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET rather than defaulting it to sessionSecret). Anything else — 'Production', 'prod', 'staging' — is neither dev (so the secrets are still demanded, making it look correctly configured) nor production (so all four protections switch off). And with NODE_ENV unset entirely the process boots with the committed dev fallbacks for SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, IMPERSONATION_SECRET, MFA_MASTER_KEY and HASH_PEPPER.
impact: No impact on the Monday release: NODE_ENV is pinned to 'production' by both apps/api/Dockerfile:83 and the literal at docker-compose.prod.yml:35, and .env.prod cannot override it. The residual is latent: the day someone stands up a second cell with NODE_ENV=staging, the dev-only PlanDemoController (whose own header says POST /demo/books 'performs a REAL, unvalidated book write that bypasses the race-safe quota authority') becomes reachable, RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED starts being honoured, and STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET silently falls back to SESSION_SECRET.
evidence: EXECUTED. Booted the API against the live audit env and probed a real seeded tenant slug. NODE_ENV=production: `GET /t/probes1-x9/plan` → 404, `/plan/usage` → 404 (NonProductionOnlyGuard firing). NODE_ENV=Production: → 401, 401. NODE_ENV=staging: → 401, 401 (guard passed; only authentication is left). Also executed: `NODE_ENV=Production` with STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET unset → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200 (production refuses: 'Missing required env var: STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET'). Also executed: `NODE_ENV=staging RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true` → BOOTED_OK (production exits 1 with 'refusing to boot').
