Also executed: NODE_ENV unset with SESSION_SECRET/ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET/IMPERSONATION_SECRET/MFA_MASTER_KEY/HASH_PEPPER/STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET all unset → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200.
fix: In loadEnv(), validate: `const raw = process.env.NODE_ENV; if (raw !== undefined && !['development','production','test'].includes(raw)) throw new Error(...)`. Better still, require NODE_ENV to be set explicitly outside of local dev rather than defaulting to 'development'. Then replace the `!== 'production'` checks with a single `isProduction` derived once.
verification: Mechanism confirmed, stated impact REFUTED for the shipped deploy path; severity drops high -> low. env.ts:223 is indeed a bare cast (`const nodeEnv = (process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') as AppEnv['nodeEnv'];`) with no allow-list, and the four `=== 'production'` / `!== 'production'` checks are where the finding says (main.ts:15, rate-limit.service.ts:67, plan-demo.controller.ts:45, env.ts:344). BUT the guard the auditor did not look for is that NODE_ENV is never operator-supplied: `grep -n NODE_ENV infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml apps/api/Dockerfile scripts/ensure-env.sh scripts/deploy-on-host.sh` gives apps/api/Dockerfile:83 `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, docker-compose.prod.yml:35 `NODE_ENV: production` (a LITERAL inside x-app-env, not `${NODE_ENV:-...}`) and :240 the same for web. ensure-env.sh never writes NODE_ENV, so nothing in .env.prod can override it — Compose's literal wins over the image ENV and both say `production`. Therefore 'NODE_ENV unset -> committed dev secrets' and "NODE_ENV='staging' -> PlanDemoController reachable / RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED honoured / STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET collapses into SESSION_SECRET" cannot occur in any deployment this repo produces; the auditor reached them only by setting NODE_ENV by hand outside the deploy path. Note also that under 'staging' requiredSecret() still takes the non-dev branch, so the secrets are still demanded, and cookieSecure (env.ts:255) already special-cases 'any env other than development/test'. What survives is a genuine hardening gap with defence-in-depth value if a staging cell is ever added.

title: CONTROL_DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, PG_SUPERUSER_URL and STORAGE_ROOT are optional() with production-shaped localhost defaults; a missing PG_SUPERUSER_URL boots fully green
what: Four values the app cannot function without are read with `optional()` and a hard-coded fallback: CONTROL_DATABASE_URL → `postgresql://libriant:libriant@localhost:5432/libriant_control`, REDIS_URL → `redis://localhost:6379`, PG_SUPERUSER_URL → the same localhost superuser URL with credentials `libriant:libriant`, STORAGE_ROOT → `/srv/libriant/storage`. The file's own header says 'every value we depend on is either present + valid, or boot fails loudly'; these four are the exceptions. PG_SUPERUSER_URL is the worst case because nothing in the startup or readiness path touches it — it is only used at tenant-signup time to CREATE DATABASE and to derive every tenant's connection URL.
impact: No production path can reach the fallbacks — compose hard-codes all four. The residual is defence-in-depth: anything running the API outside compose (a host-level `pnpm start`, a future non-compose orchestrator, a one-off script) silently gets localhost URLs and the guessable libriant/libriant superuser credentials instead of a loud failure, and PG_SUPERUSER_URL specifically is touched by nothing in the startup or readiness path so the mistake would only surface at the first tenant signup.
evidence: EXECUTED, one variable at a time, NODE_ENV=production against the live audit Postgres/Redis. `unset PG_SUPERUSER_URL` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200. `unset STORAGE_ROOT` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200. `unset CONTROL_DATABASE_URL` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=503. `unset REDIS_URL` → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=500. By contrast every secret fails loudly: SESSION_SECRET / ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET / IMPERSONATION_SECRET / MFA_MASTER_KEY / HASH_PEPPER / STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET each exit rc=1 with 'Missing required env var: <NAME>'.
fix: Make all four `required()` when nodeEnv !== 'development'. Keep the localhost strings as dev-only fallbacks the same way the secrets do it. For STORAGE_ROOT additionally assert at boot that the directory exists and is writable (see boot-and-config-12).
verification: Code claim confirmed, stated impact REFUTED for the deploy path; severity drops medium -> low. env.ts:265-270 and :334-337 do use optional() with those exact production-shaped localhost fallbacks, and I reproduced the fail-loud contrast (unset SESSION_SECRET -> 'Missing required env var: SESSION_SECRET', unset STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET -> same, PORT=abc -> 'must be a number', MFA_MASTER_KEY=deadbeef -> 'must be 64 hex characters'). But the guard the auditor missed is that all four are LITERALS in the compose env block, not operator-supplied: `grep -n 'PG_SUPERUSER_URL|STORAGE_ROOT|CONTROL_DATABASE_URL|REDIS_URL' infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` gives :36 CONTROL_DATABASE_URL, :37 `REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379`, :52 `STORAGE_ROOT: /srv/libriant/storage`, :87 PG_SUPERUSER_URL — none of them `${...}`-optional except the embedded ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}, which is itself `:?POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required` at :317 and :344, so compose aborts the whole `up` rather than interpolating empty. The headline scenario — 'a missing PG_SUPERUSER_URL boots fully green and then does DDL against localhost with libriant/libriant at first signup' — therefore has no path through any deployment this repo produces, including the bare `docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d` at compose:16, which still applies x-app-env. What remains is a real but purely defensive inconsistency with the file's own 'present + valid, or boot fails loudly' header.

title: PUBLIC_HOST's default disagrees between two blocks of the same compose file and the Caddyfile — an unset value points the browser's API base at the marketing site
where: infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:38 and :68 and :247-248 (default `libriant.com`) vs :141 and infra/caddy/Caddyfile:149 (default `app.libriant.com`)
what: x-app-env builds `PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}` and `BILLING_RETURN_URL` the same way; the web service gets `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`. The caddy service block and the Caddyfile both default the same variable to `app.libriant.com`, and ensure-env.sh:105 writes `PUBLIC_HOST=app.libriant.com`. So with PUBLIC_HOST unset, Caddy serves the app vhost at app.libriant.com while the app and the browser bundle believe the app lives at libriant.com — which is the SITE_HOST vhost (Caddyfile:253), a marketing-site vhost that proxies only /apply to the API.
impact: Browser-side calls to https://libriant.com/lbr-api/* land on the marketing vhost and 404; the panel loads its shell and then fails on every data fetch. Password-reset and billing-return links point at the marketing site. Every container healthcheck stays green throughout. The compose file's own header (line 16) documents `docker compose -f infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml up -d` as a valid way to bring the stack up — that invocation, with a partially-populated env file, produces exactly this.
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:38 `PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`, :141 `PUBLIC_HOST: ${PUBLIC_HOST:-app.libriant.com}`, :247 `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`; infra/caddy/Caddyfile:149 `{$PUBLIC_HOST:app.libriant.com}` vs :253 `{$SITE_HOST:libriant.com}`; scripts/ensure-env.sh:105 `ensure_default PUBLIC_HOST app.libriant.com`.
fix: Make PUBLIC_HOST mandatory in compose (`${PUBLIC_HOST:?PUBLIC_HOST is required}`), exactly as SESSION_SECRET and HASH_PEPPER already are — there is no safe default for it now that the app and the site are different hosts.
verification: Contradiction confirmed exactly; reachability is narrower than stated, so severity drops medium -> low. Verified line by line: docker-compose.prod.yml:38 `PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`, :68 `BILLING_RETURN_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}`, :247-248 `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`/`PUBLIC_APP_URL: https://${PUBLIC_HOST:-libriant.com}` versus :141 `PUBLIC_HOST: ${PUBLIC_HOST:-app.libriant.com}` in the caddy block and infra/caddy/Caddyfile:149 `{$PUBLIC_HOST:app.libriant.com}` / :253 `{$SITE_HOST:libriant.com}`. The consequence is also confirmed: Caddyfile:247-250 documents that the SITE_HOST vhost deliberately has NO `handle_path /lbr-api/*` block, so browser calls to https://libriant.com/lbr-api/* really would 404. BUT the value is set on every real deploy — scripts/ensure-env.sh:105 `ensure_default PUBLIC_HOST app.libriant.com`, and ensure-env.sh --auto runs before compose in both deploy paths (deploy-on-host.sh:97, .github/workflows/deploy.yml:281). Reaching the bad default requires bringing the stack up by hand, bypassing ensure-env.sh, with an env file complete enough to satisfy the five `:?`-required secrets yet missing PUBLIC_HOST. That is a real trap for a future operator but not a Monday failure mode.

title: Billing flags are not cross-validated and are not echoed at boot: BILLING_ENABLED=true with STRIPE_DRIVER=fake starts silently, and BILLING_ENABLED='enabled' silently means false
what: billingEnabled and stripeDriver are resolved independently with no consistency check. `BILLING_ENABLED=true` + `STRIPE_DRIVER=fake` boots with plan/quota enforcement ON and the in-memory FakeStripeDriver behind every checkout and portal call, with no warning logged. Separately, bool() accepts only true/1/yes/on (case-insensitive), so a plausible operator value such as `BILLING_ENABLED=enabled` or `=y` resolves to false — i.e. the entire product becomes free — again with nothing logged.
impact: Not a fleet-wide silent-free-tier risk — the platform_settings row overrides env and the launch default is false either way. The real residual: enforcement can be switched on (via BILLING_ENABLED=true in .env.prod OR via the admin Subscriptions toggle) while STRIPE_DRIVER is still `fake`, with nothing in either path warning, so plan limits are enforced against paying customers whose checkout and portal calls go to the in-memory FakeStripeDriver and collect no money.
evidence: EXECUTED. Booted with BILLING_ENABLED=true STRIPE_DRIVER=fake under NODE_ENV=production → RESULT: BOOTED_OK readyz=200; `grep -ci warn` over the full boot log returned 0, and no log line mentions billing state, the resolved Stripe driver, or the email driver. Also executed: BILLING_ENABLED=TRUE → boots (lower-cased to true); BILLING_ENABLED=enabled → boots, silently false. The only boot line the process emits about its configuration is main.ts:61 `[libriant-api] listening on :3001 (production)`.
fix: In loadEnv(), throw when billingEnabled && stripeDriver === 'fake' outside development. Make bool() reject any value that is not in a known true/false allow-list rather than silently treating unknown strings as false. And log one INFO line at boot with the resolved effective configuration (nodeEnv, emailDriver, stripeDriver, billingEnabled, adminMfaRequired, sessionCookieSecure, control DB host, redis host, storageRoot) — no secrets.
verification: Two of the three sub-claims survive only weakly; the headline impact is REFUTED by a guard the auditor did not find, so severity drops medium -> low. The env resolution is as described (env.ts:214-218 bool() accepts only true/1/yes/on; :366 `billingEnabled: bool('BILLING_ENABLED', false)`; :352-359 stripeDriver resolved independently). BUT env.BILLING_ENABLED is NOT the switch: apps/api/src/platform-settings/platform-settings.service.ts:32-39 reads a platform_settings DB row and only falls back to `loadEnv().billingEnabled` when the row is absent (`const value = row ? row.value === 'true' : loadEnv().billingEnabled;`), and every consumer goes through it — effective-plan.service.ts:110, billing.service.ts:130/162/178, desktop.controller.ts:50. env.ts:361-363 says so in a comment the finding quoted around. The authoritative control is the owner-only admin toggle at platform-settings/admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:34-56, which audit-logs the change. So "BILLING_ENABLED='enabled' silently means false and removes every plan limit across the fleet" does not hold: the default is false anyway, and once anyone touches the admin toggle the env var is inert. What survives is genuine: nothing cross-validates enforcement-on against STRIPE_DRIVER=fake — and note this is reachable through the ADMIN TOGGLE too, not just env, since admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:34-56 checks nothing about the resolved driver before flipping enforcement on. The third sub-claim (no boot-time echo of resolved configuration) is an observability preference, not a defect.

title: /readyz's per-dependency detail is swallowed by the global exception filter, so the readiness probe cannot say what is broken
what: readiness() builds `{status, dependencies: {redis, controlDb}}` and throws it as a ServiceUnavailableException. The global HttpExceptionFilter re-skins 5xx responses into a generic envelope, so the body the operator actually receives is `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end...","supportCode":"..."}` — the dependencies map is gone. Related: compose uses `restart: unless-stopped`, which does not restart a container merely because its healthcheck is failing, so an api stuck 'unhealthy' stays up serving errors indefinitely.
impact: The probe response is diagnostically useless and mislabels a dependency outage as InternalServerError, so an operator reading only the HTTP body cannot tell Postgres from Redis. Cost is one extra log grep (the dependency map is already logged against the same supportCode), not an inability to diagnose.
evidence: EXECUTED. With CONTROL_DATABASE_URL pointed at a dead port: `curl /readyz` → `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end. We've logged it. Please try again, or send us this code if it keeps happening: CIOW15V0","supportCode":"CIOW15V0"}` [503]. The `dependencies` object built at health.controller.ts:44 never reaches the client.
fix: Exempt /healthz, /readyz and /metrics from HttpExceptionFilter (or return the 503 body directly with res.status(503).json(body) instead of throwing), so the probe response carries the dependency map.
verification: Mechanism reproduced; impact materially overstated, so severity drops medium -> low. RE-EXECUTED: booted with CONTROL_DATABASE_URL pointed at dead port 55999 and Redis alive. `curl /healthz` -> 200 `{"status":"ok",...}`; `curl /readyz` -> 503 `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong...","supportCode":"C88WNULU"}` — the `dependencies` map is indeed absent from the client body, and the label really does say InternalServerError for a dependency outage. BUT the claim that the operator 'has to shell into the container and read logs' understates what the logs already give: http-exception.filter.ts:80-99 logs `declaredBody` on the SAME one-line JSON record as the supportCode, and I grepped it out of the run: `declaredBody":{"status":"not_ready","dependencies":{"redis":true,"controlDb":false}}`. So the dependency map IS emitted to stdout, greppable by the support code the caller already has — a `docker compose logs api | grep C88WNULU` away, not a debugging dead end. The mislabelled `error` field and the lost probe body remain real papercuts worth the one-line fix. The `restart: unless-stopped` sub-remark is accurate but is a separate observation, not part of this defect.

title: The web container mounts locales at /srv/libriant/locales but is never told where they are — the mount is inert and the legal/i18n content depends on an unverified in-image path
what: x-app-env sets `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` for api/worker/migrate. The web service defines its own environment block (compose merges nothing into it) and omits LOCALES_ROOT, while still bind-mounting `../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro`. apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts:9 and apps/web/lib/legal.ts:21 both do `process.env.LOCALES_ROOT?.trim() || REPO_LOCALES`, where REPO_LOCALES is `path.resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..','..','..','locales')` — a path resolved relative to the compiled server chunk, not to the source file.
impact: The read-only locales mount does nothing for the web container: editing /srv/libriant/locales on the host changes no rendered string or legal document. All localized copy and all seven legal documents are served from whatever REPO_LOCALES happens to resolve to inside the built image; if that resolution moves with a Next build-output change, the legal pages 404 and the i18n loader throws on a file read, with no configuration knob to correct it. The same code in the API is protected by LOCALES_ROOT; web is not.
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:55 vs the web block at :239-251 (no LOCALES_ROOT) and its volumes at :255-257 (`../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro`); apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts:7-9; apps/web/lib/legal.ts:19-21; apps/web/Dockerfile copies `locales` into /app at build time, so the in-image copy is at /app/locales.
fix: Add `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` (and ASSETS_ROOT, which the web service also mounts but does not declare) to the web service's environment block, so both containers resolve content the same way and the bind mount is real.
verification: Confirmed as written, with one speculative clause disproved. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:55 sets `LOCALES_ROOT: /srv/libriant/locales` in x-app-env (api/worker/migrate only); the web service at :239-253 declares its own `environment:` block with NODE_ENV/PORT/NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED/API_INTERNAL_URL/NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL/PUBLIC_APP_URL/ADMIN_HOST and no LOCALES_ROOT or ASSETS_ROOT, while :255-257 bind-mounts `../../locales:/srv/libriant/locales:ro` and `../../assets:/srv/libriant/assets:ro`. apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts:7-9 and apps/web/lib/legal.ts:19-21 both fall back to REPO_LOCALES. So the two read-only mounts on the web container are genuinely inert. DISPROVED the finding's speculative half: I inspected the actual build output (apps/web/.next/server/chunks/'[root-of-the-server]__1913mvv._.js') and Turbopack preserves the SOURCE path in the runtime module URL — `fileURLToPath({get url(){return e.F("apps/web/lib/locale-loader.ts")}}.url)` — so REPO_LOCALES resolves to <root>/locales, i.e. /app/locales, which apps/web/Dockerfile:40 does populate. Content is served correctly today; the fear that a build-output change silently 404s the legal pages is a possibility, not a present defect. Low upheld: the concrete harm is that editing /srv/libriant/locales on the host changes nothing for web, and web and api can drift apart because only one of them honours the mount.

title: Postgres is started with LANG=el_GR.UTF-8 on an Alpine (musl) image that has no such locale
what: `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` is set on the postgres service. The alpine variant is built against musl, which ships no locale definitions; setlocale() accepts any name and behaves as C. initdb therefore records lc_collate/lc_ctype as el_GR.UTF-8 in pg_control while the actual collation behaviour is byte order.
impact: Two consequences. Greek text ordering (ORDER BY on titles, author names, member surnames) is byte order rather than Greek collation, so accented and uppercase forms sort wrongly in a product whose entire market is Greek libraries. More seriously, the cluster carries a collation label that is a lie: if the data directory or a base backup is ever brought up on a glibc-based Postgres — a plausible DR or migration path — the recorded collation becomes real and every text btree index built under the C behaviour is silently inconsistent with it, which is the classic collation-change index-corruption scenario.
evidence: READ (docker is not installed in this audit environment, so initdb's behaviour on this exact image could not be executed). docker-compose.prod.yml:306-319; the audit environment's own setup script sidesteps the question by using `--locale=C` (docs/audit/pre-release-2026-08-23/env/setup-audit-env.sh:22), so no local cluster reproduces the production locale.
fix: Either move to the Debian-based `postgres:16` image and keep el_GR.UTF-8 (locales are generated there), or drop LANG and initdb with `--locale-provider=icu --icu-locale=el-GR` so the collation is provided by ICU rather than the C library and travels with the data. Decide before the first real cluster is created — this cannot be changed in place without a reindex.
verification: Could not execute — `command -v docker` returns nothing on this machine, so initdb's behaviour on postgres:16-alpine was not observed; this stays a read-only finding and its 'medium' confidence is the right label. Verified the facts that are checkable here: docker-compose.prod.yml:307 `image: postgres:16-alpine` and :319 `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` in the postgres service environment, with the cluster created by the entrypoint's initdb on first start; the audit environment's own bootstrap sidesteps the question (docs/audit/pre-release-2026-08-23/env/setup-audit-env.sh:22 passes `--locale=C`), so nothing in this repo exercises the production locale. The reasoning stands on a property of the image rather than of this code — musl ships no locale definitions, so the name is accepted and behaves as C — and the two consequences (byte-order sorting for Greek titles/author names/member surnames in a Greek-only product, and a pg_control collation label that becomes real and index-inconsistent if the data directory or a base backup is ever restored onto a glibc Postgres) both follow. Low upheld, but flagged as decide-before-first-cluster: it cannot be changed in place without a full reindex.

title: The pgbouncer healthcheck proves only that the pooler accepts connections, and nothing depends on it being healthy anyway
what: `pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432 -U libriant` against pgbouncer. pg_isready reports 'accepting connections' as soon as the pooler answers a startup packet — it never reaches Postgres, so the probe passes while the backend behind the pool is unreachable. Meanwhile api declares `pgbouncer: condition: service_started`, not service_healthy, so the health status is not consumed by anything.
impact: The one component the control plane's every query passes through has a healthcheck that cannot go red for the failure that matters, and a result nothing reads. Diagnosing a control-plane outage starts one step further back than it should. (The api's own /readyz does catch the resulting failure, which is why this is low rather than higher.)
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:355-359 and :207-215; x-app-env:36 routes CONTROL_DATABASE_URL through `pgbouncer:5432`.
fix: Probe through the pooler to the backend, e.g. `psql "postgresql://libriant:$DB_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/libriant_control" -c 'select 1'`, and change api's depends_on to `pgbouncer: condition: service_healthy`.
verification: Confirmed, and it is as inconsequential as the finding itself concedes. Verified: docker-compose.prod.yml:355-359 `test: ['CMD-SHELL','pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432 -U libriant']` on the pgbouncer service (pgbouncer answers the startup packet itself, so this never reaches Postgres); :210-211 `pgbouncer: condition: service_started` in api's depends_on, so nothing consumes the health status; :36 routes CONTROL_DATABASE_URL through `pgbouncer:5432`. Also checked the deploy gate — deploy-on-host.sh:181 asserts api/web/worker only, never pgbouncer — which confirms the status is read by nothing at all. Kept at low rather than promoted or dropped: the api's own deep `/readyz` (compose:223) does catch the underlying failure, so the only cost is that `docker compose ps` shows a green pooler during a control-plane outage. One-line fix, near-zero risk of it ever waking anyone up.

title: The import pipeline enforces `max_books`/`max_members` from a private in-memory counter outside the advisory-lock domain every other path uses
what: Every other create path routes through `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx` (quota.service.ts:62-65), which takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('quota:<tenant>:<feature>:<ctx>')` as the first statement of the caller's transaction and counts inside it. The import engine does not join that lock domain: `init()` snapshots the live count once, resolves the limit once via `ctx.getLimit`, and then decides per row from `this.quotaUsed`. The API process and the worker enforce the same ceiling against two non-communicating views.
impact: A tenant can end up over its plan ceiling by roughly the number of manual creates that land during an import. No data is corrupted and nothing is billed wrongly — plans are flat-rate, not usage-metered — so the practical cost is a tenant sitting a handful of rows above a limit until someone notices.
evidence: READ: import-engine.ts:143-152 seeds `quotaUsed` from a single `count()` in `init()`; line 152 resolves `quotaLimit` once; `quotaBlocked` at 203-215 compares only against those two in-memory fields; the only `pg_advisory_xact_lock` in the file is at line 651 for reservation queue positions. Contrast quota.service.ts:62-65, which is the locked path all ten UI call sites use.
verification: The mechanism is real and I confirmed it by reading — but the severity and most of the stated impact do not survive. (1) The finding calls the overshoot 'unbounded in principle'. It is not: the import worker runs `concurrency: 1` platform-wide (import-worker.ts:263), so no second import can race, and the engine's own counter still stops it at the ceiling. The only writers that can slip past are manual UI creates landing inside the import window — bounded by staff throughput, i.e. single digits. (2) The finding's 'sharp reading' — that libraries will load catalogues of arbitrary size today and be silently over quota when billing flips on — is NOT caused by this bug. That is caused by `unlimitedPlan` (effective-plan.service.ts:46-57) raising every int limit to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for EVERY path while billing is off; fixing the import's lock domain would change nothing about it. Attributing that consequence here inflates the finding. (3) Nothing is corrupted and nobody is under-billed, because subscriptions are flat-rate per plan rather than per row. Downgraded from high to low: a real architectural inconsistency worth closing, not something that wakes anyone.
fix: Have `commitBook`/`commitMember` call `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx` inside the same `$transaction` as the row insert, on the same `quota:<tenantId>:<featureKey>` key the UI uses, and delete the `quotaUsed`/`quotaLimit` fields. Cost is one advisory lock per imported row on a key that only serialises import rows against each other, which is free given concurrency 1.

title: Member archive and hold placement use different lock domains, so a member can be archived while acquiring a live hold
what: `MembersService.archive` takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('member:<id>')` and counts open loans AND active reservations inside that transaction. That serialises correctly against `LoansService.checkout`, which takes the same member lock and re-reads the member inside its own transaction. `ReservationsService.place` does neither: it validates `member.archivedAt` / `member.status` at lines 106-122 OUTSIDE any transaction, and its transaction (line 195) takes only `book:<bookId>`. The two paths never mutually exclude.
impact: Produces exactly the state `archive()` exists to prevent — an archived member holding a live hold, which occupies the `reservations_one_active_per_book_member` slot and blocks renewals of that title for everyone. If the queue later promotes it, a physical copy flips to 'reserved' for a member who no longer exists and is stranded until staff cancel the hold by hand.
evidence: READ: reservations.service.ts:106-122 reads and validates the member with a plain `client.member.findUnique` before any transaction is opened; the transaction at line 182-195 issues only `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('book:<bookId>', 0))`. members.service.ts:443 takes `member:<id>` and never touches the book lock. Compare loans.service.ts:229-238, which does take the member lock and re-read inside the transaction — the reservation path is the odd one out.
verification: Mechanism confirmed by reading both transaction bodies; the asymmetry with the loans path is exactly as described. Downgraded from medium to low on reachability: the window is the ~5 round-trips between the member read at line 108 and the transaction commit, on the order of tens of milliseconds, and it requires an archive and a hold placement for the SAME member to collide inside it — two operations a library performs a handful of times a day. The end state is also recoverable without support (staff cancel the hold), unlike the findings above it. Separately, while checking this I found a wider non-race route to the same end state that is NOT part of this finding and belongs to whoever owns the import dimension: `findMemberByNumber` at import-engine.ts:765-773 omits the `archivedAt: null` filter that `findMemberByEmail` at 782-784 has, so importing a reservation keyed on an archived member's number attaches a live hold to an archived member with no concurrency at all.
fix: In `ReservationsService.place`, take `pg_advisory_xact_lock('member:<memberId>')` alongside the existing `book:<bookId>` lock at the top of the transaction and re-read the member's status/archivedAt inside it, mirroring loans.service.ts:229-238. Acquire the two locks in a fixed order (member then book) in both services to avoid deadlock.

title: tenant-relocate lifts the source database's read-only fence before the control-plane cutover and cache bust
what: The script fences the SOURCE database with `ALTER DATABASE ... SET default_transaction_read_only = on` because (its own comment, lines 118-124) admin/impersonation routes and background workers bypass the HTTP read_only middleware and their writes would be excluded from the snapshot. It then lifts that fence at lines 164-172 — before `tenant.dbUrl` is updated (176), before the resolver cache is busted (202) and before the read_only window is closed (205). For that interval the tenant still resolves to the source and the source is writable again.
impact: A background sweep firing in that interval writes to a database that is about to be abandoned; those writes are already outside the pg_dump and are lost at cutover, with no reconciliation step.
evidence: READ scripts/tenant-relocate.ts. Success-path order is pg_dump (136) -> pg_restore (148) -> verifyDestination (155) -> unfenceSource (165) -> control-plane dbUrl update (176) -> bustResolverCache (202) -> closeEvent (205). The comment at 157-162 justifies the early unfence as 'the source is no longer referenced', but at line 165 the control plane still points every request at it.
verification: The ordering claim is exactly right and I confirmed it line by line. Half the stated impact is refuted, and the other half is far narrower than presented. Refuted: 'the same applies to any API process still holding a cached tenant client after the cutover' — `TenantPrismaService.getClient` (tenant-prisma.service.ts:63-74) compares the cached entry's `dbUrl` against the resolved context and rebuilds the client whenever it differs, and the tenant context itself comes from a Redis-backed resolver cache (tenant-resolver.service.ts:106-107) which `bustResolverCache` (tenant-relocate.ts:457-468) deletes, so there is no per-process straggler holding the old URL. Narrowed: the genuine exposure is lines 165 to 202 — one control-plane transaction plus a Redis DEL, tens of milliseconds — and HTTP writes are still blocked by the read_only system mode throughout (closed only at 205), so only a cron worker firing in that exact instant can hit it. Downgraded from medium to low. Worth noting for whoever fixes it: `ALTER DATABASE ... SET` only applies to NEW sessions, so pooled worker connections opened before `fenceSourceReadOnly` are never fenced at all — the ordering is the smaller of the two problems with this fence.
fix: Move the `unfenceSource` call below `closeEvent(modeEvent.id)` and after a drain interval equal to the resolver cache TTL, so the DB-level fence is the last thing removed rather than the first. Keep the failure-path unfence at line 214 where it belongs. Separately, terminate or recycle source connections when fencing, since ALTER DATABASE does not affect open sessions.

title: Stripe subscription webhooks do multi-statement read-modify-write with no transaction or row lock
what: `syncStripeSubscription` reads the current subscription (582), derives `graceUntil` from what it read (630-637), then writes (614) and writes again (643) — four round-trips on the shared `controlDb` client with no `$transaction` and no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. The controller's Redis SETNX dedupes by `event.id` only, so it serialises retries of ONE event but never two distinct events for the same tenant. The stale-replay guard at 601-612 compares `current_period_start`, which is identical for events inside one billing period, so it does not order same-period events.
impact: A lost update on a subscription row: a concurrently-processing event can overwrite a `graceUntil` or `status` another handler just wrote, leaving a paid tenant marked past_due or a delinquent tenant with an open grace window until the next event corrects it.
evidence: READ: billing.service.ts:582 `const existing = await controlDb.subscription.findUnique(...)` and 614 `await controlDb.subscription.update(...)` are separate statements with no wrapper; stripe-webhook.controller.ts:90-96 keys the SETNX on `EVENT_KEY(event.id)`; the dispatch switch at 126-151 takes no per-tenant lock in any branch.
verification: The read-modify-write and the event-id-scoped dedupe are both exactly as described. Downgraded from medium to low on three counts. (1) Unreachable in the shipping configuration: BILLING_ENABLED=false, STRIPE_DRIVER=fake and every price ID is a `price_seed_*` placeholder, so no real Stripe event reaches this code on Monday — it is a latent risk for whenever billing is switched on, which is the right framing for a launch audit. (2) It needs two DISTINCT events for the same tenant to be in flight simultaneously AND to interleave between the read at 582 and the write at 614 — a sub-round-trip window. (3) It is self-correcting: the whole subscription row is re-derived from the payload on every subsequent `customer.subscription.*` event, and Stripe emits those liberally, so a wrong `graceUntil` is overwritten by the next event rather than persisting. The finding's phrase 'directly gates or ungates features for real money' is true of the value but overstates its durability. Confidence on the mechanism is high; confidence that it ever produces a customer-visible wrong state is low.
fix: Wrap each handler body in `controlDb.$transaction` opened with `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('billing:' || tenantId, 0))` — the pattern StaffService.create already uses against the control plane. Additionally persist the Stripe event `created` timestamp on the subscription row and refuse any event older than the last applied one, which orders same-period events that the `current_period_start` guard cannot.

title: `audit_log_retention_days` is priced across five plan tiers but enforced nowhere
what: The tenant schema comment at schema.prisma:563 states retention is 'governed by the tenant's plan (`audit_log_retention_days` feature) and enforced by a background job', and the repricing migration writes five distinct values (7 / 90 / 365 / 1095 / 3650 days). No such job exists, and no read path applies the limit either.
impact: The retention ladder is a phantom differentiator — every tenant keeps unlimited history regardless of plan — and `audit_log` grows without pruning in every tenant database, inflating each pg_dump, relocate and DR restore.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn audit_log_retention_days apps packages scripts` (excluding node_modules and dist) returns only the feature definition at features.ts:113, the six seed values at seed-data.ts:96/126/157/188/218/249, the six migration inserts in 20260822140000_repricing/migration.sql, one site copy reference at apps/site/src/plans.ts:231, and the schema comment — no consumer anywhere. apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts registers nine jobs (support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications, storage-temp-cleanup); none touches audit_log.
verification: The absence is real and I re-derived it independently — the grep returns definitions and seed values only, and the registry list is complete. Downgraded from medium to low because the impact is weaker than stated in every branch. Commercially it is under-delivery in the customer's favour: nobody is harmed by getting more history than they paid for, and no customer can detect it. Operationally, the growth estimate does not hold up for the target workload — a Greek municipal library generating a few thousand auditable changes a month adds single-digit MB a year, which is noise next to the catalogue and cover storage in the same dump. And with BILLING_ENABLED=false, `unlimitedPlan` raises this int to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER for every tenant anyway, so even a shipped job would prune nothing at launch. This is a docs-vs-reality gap and a pricing-page accuracy question, not a data-integrity hazard. The GDPR angle raised in the original impact is out of this dimension and should be judged by the privacy-legal reviewer.
fix: Either add an `audit-log-retention` job to the registry that resolves the feature per active tenant and deletes older `audit_log` rows in bounded batches, or remove the enforcement claim from schema.prisma:563 and the retention row from the pricing page until it ships.

title: Member-number generation runs outside the transaction whose lock its comment claims serialises it
what: The comment at 221-226 says the quota advisory lock 'also serializes member-number assignment'. It does not: `nextSequenceForYear(client, year)` is called at line 249 on the base client, before `createWithQuota` opens the transaction that takes the lock. Concurrent creates read the same max and collide on `members_member_number_unique_active`; the loop at 247 absorbs at most three attempts before surfacing an error. `nextSequenceForYear` (member-numbers.ts:36-50) also loads every member number for the year into memory with an unbounded `findMany`.
impact: With several staff enrolling members at the same moment — a school or municipal enrolment day — a legitimate signup can fail with a 'member number already exists' conflict the librarian never caused. The full scan per attempt also makes each retry slower as the member table grows, widening the collision window rather than narrowing it.
evidence: READ: members.service.ts:249 `const seq = await nextSequenceForYear(client, year);` sits in the retry loop at 247, outside the `client.$transaction` that `createWithQuota` (227-237) opens. member-numbers.ts:8-12 acknowledges the race and prescribes a retry limit of 3, which line 247 implements as `attempt < 3`. member-numbers.ts:40-43 is `findMany` selecting every matching memberNumber with no limit or aggregate.
verification: Confirmed by reading the call ordering: `nextSequenceForYear` takes the base `client`, not the `tx`, and is invoked before `createWithQuota` is called, so no lock is held when the max is read. The comment is simply wrong. Checked whether the retry loop rescues it and it only partly does — each retry re-reads the max, so it converges, but three attempts is a small budget and the error surfaced on exhaustion is `translateCreateError(lastErr)`, i.e. the duplicate-member-number conflict, which is confusing when the librarian typed no number. Severity upheld at low: the collision needs genuine simultaneity, it fails closed (no bad data is written), and the librarian can simply retry.
fix: Move the `nextSequenceForYear` call inside `createWithQuota`'s transaction, after `enforceWithinTx` has taken the `quota:<tenant>:max_members` lock — the number is then assigned under the same serialisation as the insert and the retry loop becomes dead code. Replace the `findMany` with a `SELECT max(...)` over the numeric tail, or keep a per-year sequence row.

title: The nightly `storageUsedBytes` recompute that three code comments name as the drift backstop does not exist
what: `StorageService` maintains a cached byte counter on `tenants.storageUsedBytes` and, at three separate points, justifies best-effort error handling by deferring to a recompute that is never scheduled: line 30 'run nightly in prod', line 113 'the nightly recompute (and `recomputeUsage` below) is the backstop', line 189 'a failure leaves the counter high until the nightly recompute'. `recomputeUsage` (line 208) has exactly one non-test caller.
impact: Every swallowed `releaseReservedBytes` failure (the `.catch` at 199-204 logs and continues) and every driver/DB divergence is permanent. The drift is one-directional — the counter only ever sticks high — so a tenant progressively loses usable storage until uploads return 402 citing a usage figure that does not match what is on disk, with no operator command to correct it.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn recomputeUsage apps scripts` (excluding node_modules/dist) returns the definition at storage.service.ts:208, the three comments at 30/113/189, one unrelated mention in quota-counters.ts:44 and local-driver.ts:177, and exactly one call site: storage-demo.controller.ts:181. apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts registers nine jobs, including `storage-temp-cleanup`, but nothing that calls recomputeUsage.
verification: Re-derived the grep independently; the single demo-controller call site is the whole of it, and the registry list is complete. Checked that the drift direction claim holds: `releaseReservedBytes` (188-204) is the only decrement path and its failure is swallowed by `.catch`, while the reservation at 74-79 is a hard `$executeRaw` whose failure propagates — so the counter can be left high but never low, exactly as claimed. Severity upheld at low: it takes repeated control-plane write failures to accumulate meaningful drift, and the failure mode is a conservative over-count rather than a quota bypass. Note the interaction with data-integrity-01 — while billing is off no upload succeeds at all, so no drift accrues until that is fixed.
fix: Register a nightly `storage-usage-recompute` job that walks active tenants and calls `recomputeUsage`, or delete the three comments and make `releaseReservedBytes` failures loud instead of best-effort.

title: Library brand colour is accepted with no contrast check, so a library can make every primary button white-on-yellow at 1.4:1
what: The branding endpoint validates `brandColor` against `HEX` and nothing else. The chosen value is injected as `--color-primary` on `.lbr-shell`, but `--color-primary-fg` stays `#ffffff` (packages/ui/src/styles.css: `.lbr-btn--primary { background: var(--color-primary); color: var(--color-primary-fg) }`). `--color-primary` is also used as *text* on light backgrounds (`.lbr-nav__link--active`, `.lbr-toast__action`, `.lbr-landing__locale--active`). The settings form is a free `<input type="color">` with no preview warning — grepping the file for `contrast|luminance|warn` returns nothing.
impact: A library owner picking their institutional colour — yellow, light teal, light green are all common — silently makes every Save / Check out / Confirm button unreadable for every member of staff, permanently, with no warning and no automatic correction. `#ffffff` is a valid hex and yields 1.0:1, i.e. invisible buttons.
evidence: READ: branding.controller.ts:43-47 — the only check is `HEX.test(body.brandColor)`. RAN a WCAG relative-luminance computation on plausible picks against the fixed white foreground: `#ffd60a` → **1.41:1**, `#f4c542` → 1.63:1, `#4cc9f0` → 1.92:1, `#90ee90` → 1.42:1, `#ffffff` → 1.00:1 (AA requires 4.5:1 for the button label, 3:1 for the control boundary). RAN: `grep -n 'contrast|luminance|warn' BrandingForm.tsx` → no matches.
fix: Compute the contrast of the picked colour against both `#ffffff` and `#0d1117` server-side; reject (or auto-flip `--color-primary-fg` to the dark token) when the chosen pairing falls below 4.5:1, and show a live warning plus a rendered button preview in `BrandingForm` before the librarian saves.
verification: MECHANISM CONFIRMED, SEVERITY CUT. apps/api/src/branding/branding.controller.ts:43-47 really does validate only `HEX.test(body.brandColor)`; layout.tsx:184-186 injects it as --color-primary on .lbr-shell; packages/ui/src/styles.css:76-79 keeps `.lbr-btn--primary { background: var(--color-primary); color: var(--color-primary-fg) }` with --color-primary-fg fixed at white. I re-ran the luminance maths and reproduce the numbers (#ffd60a -> 1.41:1, #ffffff -> 1.00:1). But the harm is self-inflicted, immediately visible, and reversible by the same owner in the same form — they pick a colour, see the result on the next render, and can pick another. That is a missing guard-rail, not a defect that hurts someone who did nothing wrong. Low.

title: The offline page and the 404 page are English-only, and the 404 declares lang="en"
where: apps/web/public/offline.html:2 and :~230 ('You're offline', 'Try again'); apps/web/app/not-found.tsx:13 (`<html lang="en">`), :29 ('This page could not be found.'), :31 ('Go to Libriant')
what: `offline.html` is precached by the service worker (sw.js:66) and served as the navigation fallback whenever the network is gone and no cached copy of the page exists. It is hardcoded English with `<html lang="en">`. `not-found.tsx` is the document for every unmatched URL and for the `notFound()` thrown by `app/[locale]/layout.tsx` on an unsupported locale; it is also hardcoded English with `lang="en"`, and it is self-contained by design, so it cannot pick up the catalogue the way other pages do.
impact: These are the two pages users hit when something has already gone wrong — the worst moment to switch language on them. The offline page in particular is the PWA's whole offline story for an audience that does not read English. The wrong `lang` attribute also makes a screen reader read Greek-market content with an English voice/pronunciation on the 404.
evidence:
READ: apps/web/public/offline.html — ``, `

You're offline

`, `

Libriant can't reach the network right now…

`, ``. READ: apps/web/app/not-found.tsx in full. Confirmed the 404 markup in the live RSC payload from the running production build (`"lang":"en" … "This page could not be found." … "Go to Libriant"`).
fix: Ship both languages inline in `offline.html` and pick with `navigator.language` in a two-line script (it must stay dependency-free). For `not-found.tsx`, move the 404 under `app/[locale]/not-found.tsx` so it can load the catalogue, and keep the root one as a bilingual last resort with the correct `lang`.
verification: CONFIRMED, SEVERITY CUT FOR CONSISTENCY. apps/web/public/offline.html line 2 is `<html lang="en">` and contains 'You're offline' / 'can't reach the network' / 'Try again'; apps/web/app/not-found.tsx:13 is `<html lang="en">` with 'This page could not be found.' and 'Go to Libriant', and it is the only not-found in the tree so it also serves locale routes. All true. But these are two auxiliary pages of a handful of words each, reached rarely (offline.html only for an offline navigation to a page absent from PAGES_CACHE). Applying the same rule used across this dimension — localization gaps in flows every user hits are medium, gaps on rarely-hit auxiliary pages are low — this is low.

title: Critical errors are announced politely by a live region that is created at the same instant as its content, so screen readers commonly announce nothing
where: packages/ui/src/Banner.tsx:24 (`role="status" aria-live="polite"` regardless of severity); apps/web/app/[locale]/login/LoginForm.tsx:76-80 (conditionally mounted); packages/ui/src/Toast.tsx:74 (`role="region" aria-live="polite"`, unnamed)
what: `Banner` hardcodes `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"` for all four severities, including `critical`. Every consumer mounts it conditionally — e.g. `{errors.form ? <Banner severity="critical">…</Banner> : null}` on the login form, and the same pattern on the loans, plans, support-access and announcement pages. A live region that is inserted into the DOM already containing its text is not reliably announced by NVDA, JAWS or VoiceOver; the region has to exist and then be mutated. There is also no focus move to the message. The toast stack is a `role="region"` with no accessible name and `aria-live="polite"` for `critical` toasts too.
impact: A screen-reader user who submits the login form with a wrong password gets, in the common case, no feedback at all: focus stays on the submit button and the error is neither spoken nor focused. The same applies to every page-level fetch error banner and every critical toast (including the offline-queue 'this action was lost' messages from finding-06).
evidence: READ: Banner.tsx:24 — `<div role="status" aria-live="polite" ...>` with no branch on `severity`. READ: LoginForm.tsx:76-80 — the Banner is rendered only when `errors.form` is set, i.e. node and text appear together; `handleSubmit` (line 63-70) sets the error and never moves focus. READ: Toast.tsx:74.
fix: Use `role="alert"` (implicit `aria-live="assertive"`) for `severity="critical"` in `Banner`, keep `status` for the rest. Render a permanently-mounted, empty live region in the auth card and the tenant shell and write the message into it, rather than mounting the region with the message. Move focus to the error banner (`tabIndex={-1}` + `.focus()`) after a failed submit. Give the toast stack an `aria-label` and use `role="alert"` on individual critical toasts.
verification: PARTLY REFUTED. The code is as described: packages/ui/src/Banner.tsx:24 hardcodes `role="status" aria-live="polite"` with no branch on severity; LoginForm.tsx:76-80 mounts the Banner only when errors.form is set and handleSubmit (:64-71) never moves focus; Toast.tsx:74 is an unnamed role="region". But the impact does not follow as stated. 'A live region inserted with its content is not announced' is folklore that modern NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver frequently contradict — behaviour is AT- and version-dependent, and the auditor did not test with any screen reader (proved_by: read-only, confidence: medium, by their own admission). WCAG-wise there is no clear failure either: SC 4.1.3 Status Messages is satisfied by role=status. What remains is genuine but minor — critical severity should map to role="alert", and a failed submit should move focus. Low.

title: The sidebar's Billing item is a hardcoded English string with no catalogue key — it appears the moment subscriptions are enabled
what: `...(isAdmin && billingEnabled ? [{ href: \`${base}/billing\`, label: 'Billing' }] : [])` — every other entry in the `links` array uses `t('common.nav.*')`. There is no `nav.billing` key in either catalogue: `locales/el/common.json` contains `nav.catalog, nav.members, nav.loans, nav.reservations, nav.settings, nav.staff, nav.help, nav.language, nav.menu, nav.closeMenu, nav.desktop` and nothing else.
impact: The item is hidden today because `billingEnabled` is false, so this is invisible in every current test and every screenshot. The moment `BILLING_ENABLED=true` is set, the Greek sidebar grows an English 'Billing' row next to Κατάλογος / Μέλη / Δανεισμοί. The translation-parity CI gate cannot catch it, because the key does not exist in either language.
evidence: READ: SidebarNav.tsx:89. RAN: `python3 -c "import json; print(list(json.load(open('locales/el/common.json')).keys()))"` → no `nav.billing`. RAN the repo-wide key-usage cross-check (792 distinct `t('...')` keys against 1027 catalogue keys): zero missing keys — because this string never goes through `t()` at all, which is exactly why the existing gate misses it.
fix: Add `nav.billing` to `locales/en/common.json` and `locales/el/common.json` and use `t('common.nav.billing')`. Extend `scripts/check-translations.ts` (which today only checks en/el key parity) with a lint rule that flags string literals in JSX text and `label`/`title`/`aria-label`/`placeholder` props inside `apps/web/app/[locale]/t` and `packages/ui` — that scan found 23 such literals in tenant-facing code.
verification: CONFIRMED, SEVERITY CUT. SidebarNav.tsx:89 is verbatim `...(isAdmin && billingEnabled ? [{ href: `${base}/billing`, label: 'Billing' }] : [])`, and every sibling at :82-93 uses t('common.nav.*'). Dumped locales/el/common.json: nav keys are catalog, members, loans, reservations, settings, staff, help, language, menu, closeMenu, desktop — no nav.billing in either catalogue, so the parity gate genuinely cannot see it. All true, and the observation about why the CI gate misses it is the useful part. But the defect itself is one English word in one dormant, admin-only sidebar row. Low.

title: FormField marks fields required visually only — the input carries no required/aria-required
what: The `required` prop renders `*` — correctly hidden from assistive tech — but the `React.cloneElement` call that injects `id`, `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid` into the child does not inject `required` or `aria-required`. So the only signal that a field is mandatory is an asterisk explicitly hidden from screen readers.
impact: Screen-reader users filling in signup, checkout, new member or new book forms cannot tell which fields are mandatory until submission fails — and, per finding-20, the failure is frequently not announced either. WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions.
evidence: READ: FormField.tsx:59-71. The `cloneElement` props object is `{ id, 'aria-describedby': describedBy, 'aria-invalid': ..., invalid: ... }` — no `required`.
fix: Add `'aria-required': required || undefined` to the cloned props (prefer `aria-required` over the native `required` attribute so browser-native validation bubbles do not fight the app's own `noValidate` handling).
verification: CONFIRMED. packages/ui/src/FormField.tsx:58-63 renders the asterisk inside `<span aria-hidden="true">`, and the cloneElement props object at :65-70 is exactly `{ id, 'aria-describedby', 'aria-invalid', invalid }` — no required, no aria-required. So the mandatory-field signal is the one thing explicitly hidden from assistive tech.

title: Every modal injects a spurious banner and contentinfo landmark, so a loan detail page reports three page headers and three footers
what: `<header>` and `<footer>` map to the `banner` and `contentinfo` landmarks unless they are scoped inside `article`, `aside`, `main`, `nav` or `section`. `<dialog>` is not in that list, so both elements inside a Modal become top-level landmarks. Because `LoanActions` mounts three Modals at once (see finding-12), a loan detail page contains three `banner` landmarks and three `contentinfo` landmarks in addition to the shell's own.
impact: Landmark navigation — a primary screen-reader way to move around a page — becomes useless on the busiest pages: 'banner' should be a unique, page-level region and instead lists four indistinguishable entries. Not blocking, but it degrades the same users already hurt by findings 12, 13 and 14.
evidence: RAN: rendered the Modal markup in the browser and read the accessibility tree, which reported `dialog > banner > heading` for each of the three dialogs — the `<header>` is exposed as a `banner` landmark, confirmed by the tool's own tree output.
fix: Replace `<header>`/`<footer>` inside `Modal` and `HelpDrawer` with `<div>`s (the class names already carry all the styling), or wrap the dialog's contents in a `<section>`.
verification: CONFIRMED on the spec, which is the load-bearing part. packages/ui/src/Modal.tsx:70 `<header className="lbr-modal__header">` and :85 `<footer className="lbr-modal__actions">`; HelpDrawer.tsx:60 the same. Per HTML-AAM, header/footer map to banner/contentinfo unless scoped inside article, aside, main, nav or section (or the equivalent roles); <dialog> maps to role=dialog and is not in that list, so the mapping to banner/contentinfo applies. Combined with the three-modals-mounted-at-once fact independently confirmed under frontend-12, a loan detail page really does carry four banner landmarks. Low is the right weight — landmark clutter, no functional loss.

title: Combobox reports an expanded listbox that does not exist, points aria-controls at a missing id, and puts a role=alert li inside a listbox
what: `aria-expanded={open}` is bound to the `open` state alone, but the `<ul role="listbox">` is rendered only when `open && query.trim().length >= minQueryChars` — so focusing the input with an empty query reports 'expanded' with no popup present, and `aria-controls={listboxId}` dangles. Inside the listbox, the loading, error and no-matches rows are `<li>` elements without `role="option"`, and the error row additionally carries `role="alert"` — neither is a permitted child of `role="listbox"`. There is also no live region reporting how many results were found.
impact: The member and book pickers in checkout and place-hold are the two most-used custom widgets in the product. A screen-reader user is told a list is open when it is not, is given no result count, and encounters children the listbox role does not permit — behaviour varies by AT but is wrong everywhere.
evidence:
READ: Combobox.tsx:150-153 (`aria-expanded={open}` / `aria-controls={listboxId}`) against :157 (`{open && query.trim().length >= minQueryChars ?
    `), and :168-171 (`
  • {error}
    • `).
fix: Bind `aria-expanded` to the same condition that renders the listbox. Render the loading/error/empty rows outside the `<ul>` (in a sibling `<div role="status">` that also announces the result count), leaving the listbox containing only `role="option"` children.
verification: CONFIRMED verbatim. apps/web/components/Combobox.tsx:160 `aria-expanded={open}` and :161 `aria-controls={listboxId}` against :164 `{open && query.trim().length >= minQueryChars ? <ul id={listboxId} role="listbox">` — so an empty focused input reports expanded with a dangling aria-controls. Inside the listbox, :166-176 render loading / error / no-matches as plain `<li className="lbr-combobox__option--inert">` with no role=option, and the error one carries role="alert" — neither is a permitted child of role=listbox.

title: Footer legal links are 17 px tall on mobile, under the WCAG 2.2 minimum target size, and the coarse-pointer rule does not cover them
where: packages/ui/src/styles.css:1448-1462 (`@media (pointer: coarse)` list) and the `.lbr-legal-links__item` / `.lbr-powered-by` rules
what: The coarse-pointer block enlarges `.lbr-btn`, `.lbr-nav__link`, `.lbr-modal__close`, `.lbr-help-drawer__close`, `.lbr-banner__dismiss`, `.lbr-toast__close`, `.lbr-toast__action`, `.lbr-combobox__clear` and `.lbr-help-button` to 44 px, but not `.lbr-legal-links__item` or `.lbr-powered-by`. `.lbr-legal-links` uses `gap: var(--sp-1) var(--sp-3)`, i.e. 4 px of vertical spacing, so the spacing exception in SC 2.5.8 does not rescue them.
impact: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA — 24×24 CSS px. Measured targets are 17 px tall. These are the Terms, Privacy, Cookies and Legal Notice links required by the GDPR/consent work, so they are the links a regulator or a user with a motor impairment is most likely to try to tap.
evidence: RAN: loaded `/el` from the production build at 375×812 (mobile preset, touch emulation) and audited every focusable element's bounding box. Under-24 px results: `A.lbr-powered-by 184x16`, `A.lbr-legal-links__item 86x17 "Όροι Χρήσης"`, `132x17 "Πολιτική Απορρήτου"`, `112x17 "Πολιτική Cookies"`, `115x17 "Νομική Σημείωση"`. No other element failed, and `document.documentElement.scrollWidth` was exactly 375 with zero horizontally-overflowing elements — the responsive layer itself is sound.
fix: Add `.lbr-legal-links__item` and `.lbr-powered-by` to the `@media (pointer: coarse)` block with `min-height: 44px; display: inline-flex; align-items: center`, or raise the vertical gap on `.lbr-legal-links` to 24 px so the spacing exception applies.
verification: CONFIRMED at source (I did not re-run the browser measurement, but the CSS makes the result deterministic). packages/ui/src/styles.css:1447-1464 is the `@media (pointer: coarse)` block and its selector list is exactly .lbr-btn, .lbr-nav__link, .lbr-modal__close, .lbr-help-drawer__close, .lbr-banner__dismiss, .lbr-toast__close, .lbr-toast__action, .lbr-combobox__clear, .lbr-help-button — .lbr-legal-links__item and .lbr-powered-by are absent. :1558-1568 gives .lbr-legal-links `gap: var(--sp-1) var(--sp-3)` (4px row gap) and .lbr-legal-links__item `font-size: var(--fs-sm)` with no padding or min-height, so the target box is the ~17px line box the auditor measured, and the 4px row gap rules out the SC 2.5.8 spacing exception. The inline-in-a-sentence exception does not apply either — these are flex items, not running text.

title: The static cache version is pinned to v1, so it is never invalidated and grows across every deploy
what: `STATIC_CACHE = \`lbr-static-${VERSION}\`` with a literal `'v1'` that nothing bumps. The `activate` handler deletes only `lbr-` caches not in `ALL_CACHES`, and `ALL_CACHES` always contains the same three names, so nothing is ever evicted. `isImmutableAsset` sends every `/_next/static/*` chunk and every path ending in a static extension to `cacheFirst`, which writes and never expires. Over successive deploys the cache accumulates one full set of hashed chunks per release. `offline.html` is also precached into this never-cleared cache (sw.js:66), so a corrected offline page will not reach a browser that already installed the old one.
impact: Unbounded storage growth on long-lived circulation-desk browsers, and — more awkwardly — a fix to `offline.html` (see finding-18) will not actually ship to existing installs, because `cache.add(OFFLINE_URL)` only runs on install and `caches.match(OFFLINE_URL)` prefers the stale entry. Not urgent on day one; it becomes a support problem after a few releases.
evidence: READ: sw.js:19, 22-30, 62-72, 77-83, 95-104. `VERSION` appears exactly once and is a literal.
fix: Derive `VERSION` from the build id (inject it by generating `sw.js` at build time from a template, or append `?v=<buildId>` to the registration URL and read it in the worker) so each deploy gets fresh cache names and the activate handler evicts the previous set. Fetch `offline.html` with `cache: 'reload'` in the install step.
verification: CONFIRMED, and one implication is stronger than the finding states. apps/web/public/sw.js:19 `const VERSION = 'v1'` appears exactly once and is a literal; :77-83 activate deletes only lbr-* caches absent from ALL_CACHES, which is always the same three names. Additional point I verified: sw.js is a static file in /public that is byte-identical between deploys, so the browser sees no byte change and never even re-installs the worker — which means `cache.add(OFFLINE_URL)` at :66 never re-runs and a corrected offline.html genuinely cannot reach an existing install. Low: storage growth is slow and nothing breaks on day one.

title: The offline bar, the pending-queue pill and the toast stack all occupy the bottom-right corner and none respects the iOS safe area
where: apps/web/components/ServiceWorkerManager.tsx:33-45 (full-width bottom bar, z-index 2000); apps/web/components/OfflineQueueProvider.tsx:200-218 (bottom-right pill, z-index 1900); packages/ui/src/styles.css `.lbr-toast-stack` (bottom-right, z-index 9000, no safe-area padding)
what: Three fixed overlays anchor to the bottom of the viewport. When the device is offline with queued actions — the exact state the offline feature exists for — the pending pill (z-index 1900) sits underneath the full-width offline bar (z-index 2000), and any toast (z-index 9000) covers both. Only the offline bar and the pill add `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`; `.lbr-toast-stack` uses a plain `bottom: var(--sp-5)`.
impact: On a phone or an iPad at the desk, the '3 actions pending' indicator is obscured by the offline banner precisely when the librarian needs to know whether their checkouts are queued. On a notched iPhone the toast close button can land under the home indicator and be hard to tap.
evidence: READ: ServiceWorkerManager.tsx:33-45 (`position:'fixed', left:0, right:0, bottom:0, zIndex:2000`, `paddingBottom: calc(... + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px))`); OfflineQueueProvider.tsx:200-218 (`right`/`bottom: calc(var(--sp-3) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px))`, `zIndex:1900`); styles.css `.lbr-toast-stack { bottom: var(--sp-5); right: var(--sp-5); z-index: 9000 }` — no `env()`.
fix: Stack the three in one bottom-anchored flow container rather than overlapping fixed layers, or raise the queue pill above the offline bar and offset it by the bar's height when both are shown. Add `bottom: calc(var(--sp-5) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px))` to `.lbr-toast-stack`.
verification: CONFIRMED. apps/web/components/ServiceWorkerManager.tsx:33-45 — position fixed, left:0 right:0 bottom:0, zIndex 2000, with env(safe-area-inset-bottom). apps/web/components/OfflineQueueProvider.tsx:200-218 — position fixed, right var(--sp-3), bottom calc(var(--sp-3) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom)), zIndex 1900. The pill sits ~12px off the bottom edge with a lower z-index than a full-width bar that starts at bottom:0 and is taller than that, so it is fully covered whenever both show — which is exactly the offline-with-queued-actions state. packages/ui/src/styles.css:591 `.lbr-toast-stack { bottom: var(--sp-5) }` with no env() — confirmed.

title: The help-article HTML sanitizer is a regex denylist with proven bypasses, feeding dangerouslySetInnerHTML under a CSP that allows inline script
what: renderHtml() runs `marked` (which passes raw HTML straight through) then sanitizeHtml(), four `.replace()` calls that strip active-content tags, `on*=` handlers, and `href|src="javascript:`. The scheme regex requires a quote immediately after `=`, so an unquoted attribute slips past; it matches the literal string `javascript:`, so an HTML-entity-encoded scheme slips past; and it only looks at href/src, so SVG's `<animate attributeName=href values=javascript:...>` slips past. The stored bodyHtml is then injected with dangerouslySetInnerHTML inside the authenticated tenant shell. The CSP set at apps/web/next.config.mjs:57 is `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, which permits javascript: URL execution, so there is no containment layer behind the sanitizer. The file's own comment claims the function exists as 'defense-in-depth so a future content edit (or an admin-authored-help feature) can't introduce stored XSS' — that claim is false.
impact: Today the only author is someone with commit access, so this is not remotely exploitable — the harm is that the guard the team believes they have does not hold. The moment help content becomes admin-authored (the comment anticipates exactly that), or a markdown file is added via a dependency/vendor/AI-assisted edit that nobody reads as HTML, it becomes stored XSS in the tenant shell against every librarian in every library, with a CSP that will not stop it.
evidence:
EXECUTED. Ran marked@18.0.10 + a verbatim copy of sanitizeHtml over 12 payloads. Survivors: `x` -> output `

x

` (unquoted attribute, regex needs a quote); `[click](javascript:alert(1))` -> ``; `` -> passed through verbatim; `
fix: Replace sanitizeHtml() with an allowlist sanitizer — `sanitize-html` or `isomorphic-dompurify` — configured with an explicit allowed tag/attribute set and `allowedSchemes: ['http','https','mailto']`. The dependency is already justified by the comment in the file. Do it before any admin-authored help feature ships, not after.
verification: The mechanism is real; the severity was not. I re-ran the four claimed bypasses against a verbatim copy of sanitizeHtml (scripts/ingest-help-articles.ts:109-122) and all four survive unchanged: `x`, ``, and `

title: A NUL byte in any text query parameter produces an HTTP 500, including on the unauthenticated /help/articles endpoint
what: Query strings are passed to Prisma/Postgres without stripping U+0000. Postgres rejects a NUL in a text value with SQLSTATE 22021 ('invalid byte sequence for encoding UTF8: 0x00'), Prisma throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError, and HttpExceptionFilter turns it into a 500 with a support code. No DTO validation runs on query parameters at all — validateDto is only applied to request bodies (main.ts:47 documents that there is no global ValidationPipe), and the query helpers in platform/query.ts only cover numeric params.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can generate 500s at will against /help/articles?q=%00 — every one writes a full error record with a stack trace to the logs and mints a support code. That is a cheap log-flood / alert-fatigue lever on a public endpoint, and it will pollute whatever error budget or paging the team wires up. For signed-in users it is a plain robustness defect: a paste containing a stray NUL turns a search box into 'something went wrong'.
evidence: EXECUTED. All returned 500: `GET /help/articles?q=%00` with NO cookie (unauthenticated), `GET /t/probes1-x9/members?q=%00`, `.../catalog/books?q=%00`, `.../catalog/authors?q=%00`, `.../audit?after=%00`. The same endpoints with normal input return 200. API log for the audit case: `Invalid prisma.auditEvent.findMany() invocation: Database error. Code: 22021. Message: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00 ... at async AuditService.list`.
fix: Add a tiny middleware (or extend platform/query.ts with a `parseText(raw)` helper used by every string @Query) that strips control characters including U+0000 from query values before they reach a service. Strip, don't reject — a NUL is never meaningful search input.
verification: REPRODUCED exactly as written — all five 500s, including the unauthenticated one: `GET /help/articles?q=%00` -> 500 with supportCode 4NPRES38 and no cookie; `?q=abc` -> 200. `/t/ver-up/members?q=%00`, `/catalog/books?q=%00`, `/catalog/authors?q=%00`, `/audit?after=%00` -> 500 each. Read-verified there is no global query validation (main.ts:46-50 documents the absent ValidationPipe). SEVERITY REDUCED because the stated impact does not carry a medium. The request is not amplified — a NUL query costs the server no more than a normal one, so this is not a DoS lever, it is one error-level log line per request. Any anonymous request to any public endpoint already produces a log line; the only delta is the level and a stack trace, and nothing is wired to page on error rate yet (nothing is deployed). The user-facing half — 'a paste containing a stray NUL turns a search box into something went wrong' — is real but vanishingly rare. Low: a genuine robustness defect with a two-line fix, not something that wakes anyone at 3am.

title: Deeply nested JSON on unauthenticated endpoints blows the stack inside class-transformer and returns 500
what: validateDto passes the raw parsed body to class-transformer's plainToInstance before any structural check. class-transformer walks the object recursively with no depth bound, so a body like `{"a":{"a":{...}}}` nested ~5000 deep — well under the 100 KB body cap, so it is accepted by the parser — overflows the V8 stack with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` inside TransformOperationExecutor.getKeys. Reachable unauthenticated on /auth/login and /auth/signup, and on every authenticated write.
impact: A 40 KB request from anyone on the internet produces a 500 plus a full RangeError stack trace in the logs. Cheap unauthenticated error-log flooding, same alert-fatigue problem as finding 05. It is contained today because the throw happens synchronously inside an async handler and Nest catches it — but main.ts:74-80 installs `process.on('uncaughtException', ... process.exit(1))`, so any future refactor that moves this work outside a caught async boundary turns the same request into a process kill.
evidence: EXECUTED. Depth 5000: `POST /auth/login` (no auth) -> 500, `POST /auth/signup` (no auth) -> 500. Depth 2000 -> 400 (validation, fine). Depth 20000/60000 -> 413 (body cap). API log: `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded at TransformOperationExecutor.getKeys (class-transformer@0.5.1/src/TransformOperationExecutor.ts:527:17)`. Server stayed up (healthz 200) throughout.
fix: Add a depth guard at the top of validateDto: walk the raw value iteratively and throw BadRequestException past a modest depth (8 is more than any DTO here needs) before plainToInstance ever sees it. Same helper protects every controller at once.
verification: REPRODUCED. A 5,000-deep `{"a":{...}}` body (~40 KB) to /auth/login with no credentials -> 500; the same to /auth/signup -> 500; depth 2,000 -> 400 (validation). /healthz stayed 200 throughout. Read-verified validate-dto.ts:22-25: the only pre-check is `typeof raw !== 'object'`, then plainToInstance runs on the raw value. main.ts:73-79 does install process.on('uncaughtException', ... process.exit(1)) as claimed. SEVERITY REDUCED for the same reason as finding 05: today this is one error log per request with no amplification and no process impact — I confirmed the server survives. The escalation argument ('a future refactor that moves this outside a caught async boundary turns the same request into a process kill') is speculation about code that does not exist; a medium cannot rest on it. Low, and it shares a single fix with finding 05 (one guard helper at the top of validateDto plus query sanitising).

title: Uploads trust the client's Content-Type entirely; no magic-byte check and no multer fileFilter
where: apps/api/src/storage/storage.service.ts:56 (ALLOWED_TYPES check against input.contentType), callers at catalog/covers.controller.ts:41, members/photos.controller.ts:40, branding/branding.controller.ts:57
what: The MIME allowlist is applied to `file.mimetype`, which is whatever the client typed in the multipart part header. The file bytes are never sniffed, and FileInterceptor is configured with `limits: { fileSize }` only — no fileFilter. So arbitrary content can be stored under an image resource type by lying about the Content-Type. The team is aware: allowed-types.ts:4 says 'Clients can lie about Content-Type, so we ALSO serve uploaded files with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff'.
impact: Low as shipped — the attachment + nosniff pairing does neutralise the 'HTML uploaded as JPEG' rendering attack, and the storage layer names files itself so the extension cannot be attacker-chosen. The residual is that tenant storage will accumulate files whose type is a lie, which matters if a future feature ever serves these inline (an OPAC public cover endpoint, a PDF viewer, an email attachment) and drops one of the two headers. It also means the per-resource allowlist provides no actual guarantee about what is on disk.
evidence: EXECUTED. `POST /t/probes1-x9/storage/covers` with an HTML body declared as `type=image/png` was accepted (201, ref covers/cmt5mnlskf8250764cdd8.png) and read back byte-identical as `<html><script>alert(1)</script></html>`. The same file declared honestly as text/html was correctly rejected 415. Also verified the good news: a filename of `../../../../tmp/pwn.png` had no effect — LocalDriver.put ignores originalname for the path and generates `covers/<cuid>.png`, and safeResolve() refuses any ref containing '..'.
fix: Add a magic-byte check in StorageService.put for the image resource types (the first 12 bytes distinguish JPEG/PNG/WebP/GIF unambiguously) and reject on mismatch with the declared type. Keep attachment + nosniff regardless.
verification: REPRODUCED, including the negative controls. `POST /t/ver-up/storage/covers` with an HTML body declared `type=image/png` -> 201, ref covers/cmt5ndvrtbc9292e126b7.png; the same bytes declared honestly as `text/html` -> 415. A part filename of `../../../../tmp/pwn.png` was ignored — the driver generated covers/<cuid>.png and /tmp/pwn.png does not exist. Read-verified storage.service.ts:55-60 tests ALLOWED_TYPES against input.contentType only, and import.controller.ts-style fileFilter is absent from all three FileInterceptor configs. The severity is honestly self-assessed by the original finding — attachment + nosniff do neutralise the rendering attack today (and my finding-08 browser test shows the headers really are on every response), so low is correct.

title: The public /apply throttle fails open, and the only bot defence behind it is a honeypot field
what: RateLimitService.hit() fails closed only for keys starting with 'signup:'; every other bucket returns `{ allowed: true }` on a Redis error. The /apply bucket is keyed `apply:iph:<hash>`, so a Redis outage removes the form's only throttle entirely (the code comments this as intentional: 'Fails OPEN - a Redis outage must not eat leads'). The remaining bot defence is a single honeypot input named `website`. Each accepted submission writes a row to the control-plane applications table and enqueues an outbound notification email to the operator.
impact: During any Redis blip — or permanently, via finding 02's header rotation — the launch marketing form accepts unlimited submissions. Each one is a control-plane row plus an email to the operator's inbox, so the practical outcome is an inbox flood and a polluted lead table at the exact moment the Greek launch campaign is driving real traffic to that page. Trivially automated; the honeypot stops only naive scrapers.
evidence: READ: rate-limit.service.ts:78 `const failClosed = key.startsWith('signup:')` and :102 the catch branch returns `{ allowed: true, ... }` for everything else; applications.service.ts:112 keys the bucket `apply:iph:<sha256>`. EXECUTED (the header-rotation half): 8 submissions with rotating X-Real-IP all returned 303 and persisted, taking the applications table to 13 rows.
fix: Add a second bucket for /apply that is not IP-derived and fails closed — a global 'applications per hour' ceiling is fine here because, unlike signup, refusing a burst of applications for a few minutes is a far smaller harm than an unbounded flood. Given the campaign traffic, a Turnstile widget on the form is the cheaper real fix.
verification: Read-verified line by line. rate-limit.service.ts:78 `const failClosed = key.startsWith('signup:')`; the catch branch at :103-105 returns `{ allowed: true, count: 0, retryAfterSec: 0 }` for every other key. applications.service.ts:112 keys the bucket `apply:iph:<sha256>` and :118 comments the fail-open as intentional. The honeypot is the single check at applications.controller.ts:65 (`if (typeof body.website === 'string' && body.website.trim() !== '')`), and the throttle at :80 runs after validation. Kept at low and kept as a separate finding from 02: the header-rotation half is a duplicate of 02, but the Redis-outage half is independent of it and would still bite after 02 is fixed.

title: Password fields have a minimum length but no maximum
what: SignupDto.password and PasswordResetCompleteDto.newPassword are `@MinLength(12)` with no `@MaxLength`. Every other string field in these DTOs is bounded with @Length. LoginDto.password and CompleteSetupDto.newPassword are correctly bounded at 200.
impact: Small. The 100 KB body cap bounds the input and bcryptjs truncates at 72 bytes, so there is no hashing-cost amplification.
