The concrete harm is inconsistency: a user can set a 90 KB password at signup that LoginDto's `@Length(1, 200)` will then refuse at login, locking them out of the account they just created.
evidence: READ. signup.dto.ts:45-47 `@IsString() @MinLength(12, ...) password!: string;` with no @MaxLength; password-reset.dto.ts:21-22 the same for newPassword. Contrast login.dto.ts:22 `@Length(1, 200) password!: string;`.
fix: Add `@MaxLength(200)` to both, matching LoginDto.
verification: Upgraded from read-only to EXECUTED, and the lockout is real. Read confirmed signup.dto.ts:45-47 and password-reset.dto.ts:21-22 carry @MinLength(12) with no @MaxLength, against login.dto.ts:19-20 `@Length(1, 200)`. Then I drove it: signup with a 300-character password -> 201, account created. Login with that same password -> 400 `["password must be shorter than or equal to 200 characters"]`. Login with just its first 72 characters -> 200. So a user who sets a >200-char password is locked out of the library they just created, and the only way back in is to guess that bcrypt silently truncated their secret at 72 bytes. Low is right — it needs an unusual password — but this is a real self-lockout, not a style nit, and the fix is one decorator.

title: The container's pg_dump major version floats while the server is pinned at 16 — the exported SQL dump may not restore where the site promises it will
what: The api/worker image does `RUN apk add --no-cache openssl tini postgresql-client` (Dockerfile:22) with no version pin, so the pg_dump major is whatever the current node:26-alpine base's Alpine release defaults to (17 or 18 today, rising with each base bump), while the server is deliberately held at postgres:16-alpine. Dumping an older server with a newer client is supported, but the emitted header carries the client's settings: a pg_dump 18 dump opens with `SET transaction_timeout = 0;`, a parameter PostgreSQL 16 and earlier do not recognise, and psql aborts on it. docs/server-handbook.md §8 records this exact failure measured against this cluster ('dumping 16 with the 18 client produces SET transaction_timeout = 0;, and the restore aborts'), for backups — the same hazard applies to the customer-facing export and is not mentioned anywhere near it. The dump also emits `\restrict`/`\unrestrict` meta-commands that only recent psql builds understand.
impact: The SQL export is the site's load-bearing answer to 'and what if you disappear?': '/en/about — The SQL copy does not depend on us in order to be read: it restores onto any PostgreSQL server, by any technician'; '/en/migration — a complete copy of your library's database, made with pg_dump, without owners and privileges, which restores into any PostgreSQL installation.' A library whose technician restores onto their own PostgreSQL 15 or 16 gets an error, at exactly the moment the promise is being tested. Nobody would find out before then, because nothing in CI restores an export.
evidence: READ Dockerfile:22 — unpinned `postgresql-client`. READ export-processors.ts:349-353 — `execFileP('pg_dump', ['--no-owner','--no-privileges','--format=plain','--file',outPath])`. READ server-handbook.md §8, the version-skew note. EXECUTED the export end to end against the live audit environment (processExportJob on a real tenant): `AFTER {"status":"completed","fileName":"libriant-lrp-6e683b-2026-08-23.sql","bytes":37023,"error":null}`, and the produced file restored cleanly into a fresh database (`psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f <dump>` → exit 0, 15 tables) — but with the local pg_dump 16.15, which is the version-matched case, not the container's. The dump header reads `Dumped by pg_dump version 16.15` and contains `\restrict`. Docker is not available in this environment, so the container's actual client major could not be measured.
fix: Pin the client to the server major in apps/api/Dockerfile — `apk add --no-cache postgresql16-client` — and add a CI step that takes a tenant export and restores it into a stock postgres:16 container, asserting exit 0. That test is the only thing that keeps the /en/about promise honest as base images move.
verification:
I MEASURED THE FAILURE THE FINDING ASSERTS AND IT IS NOT WHAT THE FINDING SAYS. Against the live audit Postgres 16.15 I ran a file containing `SET statement_timeout = 0; SET transaction_timeout = 0; \restrict abc123; CREATE TABLE t...; INSERT...; \unrestrict abc123`:
  psql -f  (default)          → `ERROR: unrecognized configuration parameter "transaction_timeout"`, then `CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT 0 1`, **exit 0**, and `select count(*) from t` → 1.
  psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f  → same ERROR, **exit 3**.
So the finding's core sentence, 'psql aborts on it', is false for the default invocation a library's technician would use — the restore emits one scary line and completes. It aborts only under ON_ERROR_STOP, which the customer-facing promise does not require. The `\restrict`/`\unrestrict` claim is also wrong in the direction that matters: psql 16.15 accepted both silently (they were backported), so they are not a compatibility hazard for a 16 target. THE UNDERLYING HYGIENE DEFECT IS REAL: READ apps/api/Dockerfile:19-22 — `FROM node:26-alpine` then `RUN apk add --no-cache openssl tini postgresql-client`, unpinned, while the server is held at postgres:16-alpine; and READ export-processors.ts:349-353, which shells to that pg_dump. The handbook's own note at :527-533 records the skew hazard for backups and says backup.sh is safe only because it runs inside the postgres container — the customer export does not. AND THE CONTAINER'S ACTUAL CLIENT MAJOR IS STILL UNMEASURED: `which docker` → not found in this environment, and only postgresql@16 is installed locally, so nobody — the original auditor or me — has observed what apk actually installs. Downgraded to low: pin the client and add the CI restore test, but this does not break the export promise the way the finding claims.

title: The plan catalogue ships three feature flags the product does not have and the site explicitly disclaims — api_access, custom_subdomain, priority_support
what: The seeded catalogue grants `api_access_enabled: true` on Municipal, Central and Institutional; `priority_support: true` on Central and Institutional; and `custom_subdomain_enabled: true` on Institutional. All three contradict published copy. The site says there is no API in four places, including '/en/security — No. There is no programming interface, and we will not tell you otherwise in order to get through an evaluation', and apps/site/build.ts even lints the Greek phrase «πρόσβαση API» out of the copy as 'a claim the code does not support'. On support: '/en/about — we do not sell tiers of support: no plan buys a faster answer.' Custom subdomains cannot work at all — the `*.libriant.com` vhost in infra/caddy/Caddyfile is entirely commented out and needs a DNS-01 wildcard certificate that is not provisioned.
impact: Low today because the tenant-facing plan grid renders only name, description and price (apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/billing/PlanGrid.tsx has no feature matrix) and /t/:slug/plan is dev-only. The exposure is the moment anyone builds a comparison table from the catalogue, or an admin quotes the plan record to a prospect: the database says Municipal includes API access, and the website says the API does not exist. It also means an Institutional customer could be sold a custom subdomain the edge cannot serve.
evidence: EXECUTED `psql` pivot over plan_feature_values → `api_access_enabled` false/false/true/true/true, `priority_support` false/false/false/true/true, `custom_subdomain_enabled` false/false/false/false/true across starter→institutional. READ seed-data.ts:97-99 and the four sibling blocks. READ Caddyfile — the `*.{$PUBLIC_APEX_DOMAIN}` block is commented from `# *.{...} {` to the closing `# }`. READ build.ts:222-226 — the `terminology-drift` lint bans «πρόσβαση API» with `why: 'Glossary violation, or a claim the code does not support.'` EXECUTED `grep -rn 'api_access_enabled|priority_support' apps/web packages/i18n locales` → no matches, confirming nothing renders them today.
fix: Set all three to false across every plan in seed-data.ts until the features exist, or delete the feature keys. A catalogue that disagrees with the website is a claim waiting for a UI to surface it.
verification:
RE-EXECUTED THE PIVOT MYSELF against the live audit control plane:
  slug | api_access_enabled | priority_support | custom_subdomain_enabled
  starter false/false/false · community false/false/false · municipal TRUE/false/false · central TRUE/TRUE/false · institutional TRUE/TRUE/TRUE · on-prem-enterprise true/true/true
Matches the finding exactly. READ infra/caddy/Caddyfile:338-343 — the wildcard vhost is commented (`# *.{$PUBLIC_APEX_DOMAIN:libriant.com} {`), so custom_subdomain_enabled cannot be served. READ apps/site/build.ts:222-227 — the `terminology-drift` lint bans «πρόσβαση API» at error level with `why: 'Glossary violation, or a claim the code does not support.'` And pages.en.json (/en/about), quoted under finding 15, says in terms 'we do not sell tiers of support: no plan buys a faster answer' against priority_support=true on two plans. Low is correct — `grep -rn 'api_access_enabled|priority_support' apps/web packages/i18n locales` finds no renderer, so nothing surfaces it today; the exposure is the first comparison table anyone builds from the catalogue.

title: A tenant cannot see its own usage against its plan limits in production, so the first signal a library gets when billing turns on is the refusal itself
what: `GET /t/:slug/plan` and `GET /t/:slug/plan/usage` are mounted on PlanDemoController, which is gated by `NonProductionOnlyGuard` (plan-demo.controller.ts:72) — `enabled = loadEnv().nodeEnv !== 'production'`, throwing NotFoundException otherwise. The guard is correct for its purpose: the same controller carries `POST /t/:slug/demo/books`, a real unvalidated write that bypasses the race-safe quota authority, and that must not be reachable in production. But it takes the two read-only usage endpoints down with it. docs/billing-go-live.md flags the consequence ('A tenant cannot see their own usage in production') and then proceeds to the flip anyway.
impact: Once BILLING_ENABLED=true the real caps bite immediately against data loaded with none in force. A librarian mid-task meets a 402 with no screen anywhere in the product showing how many of their 60,000 titles or 25 staff seats are used. The handbook's related note that `storageUsedBytes` never self-heals (nothing schedules recomputeUsage) means a stale counter can refuse an upload that should succeed, again with no visible number to argue with.
evidence: READ plan-demo.controller.ts:44-53 (the guard) and :68-73 (`@UseGuards(NonProductionOnlyGuard, TenantGuard, RolesGuard, PlanGuard)`). EXECUTED against the live audit environment where NODE_ENV=test: `### PLAN USAGE 200` — the endpoint works and returns real counters, so only the production guard stands between a library and its own numbers. READ billing-go-live.md, 'Before you flip it' section.
fix: Split the two read-only endpoints out of PlanDemoController into a plain tenant controller behind TenantGuard/RolesGuard, leaving the demo write behind NonProductionOnlyGuard, and surface the numbers on the billing page. Do it before BILLING_ENABLED is flipped, not after the first 402.
verification: RE-VERIFIED IN CODE AND AT RUNTIME. READ plan-demo.controller.ts:41-52 — `NonProductionOnlyGuard.enabled = loadEnv().nodeEnv !== 'production'`, throwing NotFoundException otherwise — and :72, `@UseGuards(NonProductionOnlyGuard, TenantGuard, RolesGuard, PlanGuard)` on the whole `t/:slug` controller, which carries both the two read-only plan endpoints and the `POST /t/:slug/demo/books` write. My probe under NODE_ENV=test got `PLAN 200 / USAGE 200`, so the guard really is the only thing between a library and its own counters. docs/billing-go-live.md:109-111 flags it and proceeds anyway — read and confirmed. ONE MITIGATION THE FINDING MISSES, WHICH IS WHY LOW IS RIGHT: READ quota.interceptor.ts:95-108 — the 402 body is not opaque. It carries `feature`, `limit`, `used` and `currentPlan` alongside the message, so a librarian who hits a cap does get the numbers, provided the UI renders them. The gap is the absence of a *proactive* screen, not a refusal with no information. Low stands.

title: Prisma cursor pagination degrades linearly with page depth on every list endpoint
what: Every list method pages with `cursor: { id: after }, skip: 1` while ordering by a non-unique column plus id (books: sortTitle+id; members: sortName+id; loans: loanedAt+id; audit: occurredAt+id; reservations: status+queuePosition+placedAt+id). Prisma renders that as `WHERE (sortTitle = (SELECT sortTitle FROM books WHERE id = $1) AND id >= (SELECT ...)) OR (sortTitle > (SELECT ...))`. The OR-of-subselects is not a btree start-key, so Postgres scans the index from the beginning of the range and discards every row before the cursor. Page N costs O(N x pageSize), and walking the whole list is O(n^2).
impact: A librarian paging through a 400,000-title catalogue gets progressively slower pages, and the API burns whole-index scans doing it. It is not just a UI annoyance: the offline/PWA sync, the desktop app and any script that walks a list page-by-page pay quadratic cost against the shared Postgres.
evidence: RAN. Captured the exact SQL from Prisma's query event log, then EXPLAIN ANALYZE'd it. Page ~8,000 of books: `Index Scan using "books_sortTitle_idx" ... Rows Removed by Filter: 200000`, `Buffers: shared hit=40 read=5951 written=1331`, `Execution Time: 86.872 ms`. Last page: `Rows Removed by Filter: 399000`, `Execution Time: 190.272 ms`. Page 1 of the same query: 13 ms. The same OR-of-subselects shape was captured for members, loans and audit_log.
fix: Stop using Prisma's `cursor`. Encode the cursor as the tuple of the sort keys (`sortTitle|id`, base64) and emit a true row-value predicate — `WHERE ("sortTitle", id) > ($1, $2)` via `$queryRaw` or `Prisma.sql` — which a `@@index([sortTitle, id])` can seek directly. Add the composite indexes to match each list's orderBy.
verification: Mechanism REPRODUCED exactly. Captured Prisma's emitted SQL from the query event log for `book.findMany({cursor:{id},skip:1, orderBy:[sortTitle,id]})`: it is the OR-of-subselects the finding describes. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) of that literal SQL at depth 200,000: `Index Scan using "books_sortTitle_idx"`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 204082`, `Buffers: shared hit=6120`, `Execution Time: 32.254 ms`. So the O(depth) cost is real. IMPACT REFUTED. The finding claims 'the offline/PWA sync, the desktop app and any script that walks a list page-by-page pay quadratic cost'. There is no such consumer: grepping apps/web and apps/desktop for `nextCursor`/`after` returns only apps/web/components/DataTable.tsx (the 'Load more' button) and Combobox; apps/web/lib/offline-queue.ts is a write replay queue for circulation actions (checkout/return/renew/mark-lost), it syncs no lists. Reaching depth 200k in the UI takes ~8,000 clicks at 25 rows a page; at a realistic depth of 50 pages the filter discards ~1,250 rows, which is unmeasurable. Real defect, no realistic harm — low.

title: book-metadata-refresh full-scans the catalogue every 6 hours and can never finish a pass
what: The candidate query orders by `metadataRefreshedAt ASC NULLS FIRST`. `books_metadataRefreshedAt_idx` is a plain ascending btree, which in Postgres is NULLS LAST, so the index cannot satisfy the ordering and the planner falls back to a full scan plus top-N sort. It scans 400,000 rows to return `PER_TENANT_LIMIT = 40` (line 35), and the job ticks every 6 hours (registry.ts:59-60), i.e. 160 books/day per tenant.
impact: Four full scans of every tenant's books table per day, each producing 40 useful rows. Worse, the feature cannot converge: at 160 books/day a 400,000-title catalogue needs over 6,800 days for one pass, while `REFRESH_INTERVAL_DAYS = 30` makes rows eligible again after a month. An Institutional library's catalogue will never be enriched, so the cost buys nothing.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of the exact SQL captured from Prisma's query log: `Parallel Seq Scan on books (actual rows=130667 loops=3)`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 2667`, `Sort Key: "metadataRefreshedAt" NULLS FIRST`, `Buffers: shared hit=931 read=9124`, `Execution Time: 34.847 ms`; Prisma wall time 118 ms. Read: PER_TENANT_LIMIT=40 at line 35, 6 h interval at registry.ts:59.
fix: Change the index to match the sort — `CREATE INDEX books_metadata_refresh ON books ("metadataRefreshedAt" NULLS FIRST) WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL AND isbn13 IS NOT NULL` — and add the 'still missing a field' condition to the partial predicate so the index is a work queue rather than a table scan. Then either raise the per-tenant budget so a pass can actually complete, or make the job event-driven (enqueue a refresh when a book is created/imported without metadata) and drop the sweep.
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED: `pg_indexes` shows `books_metadataRefreshedAt_idx ... btree ("metadataRefreshedAt")` (plain ASC = NULLS LAST) while book-metadata-refresh.job.ts:118 asks for `nulls: 'first'`; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) of the real predicate gives `Parallel Seq Scan on books`, `Sort Key: "metadataRefreshedAt" NULLS FIRST`, `Buffers: shared hit=4660 read=5395`, `Execution Time: 74.541 ms`. But the severity does not follow. The job runs every 6 h (registry.ts:59-60), so this is four 75 ms scans per tenant per day — about 300 ms of scanning a day, against a dashboard that does 2 x 32,845 buffers on every single page view. The convergence arithmetic is also wrong: PER_TENANT_LIMIT=40 x 4 runs = 160 books/day, and 400,000/160 = 2,500 days, not the 'over 6,800 days' claimed. The non-convergence is a product/feature-design problem, not a performance one, and the candidate set is much smaller than 400k (only books with an isbn13 still missing a backfillable field). Low.

title: The reservations list sorts every live hold in the library to render 26 rows
what: The default list has no bookId/memberId filter and orders by `status ASC, queuePosition ASC NULLS LAST, placedAt DESC, id ASC`. The only reservation index that could help is `reservations_bookId_status_queuePosition_idx`, whose leading column is bookId — unusable without that filter. Nothing indexes `(status, queuePosition, placedAt, id)`, so Postgres seq-scans the table and sorts the whole live set for each page.
impact: Page latency scales with the size of the hold queue rather than the page size, and the four-key ordering makes performance-03's cursor problem worse (the OR-of-subselects predicate is built over the leading key only). The holds screen is the second-most-used circulation view after loans.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM reservations WHERE status IN ('queued','ready') ORDER BY status ASC, "queuePosition" ASC NULLS LAST, "placedAt" DESC, id ASC LIMIT 26` with 40,000 live holds: `Seq Scan on reservations (actual rows=40000)`, `Sort Method: top-N heapsort`, `Buffers: shared hit=591`, 9.304 ms. Prisma wall time 135 ms for the page including the three relation-batch queries.
fix: Add `@@index([status, queuePosition, placedAt, id])` on Reservation so the default ordering is an index scan, and keyset-paginate on that tuple (performance-03).
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED: reservations.service.ts:429-439 orders by status, queuePosition NULLS LAST, placedAt desc, id; `pg_indexes` on reservations shows nothing leading with `status`, only `reservations_bookId_status_queuePosition_idx`. RAN the query at 40,000 live holds (35,000 queued + 5,000 ready): `Seq Scan on reservations (actual rows=40000)`, `Sort Method: top-N heapsort`, `Buffers: shared hit=14 read=583`, `Execution Time: 14.121 ms`. That is the whole harm: 4.7 MB and 14 ms at a hold-queue size (40,000 simultaneous live holds for a 100,000-member library) that is already far beyond anything a real library sees. At a plausible few hundred live holds the scan is sub-millisecond. Real missing index, negligible cost — low.

title: No statement_timeout or query timeout is configured anywhere for tenant traffic
what: The postgres service's command sets only `shared_preload_libraries` and `max_connections` — no `statement_timeout`, no `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, no `lock_timeout`. `makeTenantPrismaClient` passes only `{ connectionString, max }` to `PrismaPg` (packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55), and the control client passes only `{ connectionString }` (packages/db-control/src/client.ts:34, so it also inherits pg's default pool of 10 rather than a deliberate figure). The only place a statement timeout is set is the export worker (export-processors.ts:29). NestJS sets no HTTP handler timeout in main.ts either.
impact: A runaway query — a two-character search over a cold 400k catalogue, a stuck lock wait, a pathological trigram scan — occupies one of the five per-tenant pool slots for as long as it takes, with nothing to shed it. Five such queries wedge that library entirely, and the requests behind them queue in pg's connection pool with no acquire deadline. There is no automatic recovery; an operator has to `pg_terminate_backend` by hand.
evidence: READ: compose command block lines 320-325; packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55-59 and packages/db-control/src/client.ts:34 show the full option set passed to PrismaPg; grep for `statement_timeout` across apps/ packages/ infra/ returns only export-processors.ts. I attempted to demonstrate unbounded pool queueing empirically and could not reproduce it cleanly in a single process, so the impact statement above is derived from configuration, not measured.
fix: Add `-c statement_timeout=30s -c idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=60s -c lock_timeout=5s` to the postgres command (with the export/import/migration paths raising it per-session where they legitimately need longer), and give the control client an explicit `max` so its budget is deliberate.
verification: Every configuration fact re-verified. docker-compose.prod.yml:320-325 passes only `-c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements -c max_connections=200`. `grep -rn 'statement_timeout|idle_in_transaction|lock_timeout' apps packages infra scripts` returns only export-processors.ts:337/345/370 (the export worker's own 60 s cap) and two DR-drill scripts. packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55-58 passes `{connectionString, max}` and packages/db-control/src/client.ts:33 passes `{connectionString}` alone, so the control client does inherit pg's default pool of 10. main.ts installs only cookieParser and the exception filter — no HTTP timeout. Kept at low and kept honest: the finding already states its impact is derived from configuration, not measured, and I did not reproduce it either. It earns its place only because performance-01/-02/-12 show queries that can run long enough for the absence to matter.

title: API responses are served uncompressed from the app host
what: `encode zstd gzip` appears only inside the `{$SITE_HOST}` block (the marketing site). Neither the `{$PUBLIC_HOST}` block (line 149) nor the `{$ADMIN_HOST}` block (line 205) has an `encode` directive, and `apps/api/src/main.ts` installs no compression middleware — the only `app.use` calls are `cookieParser()` and the exception filter. So everything under `/lbr-api/*` leaves the origin uncompressed.
impact: Mostly absorbed for browsers by Cloudflare's edge compression, so the user-visible cost is limited — but origin-to-edge egress and the desktop/PWA sync paths pay full size, and a self-hosted or direct-to-origin deployment would ship the raw bytes to the client.
evidence: RAN: serialised the real DTO shapes from the scale DB. `GET /loans?limit=100` = 60.9 KiB raw / 4.0 KiB gzip (93% saved); `GET /catalog/books?limit=25` = 15.7 KiB raw / 1.4 KiB gzip. READ: Caddyfile blocks at 149, 205, 253-264; main.ts:29-45.
fix: Add `encode zstd gzip` to the `{$PUBLIC_HOST}` and `{$ADMIN_HOST}` site blocks (one line each), or install `compression` middleware in main.ts.
verification: `grep -n encode infra/caddy/Caddyfile` returns exactly one hit, line 264, inside the SITE_HOST block. Re-read the PUBLIC_HOST block (line 149) and the ADMIN_HOST block (line 205) in full — neither has an `encode` directive, and both reverse_proxy to api:3001 for /lbr-api/*. `grep -n 'app.use|compression' apps/api/src/main.ts` returns only line 39 `app.use(cookieParser())`. Low is the right rating: the finding is candid that Cloudflare's edge compression absorbs most of it for browsers, and the residual cost is origin egress plus direct-to-origin clients.

title: Hourly storage sweep recursively walks every tenant's entire flat file tree
what: The sweep loops every active tenant and calls `driver.sweepStaleTemps`, which recurses the whole storage root with `fs.readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` (apps/api/src/storage/drivers/local-driver.ts:199-228). Refs are flat within a resource folder (`covers/<id>.jpg`, `members/<id>.jpg`), so an Institutional tenant ends up with a single directory holding hundreds of thousands of entries, and readdir materialises every Dirent into one array. It runs hourly (registry.ts:70-79) even though, as the job's own comment notes, temps only appear after a crash mid-upload — the working set is normally empty.
impact: Hourly, per tenant, the worker allocates and discards an array of every file the library owns and stats the shared storage volume for nothing. It competes for the same worker process and the same disk as exports and imports.
evidence: READ: storage-temp-cleanup.job.ts:26-41 (loop over all active tenants), local-driver.ts:199-228 (unfiltered recursive readdir with withFileTypes, recursing into every directory), registry.ts:70-79 (60-minute interval). Ref layout confirmed from covers.controller.ts / photos.controller.ts usage of `covers/<id>` and `members/<id>`.
fix: Confine the sweep to a dedicated `_tmp/` staging directory (write temps there and rename into place), so the walk is O(orphans) instead of O(files). Drop the interval to daily. Shard the resource directories by id prefix (`covers/ab/abcd....jpg`) so no directory holds 400k entries.
verification: READ storage-temp-cleanup.job.ts:25-41 (loops every active tenant, hourly per registry.ts:70-79) and local-driver.ts:199-228 — `fs.readdir(dir, {withFileTypes:true})` recursing unconditionally into every directory with no prefix filter and no depth bound. ONE CORRECTION: it does NOT stat every file. `withFileTypes` supplies the type from getdents, and `fs.stat` runs only for names matching `/\.tmp-[0-9a-f]+$/i` (isTempUpload, line 190) — so the cost is one Dirent array per directory plus the syscalls, not a stat storm. That is the whole harm: an hourly allocate-and-discard of an array of every file the library owns, for a working set that is normally empty by the job's own comment. Low.

title: School libraries are a first-class segment and children's data gets no special treatment anywhere in the product, while the DPA promises Art. 35 assistance that does not exist
what: `school` is one of the selectable library types at signup, and `Member.dateOfBirth` is a stored column. Nothing in the codebase branches on it: `grep -rniE 'minor|child|guardian|parent|under 1[368]|dateOfBirth' apps/api/src apps/web/app packages/shared/src` returns no age logic, no guardian contact field, no consent flag, no restriction on automated e-mail to a minor's address, no reduced-retention rule. The DPA acknowledges the exposure squarely — Annex I lists 'your members/patrons (which may include children)' — and then assigns 100% of it to the controller (§3.2), while §4(e) promises assistance 'with your obligations under Articles 32–36 (… DPIAs …)'. No DPIA template, no children-specific guidance and no Art. 35 material exists in the repo (see privacy-legal-08).
impact: A school library processing pupils' borrowing records is squarely inside the HDPA's high-risk criteria (data of vulnerable subjects, systematic processing) and will need a DPIA before go-live. Libriant supplies nothing, so the promise in the signed DPA is unmet from day one. Operationally, a child member's e-mail address receives automated 'you have Το Κιβώτιο overdue' messages with no way for the library to route notices to a guardian instead, and that disclosure is then retained forever in Libriant's control plane (privacy-legal-04). Nothing prevents a librarian entering a pupil's full home address and photo either, with no shortened retention.
evidence: READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:42-45 — `enum LibraryType { … school }`. RAN `grep -rniE "minor|child|guardian|parent|under 1[368]|dateOfBirth" apps/api/src apps/web/app packages/shared/src --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` → 30 hits, all false positives (damaged/manage/image/pages); zero minor-handling code. READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:47-48 — 'Categories of data subjects: your members/patrons (which may include children)'.
fix: Ship a DPIA template and a children's-data guidance note for school libraries as part of the legal layer (that is the Art. 28(3)(f) assistance already promised). In the product, add an optional guardian e-mail on Member that automated notifications prefer when `dateOfBirth` indicates a minor, and let a library set a shorter retention for minor records.
verification: Facts verified. packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:41-48 `enum LibraryType { public academic school special community other }`. `dateOfBirth` is stored (db-tenant schema; members.service.ts:212, :325-326) and RAN `grep -rniE '\bminor\b|\bguardian\b|\bchild\b|\bchildren\b|under 1[368]' apps/api/src apps/web/app packages/shared/src` → every hit is a false positive ('minor units', React `children`, BullMQ 'waiting-children'). There is no age logic. dpa.md:47-48 does list 'your members/patrons (which may include children)'. Downgraded from medium to low because the two harms asserted do not hold up. (1) 'no way for the library to route notices to a guardian instead' is refuted: the notification templates key on `member.email` (member-notifications.job.ts:213-236) and that field is free text the librarian fills in — entering the guardian's address routes the notice to the guardian, today, with no code change. (2) 'no DPIA material exists' is privacy-legal-08 restated; counting it twice inflates both. What remains is a real but modest gap: the DPA promises Art. 32-36 assistance to a segment it names, and ships none. The product-side suggestions in the fix are feature requests, not defects.

title: The DPA is never presented at signup and is not separately accepted
what: `SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS = ['terms','privacy']`, and the checkbox renders as 'Έχω διαβάσει και αποδέχομαι τους [Όρους Χρήσης] και την [Πολιτική Απορρήτου]' — two links, neither to /legal/dpa. The only hook is Terms §5: the DPA 'forms part of these Terms'. So the Art. 28 agreement is incorporated by reference into a clickwrap, is never shown, is never separately evidenced, and — like everything else — carries the draft banner and an unnamed processor when the library does go and read it.
impact: Art. 28(9) accepts electronic form, and incorporation by reference is defensible in principle, but the combination here is not: a public-body controller must be able to show it concluded an Art. 28 contract, and the record on file says only that someone ticked a box labelled 'Terms and Privacy Policy'. A DPO reviewing the onboarding will ask for the signed DPA and there will be nothing to send.
evidence: READ packages/shared/src/legal.ts:33. READ locales/el/legal.json — `"consent.pre": "Έχω διαβάσει και αποδέχομαι τους"`, `"consent.and": "και την"`, with the two links rendered at SignupForm.tsx:372-380. READ locales/en/legal/terms.md:50-51 — '…governed by our [Data Processing Agreement](/legal/dpa), which forms part of these Terms.'
fix: Add 'dpa' to SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS, name it in the consent label, and record acceptance of each of the three documents with its own version. For public bodies, back it with the counter-signed instrument from privacy-legal-10.
verification: Verified: packages/shared/src/legal.ts:33 `SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS = ['terms','privacy']`; SignupForm.tsx:371-381 renders exactly two links, /legal/terms and /legal/privacy, around locales/{el,en}/legal.json:24-26 ('I have read and agree to the … and the …'); terms.md:50-51 incorporates the DPA by reference. Downgraded from medium to low. The finding concedes the legal point against itself — Art. 28(9) accepts electronic form and incorporation by reference is effective — and then rests on the assertion that 'a DPO will ask for the signed DPA and there will be nothing to send'. That does not follow: what exists to send is the accepted Terms plus the DPA at a stable URL, which is the same instrument most SaaS vendors produce. Strip that out and the finding is a one-line fix with real procurement value (name the DPA in the consent label and add it to SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS), which is a low, not a medium.

title: The site's published retention and deletion promises for applicants are not implemented, and the notification e-mail keeps a second permanent copy
what: The public privacy notice at libriant.com promises 'If we do not go ahead together: we delete your details at the latest 12 months after we have been in touch, or immediately if you ask us to' and 'you can ask for deletion with a single email … we will answer within 30 days'. The `applications` table (libraryName, city, contactName, contactEmail, phone, currentSystem, message, consent, privacyVersion) has no purge job — SCHEDULED_JOBS contains none. Worse, applications.service.ts enqueues an admin-notification e-mail whose `bodyMarkdown` restates the applicant's details into `email_outbox`, which is also never purged, so deleting the Application row on request still leaves the applicant's name, e-mail and phone in the control plane indefinitely.
impact: A published, dated, version-pinned retention promise that the system cannot keep. The rest of that notice is genuinely careful — the IP is only ever a peppered hash with a one-hour Redis TTL, and the Application model's comment explains why no IP, country or user-agent is stored — which makes the unenforced 12-month rule the one falsifiable claim on the page. An applicant who invokes the promise gets a partial deletion at best.
evidence: READ apps/site/content/privacy.en.md §5. READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:1028-1061 (no deletedAt, no TTL). RAN `grep -rn 'application' apps/api/src/jobs/*.ts` → no matches. READ apps/api/src/applications/applications.service.ts:180 (`bodyMarkdown: body`) against the absence of any email_outbox purge.
fix: Add applications and email_outbox to the retention sweep from privacy-legal-05 (12 months for applications; null the body on delivered outbox rows within 30 days), and make the deletion-on-request path delete both the Application row and its outbox rows.
verification: Verified. apps/site/content/privacy.en.md:73-80 publishes 'we delete your details at the latest **12 months** after we have been in touch, or immediately if you ask us to' and 'you can ask for deletion with a single email'. The Application model (schema.prisma:1027-1061) has no deletedAt and no TTL, SCHEDULED_JOBS contains nothing touching it, and applications.service.ts:174-182 does enqueue an admin notification whose bodyMarkdown restates the applicant's answers into the never-purged email_outbox. Downgraded from medium to low. The clock has not started: the promise is '12 months after we have been in touch', the site has no origin yet and no application has been submitted, so no breach is possible before mid-2027. Compliance needs one DELETE statement, not a feature — and the outbox half of the finding is privacy-legal-05/-06 restated. Also worth recording against the auditor's own framing: this is the one falsifiable claim on a page whose surrounding data-minimisation is genuinely careful (see privacy-legal-20), which argues for fixing it, not for rating it above the items that touch member data.

title: No per-data-subject access or portability tooling — the only export is a full-tenant dump restricted to owner/admin
what: The library-facing export takes a format and nothing else: scope is implicitly the whole tenant. There is no 'export this member's data' action anywhere in the API or the web app. To answer one member's Art. 15 or Art. 20 request, a librarian must either produce a dump containing every other member's name, date of birth, address, phone and complete borrowing history — and then hand-extract one person's rows from it — or transcribe the member page by hand and separately reconstruct the loan, reservation and fine history.
impact: The DPA tells the controller the Service provides tools to 'access … and export Controller Personal Data directly'. For a per-subject request it does not, and the workaround (a whole-database export) is itself a fresh risk: an unencrypted file containing the entire registry, sitting downloadable for 24 hours, created every time a member asks a question. Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation cuts against making that the standard response.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/export/export.dto.ts:8-12 — `class CreateTenantExportDto { format!: ExportFormat }`, no scope or subject. READ apps/api/src/export/tenant-export.controller.ts:33-34 — `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard) @Roles('owner','admin')`. READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:98.
fix: Add `GET /members/:id/data-export` returning that member's record plus their loans, reservations, fines and the audit rows targeting them, in a machine-readable format — this is a small query and it is the Art. 15/20 answer. Pair it with the erasure endpoint from privacy-legal-03.
verification: Verified the API surface: apps/api/src/export/export.dto.ts:8-11 `class CreateTenantExportDto { format!: ExportFormat }` — no scope, no subject; tenant-export.controller.ts:33-35 is `@Roles('owner','admin')`; members.controller.ts exposes only @Get(), @Get('lookup'), @Post(), @Get(':id'). There is no per-member export. Downgraded from medium to low because the stated impact is refuted by the UI. The finding claims the librarian's only options are a whole-tenant dump or hand-transcription reconstructing the loan/reservation/fine history. Read apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/members/[id]/MemberDetail.tsx:279-292: the member page shows the record and links straight to that member's filtered views — `/t/{slug}/loans?memberId={id}&status=active` and `/t/{slug}/reservations?memberId={id}` — plus outstanding fines. Assembling one subject's data is a few screens, not a full-database dump, so the 'every Art. 15 question produces an unencrypted copy of the entire registry' scenario is not what a librarian would actually do. What survives is narrow and real: Art. 20 portability specifically requires a structured machine-readable format, there is none per subject, and dpa.md:98's 'tools to access … and export … directly' overstates what ships.

title: Cookie Policy is incomplete and its offline-cache claim is contradicted by the code
where: locales/en/legal/cookies.md (Cookies we set table; Local storage section); apps/web/lib/offline.ts:31-43; apps/web/lib/offline-queue.ts:17-33,49
what: Two defects. (a) The table lists only `libriant_session`, `libriant_admin` and `libriant_imp`. The service is fronted by Cloudflare (the site's own notice at apps/site/content/privacy.en.md §4 discloses `__cf_bm`, a 30-minute bot-management cookie); the app's Cookie Policy omits it. (b) The Local storage section says 'cached data is cleared on sign-out and on session loss'. On sign-out that is true (`clearOfflineCaches` calls `clearQueue`). On session loss it is deliberately false: `clearOfflineReadCaches` clears only the page/data caches and leaves the circulation queue intact, by design, and a queued entry carries `label` — a human-readable member name and book title ('Dune → Ada Lovelace') — for up to MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS = 18 hours.
impact: The strictly-necessary-only position that justifies not showing a consent banner is correct on the evidence (no analytics, no third-party fonts, no external scripts — CSP is `default-src 'self'; script-src 'none'; font-src 'self'` and grep finds no Sentry/GA/Plausible/Google Fonts anywhere), so this is not a banner problem. It is an accuracy problem in a published policy, and the second half understates how long member names persist on a shared circulation desk workstation after a librarian's session expires.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/cookies.md ('cached data is cleared on sign-out and on session loss'). READ apps/web/lib/offline.ts:31-43 — the A10-02 comment states the queue is left intact on a 401 on purpose. READ apps/web/lib/offline-queue.ts:29 (`label` — 'Human-readable summary for toasts ("Dune → Ada Lovelace")') and :49 (`MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS = 18 * 60 * 60 * 1000`). RAN `grep -rniE 'sentry|datadog|posthog|plausible|google-analytics|gtag|hotjar' apps packages infra` → no output; RAN `grep -rn 'fonts.googleapis|next/font/google' apps/web packages/ui` → no output.
fix: Add a `__cf_bm` row to the table (strictly necessary, Cloudflare, 30 min) and reword the local-storage paragraph: caches are cleared on sign-out and on session loss; pending offline circulation actions are kept for up to 18 hours so they can be completed, and are cleared on sign-out.
verification: Part (b) verified precisely and is the stronger half: locales/en/legal/cookies.md's Local storage section says 'cached data is cleared on sign-out and on session loss', while apps/web/lib/offline.ts:34-43 documents the opposite by design — `clearOfflineReadCaches` (the session-loss path) deliberately leaves the queue intact so 'the same user may re-authenticate and still wants their queued, idempotent offline writes to flush' — and offline-queue.ts:26 shows each entry carries `label` ('Dune → Ada Lovelace'), a member name plus a book title. Note the finding is if anything conservative: MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS (offline-queue.ts:49) is the age at which `isExpired` refuses to REPLAY an entry, not a sweep that removes it, so on a workstation nobody signs back in on, the labels persist past 18 hours. Part (a) is narrowed, not confirmed: __cf_bm is only set if the app is proxied through Cloudflare, and app.libriant.com has no DNS record while infra/caddy/Caddyfile terminates TLS directly on the Hetzner box — so the app's cookie table is not yet provably incomplete. Add the row when, and only if, the app goes behind the proxy. Severity unchanged at low.

title: The Legal Notice directs users to the EU ODR platform, which was shut down on 20 July 2025
what: The consumer-dispute section links to ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr. The ODR Regulation (EU) 524/2013 was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 and the platform ceased operating on 20 July 2025; the obligation to link to it went with it. The paragraph then hedges 'The Service is provided to organisations (B2B); consumer-ADR rules may not apply', which is the right position given Terms §2.1.
impact: A dead link presented as a statutory redress route. Small on its own, but it is the kind of detail a public-body reviewer notices and reads as 'this document was not maintained' — which, given the draft banner and the placeholders, reinforces the wrong impression at the worst moment.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/legal-notice.md:36-38 — 'the EU Online Dispute Resolution platform is available at [ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr]'.
fix: Delete the ODR paragraph (or replace it with a plain statement that the Service is B2B and that disputes go to the courts named in Terms §12) when counsel reviews the document.
verification: Verified the text: locales/en/legal/legal-notice.md:35-38 does present 'the EU Online Dispute Resolution platform is available at [ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr]' followed by the B2B hedge, and the Greek file mirrors it. The legal fact — Regulation (EU) 524/2013 repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228, the platform ceased operating 20 July 2025 — is not verifiable from this repository and rests on the auditor's knowledge, which matches mine; the finding's own 'medium' confidence is honestly stated and I have left it. Rating and fix are proportionate: delete the paragraph during the counsel review that privacy-legal-01 already requires. Severity unchanged.

title: With EMAIL_DRIVER=console in production, undelivered member notices are marked 'delivered' and their PII accumulates, while the recipient address is still logged
what: The console driver correctly withholds the body outside development — the A12-02 comment and the `isDev` branch are right, so reset tokens do not reach docker logs in production. It still logs the recipient address (`… NOT delivering "${input.subject}" to ${input.to}`), which for member notifications is a patron's e-mail address plus a subject line naming their overdue book. It also returns a synthetic providerId, so the worker writes `status: 'delivered', deliveredAt: new Date()` for a message nobody received. `createEmailDriver` falls through to console for any unrecognised value, with no production guard.
impact: Patron e-mail addresses and the titles they have out land in container logs (journald/docker, shipped and retained by whatever collects them) with no retention rule, in an environment where by definition no e-mail is being sent. And the outbox fills with member names, addresses and book titles marked delivered — data retained for a purpose that was never served, which is precisely what Art. 5(1)(b)/(e) forbid. Any future audit of 'did the member get the notice' reads a false answer.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/email/drivers/console-driver.ts:32-35 — the non-dev branch logs subject and `to`. READ apps/api/src/email/email-worker.ts:195-202 — unconditional `status: 'delivered'` after `driver.send` returns. READ create-email-driver.ts:19-21 — `default: return new ConsoleEmailDriver()`.
fix: Log only the outbox row id in the non-dev branch, not the recipient. Have the console driver mark the row `status: 'dead'` (or a new `not_sent`) outside development instead of `delivered`, and refuse to boot with EMAIL_DRIVER=console when NODE_ENV=production unless an explicit acknowledgement env var is set — the same pattern backup.sh already uses for BACKUP_ALLOW_LOCAL_ONLY.
verification: Verified and slightly strengthened. console-driver.ts:31-36: the non-dev branch withholds the body (the A12-02 comment is accurate and the isDev guard is real) but logs `"${input.subject}" to ${input.to}`. Checked what that subject actually contains — member-notifications.job.ts:43/65/88 build subjects 'Υπενθύμιση: το «${book}» λήγει σύντομα', 'Εκπρόθεσμο: «${book}»', 'Η κράτησή σας για το «${book}» είναι έτοιμη' — so the log line pairs a patron's e-mail address with the title they have out, which is exactly the borrowing record the rest of this dimension is trying to protect. email-worker.ts:195-202 does write `status:'delivered', deliveredAt: new Date()` unconditionally once `driver.send` returns, and create-email-driver.ts:19-21 falls through to console with no production guard. Severity unchanged at low: the exposure is container logs on a box that is not deployed, and the fix is three lines.

title: An aborted dr-drill.sh leaves the shared superuser role crippled (statement_timeout=1s, CONNECTION LIMIT 7)
what: The drill deliberately drifts the restoring role — `ALTER ROLE $PGUSER CONNECTION LIMIT 7; ALTER ROLE $PGUSER SET statement_timeout = '1s';` (lines 218-219) — so the post-restore assertions cannot be tautologies. The undo lives only in the 'Cleaning up' block at the very end of a successful run. The EXIT trap (line 47) is `trap 'restore_password; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT`, and `restore_password` issues only `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD`. Any abort after line 219 — `set -e` on a failed psql, a Ctrl-C, a lock wait, a concurrent process dropping a database mid-`pg_dumpall` — leaves the role with a 1-second statement timeout and a 7-connection cap.
impact: The whole stack authenticates as this one role. A cluster left in that state fails every query longer than a second and refuses the 8th connection: the API's Prisma pools, pgbouncer's server pool and the worker's per-tenant clients all break, and the symptom (`canceling statement due to statement timeout`, `too many connections for role`) points nowhere near a shell script that exited an hour ago. The script's only guard is the comment 'Never point it at production'.
evidence:
RAN, unintentionally — which is the point. My first drill invocation aborted mid-run (a concurrent process dropped a tenant database during `pg_dumpall`). Immediately afterwards, on that cluster:
```
psql -qtAX -c "SELECT rolname, rolconnlimit, rolconfig FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='libriant'"
libriant|7|{statement_timeout=1s}
```
I had to repair it by hand with `ALTER ROLE libriant RESET ALL; ALTER ROLE libriant WITH CONNECTION LIMIT -1`.
fix: Move the role reset into the EXIT trap: `trap 'undo_drift; restore_password; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT`, where `undo_drift` runs `ALTER ROLE "$PGUSER" RESET ALL; ALTER ROLE "$PGUSER" WITH CONNECTION LIMIT -1 VALID UNTIL 'infinity'`. Additionally refuse to start when the target cluster contains a `libriant_control` database (a production fingerprint) unless `--i-know-this-is-not-production` is passed.
verification: Mechanism confirmed exactly: dr-drill.sh:47 `trap 'restore_password; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT` and restore_password (lines 38-46) issues only `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD`; the drift at lines 217-220 sets `CONNECTION LIMIT 7` and `statement_timeout = '1s'` and is undone only by the successful restore later in the run, not by the trap. Any abort in between leaves the role crippled. Downgraded medium -> low on blast radius. This script is explicitly a throwaway-cluster tool: its header (lines 30-31) says 'DESTRUCTIVE: drops and recreates its own fixture databases... Never point it at production', and its only automated caller (.github/workflows/verify.yml:341-352) runs it against a dedicated postgres service container on port 5433, deliberately separated from the shared 5432 service. The impact paragraph describes production Prisma pools and pgbouncer breaking, which requires an operator to have aimed a self-described production-destroying script at production. Real defect (the trap should undo the drift, and a `libriant_control` fingerprint check is a cheap guard), but it is developer-tooling hygiene, not a launch reliability risk.

title: Library errors carrying a 4xx status are returned to the client with zero logging
what: Path 1.5 inspects any non-HttpException for a numeric `status`/`statusCode` in 400-499 and, if found, responds with that status and a canned message — and returns without a single log call. The intent is body-parser's `PayloadTooLargeError`/`SyntaxError`, but the shape is generic: Stripe's SDK errors carry `statusCode`, http-errors and most HTTP client wrappers carry `status`, and any of them thrown from a handler now produces a client-visible 4xx with no server-side record.
impact: A whole class of upstream failures becomes invisible: no support code, no log line, no metric. If the Stripe API starts returning 402/429, or the GitHub desktop-release proxy starts 404ing, the user sees "We couldn't process that request" and the operator has literally nothing to correlate — not even a count. Silent 4xx is the hardest failure mode to notice, and this path guarantees it.
evidence: READ. apps/api/src/platform/http-exception.filter.ts:63-72 — between `const clientStatus = clientErrorStatus(exception)` and `return`, there is no `this.logger.*` call, unlike both other branches which route through `handle5xx` and its single-line JSON log.
fix: Log a warn line (method, url, status, error message, constructor name) before responding on this path, and narrow the trigger: only honour the status when the exception is an instance of an expected body-parser/http-errors type (`err.type === 'entity.too.large'` / `'entity.parse.failed'`), letting everything else fall through to the 5xx path where it gets a support code and a stack.
verification: Mechanism confirmed: http-exception.filter.ts:63-70, between `clientErrorStatus(exception)` and the `return`, contains no logger call, and `clientErrorStatus` (lines 116-121) is indeed generic — it accepts any object with a numeric `status` or `statusCode` in 400-499, which does match Stripe SDK errors and http-errors. Downgraded medium -> low because the stated impact overreaches. 'The operator has literally nothing to correlate — not even a count' is false: pino-http autologging records every response, and I confirmed on the live API that a 404 produced an INFO line carrying method, url and `"res":{"statusCode":404,...}`. So 4xx on this path are countable and locatable by URL; what is lost is the exception's message and constructor name. The narrowing half of the fix (only honour the status for known body-parser/http-errors shapes, so a Stripe 402/429 is not mislabelled as user error) is the part that matters, and it is a small, contained defect.

title: No stop_grace_period on api, web or postgres — Docker SIGKILLs them 10 s after SIGTERM
what: `stop_grace_period: 60s` is set for the `worker` service and nowhere else. Every other service — api, web, caddy, postgres, pgbouncer, redis — inherits Docker's 10 s default. The API also has no internal shutdown deadline of its own: main.ts calls `app.enableShutdownHooks()` and relies entirely on Nest's `close()`, in contrast to worker.ts:227-262 which races the drain against an explicit 25 s `SHUTDOWN_DEADLINE_MS`.
impact: Two consequences. (a) Any API request still in flight 10 s after a deploy's SIGTERM is severed mid-write — an import commit, a tenant provision (measured at ~1.2 s for a small library, longer as schemas grow), a large export kickoff. (b) More serious: the official postgres image's STOPSIGNAL is SIGINT, i.e. fast shutdown, which still has to complete a shutdown checkpoint. On a 2 GB-limit Postgres with a dirty buffer pool, a checkpoint that overruns 10 s ends in SIGKILL and the next start is a WAL crash recovery — extra downtime, on the component whose death takes the whole cell with it, at exactly the moment an operator is already doing something stressful.
evidence: READ. `grep -n 'stop_grace_period' infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` → one hit, line 297, under `worker`. main.ts has `app.enableShutdownHooks()` (line 57) and no timer; worker.ts:227 defines `SHUTDOWN_DEADLINE_MS = 25_000` and races it at line 258. Separately RAN: an idle HTTP keep-alive socket does NOT block the API's shutdown (SIGTERM → process exited in 1 s with a live keep-alive agent attached), so the exposure is genuinely in-flight work, not connection draining.
fix: Add `stop_grace_period: 30s` to api and web and `stop_grace_period: 120s` to postgres (and tune `checkpoint_timeout`/`max_wal_size` so a shutdown checkpoint is bounded). Mirror worker.ts's bounded-drain pattern in main.ts: register a SIGTERM handler that races `app.close()` against a ~25 s deadline and then `process.exit`.
verification: Facts confirmed: `grep -n stop_grace_period infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` returns exactly one hit, line 297 under worker; main.ts:57 calls `app.enableShutdownHooks()` with no deadline while worker.ts:208/220/253 races a 25 s SHUTDOWN_DEADLINE_MS. Downgraded medium -> low after testing the two impact legs. (a) The Postgres-checkpoint leg is the serious one on paper, but I measured a fast shutdown of the seeded audit cluster (49 tenants) from its own log: 'checkpoint starting: shutdown immediate' -> 'checkpoint complete: wrote 1098 buffers (6.7%) ... total=0.048 s'. Two orders of magnitude under the 10 s default at launch scale; the risk is real only as the dataset grows. (b) The in-flight-work leg largely does not apply to the API: the long operations named (import commit, export generation, tenant provisioning) run in the worker, which is the ONE service that already has stop_grace_period: 60s and a bounded internal drain. The finding itself already recorded that idle keep-alive sockets do not block shutdown. Cheap fix, correct diagnosis, but it cannot produce the stated 3am event at this scale.

title: Redis has a 512 MB cgroup ceiling and no maxmemory — an OOM-kill is a full outage
what: The comment explains the deliberate choice not to set `--maxmemory` (an eviction policy could drop live BullMQ job keys), and the command passes `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`, which is inert without a `maxmemory`. But `mem_limit: ${REDIS_MEM_LIMIT:-512m}` still applies at the cgroup level. Redis therefore has no internal backpressure and no eviction; it grows until the kernel OOM-killer takes the container.
impact: There is no soft landing between 'fine' and 'killed'. And because of reliability-02, a killed Redis is not a degraded cache — it is a 100%-500 API. Growth drivers are real: BullMQ keeps `removeOnComplete: 100-1000` / `removeOnFail: 100-5000` per queue across five queues, plus session-adjacent caches, plus AOF buffers during a rewrite. Recovery is bounded (AOF on a named volume, `restart: unless-stopped`), but the outage window is a hard failure of the whole product.
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:361-371 — `mem_limit: ${REDIS_MEM_LIMIT:-512m}` with `command: ['redis-server','--appendonly','yes','--maxmemory-policy','allkeys-lru']` and no `--maxmemory`. Combined with the executed evidence in reliability-02 that a Redis outage 500s every route including /healthz.
fix: Set `--maxmemory` to ~70% of the cgroup limit with `--maxmemory-policy noeviction` — that turns an OOM-kill into write errors Redis reports and the app can log, instead of a process death, while still never evicting a BullMQ key. Export Redis memory to Prometheus (the gauge already exists: `libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes`) and alert at 70% of the limit. Once reliability-02 is fixed, this drops to a nuisance rather than an outage.
verification: Configuration confirmed verbatim: docker-compose.prod.yml:364 `mem_limit: ${REDIS_MEM_LIMIT:-512m}` with :372 `command: ['redis-server','--appendonly','yes','--maxmemory-policy','allkeys-lru']` and no `--maxmemory`. Downgraded medium -> low on two grounds. (1) I measured actual usage on the audit instance carrying 50 seeded tenants plus BullMQ keys: `libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes 1407120` — 1.4 MB against a 512 MB ceiling, roughly 350x headroom, and the launch cohort is five libraries. The finding asserts growth drivers but quantifies none, and no OOM path is demonstrated. (2) The omission is a deliberate, documented trade-off — lines 365-370 explain that eviction could drop live BullMQ job keys and name the durable sources of truth that make a container OOM recoverable. What survives as a genuine defect is smaller and worth keeping: `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` is INERT without a `maxmemory`, so the compose file reads as if a protection is configured when none is, and the existing libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes gauge has no alert rule on it.

title: Scheduled BullMQ jobs are registered with no attempts, so they never retry — contradicting the code's own comment
what: `queue.upsertJobScheduler(j.name, { every: j.intervalMs }, { name: j.name, opts: { removeOnComplete: 100, removeOnFail: 100 } })` — no `attempts`, no `backoff`. BullMQ's default is `attempts: 1`, i.e. no retry. The worker body at line 110 nonetheless re-throws with the comment "re-throw so BullMQ marks the job failed + retries". The retry never happens; recovery is only the next scheduled tick.
impact: Small in practice — every registered job is an idempotent periodic sweep, so a transient failure costs one interval. But it matters for the hourly jobs: a 2-second Postgres blip at the top of the hour costs `member-notifications` and `fine-accrual` a full hour, and the comment tells the next maintainer that a retry is happening when it is not.
evidence: READ. scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:70-74 (the upsert with no `attempts`), versus line 110 `throw err; // re-throw so BullMQ marks the job failed + retries`. Contrast apps/api/src/email/email.service.ts:79-80, which does configure `attempts: this.defaultMaxAttempts` and `backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 30_000 }`.
fix: Add `attempts: 3, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 10_000 }` to the scheduler template opts (capped well under the shortest interval so retries cannot overlap the next tick), or correct the comment to say recovery is the next tick. Pick one — the current state is a comment that lies.
verification: Confirmed by reading both sides. scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:69-74 upserts the scheduler with template opts `{ removeOnComplete: 100, removeOnFail: 100 }` and no `attempts`/`backoff`, so BullMQ's default of attempts:1 applies; runner line 110 nonetheless says `throw err; // re-throw so BullMQ marks the job failed + retries`. The contrast case is real too — email.service.ts configures attempts plus exponential backoff. Severity correctly rated low: every registered job in registry.ts is an idempotent periodic sweep, so the cost of a transient failure is one interval. The finding is honest about that. Kept because the comment actively misinforms the next maintainer.

title: Caddy has no retry budget for its single upstreams — every container recreate is a burst of user-visible 502s
what: Two `reverse_proxy api:3001` blocks set `fail_duration 10s` / `max_fails 3`; the webhook proxy (line 189) and both `reverse_proxy web:3000` blocks (lines 194, 235) set nothing. No block sets `lb_try_duration`, so with a single upstream Caddy makes exactly one attempt and returns 502 on a connection refusal. Worse, once passive health marks the sole upstream unhealthy, Caddy short-circuits every request for the full `fail_duration` even if the upstream came back immediately.
impact: Deploys are manual, single-host, and recreate containers in place — there is no second replica to shift traffic to. Every `docker compose up -d` therefore produces a window where users get raw 502s on the main HTML path (`handle { reverse_proxy web:3000 }`) rather than a brief retry. With `fail_duration 10s` on the API path, a 200 ms restart can be amplified into a 10-second blackout. Cheap to fix and it makes most deploys invisible.
evidence: READ. `grep -n 'lb_try_duration' infra/caddy/Caddyfile` → no matches. `fail_duration 10s` / `max_fails 3` appear only at lines 179-180 and 277-278; lines 189, 194 and 235 are bare `reverse_proxy` directives.
fix: Add `lb_try_duration 10s` and `lb_try_interval 250ms` to the web and api reverse_proxy blocks so Caddy rides out a container restart, and lower `fail_duration` to ~2s (or drop passive health entirely for a single upstream, where it can only hurt).
verification: Confirmed by grep over infra/caddy/Caddyfile: `reverse_proxy` appears at 171 (with fail_duration 10s / max_fails 3 at 179-180), 189 (bare), 194 (bare), 218, 235 (bare) and 273 (with fail_duration/max_fails at 277-278); `lb_try_duration` and `lb_try_interval` appear nowhere. With one upstream and no try budget Caddy makes a single attempt and returns 502 on connection refusal, and passive health on a sole upstream can only short-circuit it. Consistent with the deployment model — single host, manual `docker compose up -d`, no second replica — so a container recreate is user-visible. Severity correctly low: the window is seconds, at a moment the operator chose.

title: autoInstallPeers pulls the Prisma CLI, Prisma Studio, a MySQL driver and an embedded WASM Postgres into the production dependency closure — and with them the one open CVE
where: pnpm-lock.yaml:3-5 (`settings: autoInstallPeers: true`), pnpm-lock.yaml:4673-4678 (`@prisma/client@7.9.1` snapshot lists `prisma` and `typescript` under optionalDependencies)
what: `@prisma/client@7.9.1` declares `prisma` and `typescript` as OPTIONAL peer dependencies (`peerDependenciesMeta: {prisma: {optional: true}, typescript: {optional: true}}`). Because `prisma` is also a devDependency of packages/db-control and packages/db-tenant, pnpm resolves the peer and records it as an optionalDependency of the client snapshot. That means it survives even a `--prod` install: the Prisma CLI (41.9 MB) comes along, and with it @prisma/studio-core (42.2 MB), @prisma/dev, @electric-sql/pglite, mysql2 and effect. @prisma/config (a CLI dependency) is where the tree's single open advisory lives.
impact: Prisma Studio — a full database-browsing UI — and a MySQL client library sit in the production image of a multi-tenant library SaaS. Nothing starts them, so this is surface rather than an open door, but it is 130+ MB of code that will never be exercised, will never be patched deliberately, and is what makes `pnpm audit` non-clean. It also defeats the obvious fix for supply-chain-03: switching the Dockerfile to `--prod` alone does not remove any of it.
evidence: READ node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+client@7.9.1*/node_modules/@prisma/client/package.json — `peerDependencies: {prisma: "*", typescript: ">=5.4.0"}`, both marked optional. READ pnpm-lock.yaml:4676-4678 showing them promoted to `optionalDependencies`. RAN a clean `pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile` over only {apps/api, apps/site, packages/db-control, packages/db-tenant, packages/shared}: 444 packages, 459 MB, and `ls node_modules/.pnpm` still shows prisma@7.9.1, @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0, @prisma/dev@0.24.17, @electric-sql/pglite@0.4.3, mysql2@3.15.3.
fix: Set `autoInstallPeers: false` in pnpm-workspace.yaml and re-resolve; the Prisma CLI then only appears where it is a real devDependency, and the runtime image loses ~130 MB and the entire elkjs/mysql2/pglite subtree. Re-run the full gate afterwards — turning it off can surface genuinely missing peers, which is the point.
verification: Every technical claim checked out and is worth keeping on record. READ pnpm-lock.yaml:1002-1012 — `@prisma/client@7.9.1` declares `peerDependencies: {prisma: '*', typescript: '>=5.4.0'}` with both `optional: true`. READ pnpm-lock.yaml:4673-4679 — the snapshot promotes both to `optionalDependencies`, which is what makes them survive a `--prod` install. pnpm-lock.yaml:3-4 does set `autoInstallPeers: true`. And `pnpm audit` confirms the advisory path is rooted there: `packages__db-control>@prisma/client>prisma>@prisma/config>deepmerge-ts`. The non-obvious insight — that switching the Dockerfile to `--prod` alone does NOT remove the Prisma CLI, Studio, pglite or mysql2 — is correct and is the single most useful sentence in this dimension. Downgraded medium -> low because it is not an independent harm: it is the reason supply-chain-03's fix is harder than it looks. The finding itself concedes 'nothing starts them, so this is surface rather than an open door'. Rating the same 'unused code in the prod image' harm at medium here and again at medium/high in supply-chain-03 double-counts it. Keep it as an implementation note attached to supply-chain-03, not as a separate medium. CAVEAT on the fix: `autoInstallPeers: false` is not a free switch — it changes resolution across all nine workspaces and will surface genuinely missing peers. Do not flip it in the launch window.

title: Caddy runs as root, holds the Cloudflare origin private key and the ACME account key, and the compose file states the opposite
where: infra/caddy/Dockerfile (no USER directive anywhere), infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:113-163 (caddy service: no `user:`, no `cap_drop`, no `security_opt`), and the contradicting comment at docker-compose.prod.yml:176-179
what: The edge image is `FROM caddy:2-alpine` with nothing after it but a COPY; the official Caddy image sets no USER, so PID 1 in that container is uid 0. Compose adds no `user:`, no `cap_drop: [ALL]` + `cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]`, and no `no-new-privileges`. It is also the container that binds host 80/443/443udp (:135-138), mounts the Cloudflare Origin Certificate private key at `/etc/caddy/origin:ro` (:148), and owns the `caddy_data` volume holding the ACME account key. Meanwhile the comment at :176-179 asserts that removing `user: root` from the `migrate` one-shot "eliminates the only root container in the prod stack" — which is false.
impact: Any Caddy RCE (or a compromised base-image tag, see supply-chain-05) is root inside a container with the TLS origin private key, host ports 80/443, and reachability to both the `edge` and `app` networks. The false comment means the next person reading the stack for a security review will conclude root has already been dealt with and look no further.
evidence: RAN `grep -n USER infra/caddy/Dockerfile apps/api/Dockerfile apps/web/Dockerfile` -> only apps/web/Dockerfile:64 and apps/api/Dockerfile:97 match; the caddy image has none. READ docker-compose.prod.yml:113-163 — no `user:`/`cap_*`/`security_opt` key on the caddy service. Independent proof of uid 0: the container binds :80 and :443 with no `cap_add`, which is only possible as root under the default capability set.
fix: Either run Caddy as a non-root user with `cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]` and `cap_drop: [ALL]`, or accept root and correct the comment at docker-compose.prod.yml:178. In both cases add `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]` to every service and make the origin-key mount `:ro` readable only by the running uid.
verification: Facts verified: `grep -n USER infra/caddy/Dockerfile` -> no match (the file ends at :47 `FROM caddy:2-alpine` + :48 a COPY, nothing else), and `grep -n 'user:|cap_drop|cap_add|security_opt|read_only' infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` returns exactly ONE hit — a comment at :176 — so no service in the prod stack sets any of them. The comment at :175-179 does claim removing `user: root` from `migrate` 'eliminates the only root container in the prod stack', and that is demonstrably false. Downgraded medium -> low because the stated impact largely does not follow. Caddy must be able to read /etc/caddy/origin (docker-compose.prod.yml:148) to terminate TLS at all, so the Cloudflare origin private key is exposed to a Caddy RCE at ANY uid — dropping to non-root does not protect it. Same for the ACME account key in caddy_data and for binding :80/:443. The genuine, and much narrower, delta is post-RCE escalation and container-escape surface (no `no-new-privileges`, full default capability set). Running the upstream caddy image as root is also the vendor's own default, i.e. a hardening gap rather than a misconfiguration. The most valuable half of this finding is the false comment, which will mislead the next reviewer into thinking root has been dealt with. Fix that line regardless of whether the hardening lands.

title: There is no vulnerability gate anywhere in the pipeline — no pnpm audit, no Dependabot/Renovate, no image scan, no SBOM — and the tree already fails one
where: .github/workflows/verify.yml (four jobs: static-checks, unit-tests, integration-tests, db-migration — none audits dependencies); .github/ contains only `workflows/` (no dependabot.yml, no CODEOWNERS, no SECURITY.md); no renovate.json at the repo root
what: The verify gate runs typecheck, lint, prettier, translations, assets, unit, integration, migrations and the DR drill — and zero supply-chain checks. Nothing in CI runs `pnpm audit`. Nothing scans the built images. Nothing produces an SBOM. And because every install site uses `--frozen-lockfile`, the resolved versions are frozen forever: without Dependabot or Renovate no mechanism exists that will ever raise a dependency version again. The 2026-06-14 audit already recorded this exact gap (docs/audit/production-readiness-findings-2026-06-14.json:2172 recommends adding `pnpm audit --prod` or Dependabot) and it was not acted on.
impact: The day a Next.js, NestJS, Prisma or ioredis advisory lands, nobody here finds out. For a product holding Greek public libraries' member records under GDPR, 'we had no process for learning about known vulnerabilities' is the finding an incident review writes down. The gap is not theoretical: `pnpm audit` fails today (see supply-chain-09).
evidence: RAN `grep -rn 'pnpm audit|npm audit|trivy|grype|snyk|osv-scanner|sbom|cyclonedx'` across the repo excluding node_modules — the only matches are inside docs/audit/ (the June audit's own scripts and its unactioned recommendation). RAN `ls -a .github/` -> `workflows` only. RAN `pnpm audit --json` -> 1 high, 0 critical over 895 dependencies.
fix: Add a `supply-chain` job to verify.yml running `pnpm audit --prod --audit-level=high` (it will fail on supply-chain-09 until Prisma ships a fix, so start with `--audit-level=critical` plus a non-blocking full report). Add .github/dependabot.yml with `npm` (grouped, weekly), `github-actions` and `docker` ecosystems. Generate a CycloneDX SBOM in the build job and attach it to the image.
verification: Absence verified: `ls -a .github/` -> `workflows` and nothing else (no dependabot.yml, no CODEOWNERS, no SECURITY.md); no renovate.json at the root; verify.yml's four jobs run typecheck/lint/prettier/translations/assets/unit/integration/migrations and no dependency, image or SBOM check. RAN `pnpm audit --json` -> `{'high': 1, 'critical': 0, 'totalDependencies': 885}`. Downgraded medium -> low on two grounds. First, the central impact claim — 'the day a Next.js, NestJS, Prisma or ioredis advisory lands, nobody here finds out' — is refuted by the repo's own history: commits fe0931e (pnpm 9->11, every action to its latest major), 84e61ff (redis 8, pgbouncer 1.25.2) and 35d81ae (ioredis 6 + BullMQ 6) all landed on 2026-08-22, so a manual bump mechanism demonstrably exists and is in active use. 'No mechanism exists that will ever raise a dependency version again' is false. Second, this is an absence-of-process finding whose only concrete instance is supply-chain-09, which is itself unreachable. It stays on the list at low because it is genuinely worth doing before launch and is cheap, and because .github/dependabot.yml with the `github-actions` ecosystem is the maintainable answer to supply-chain-01.

title: One open advisory in the tree: deepmerge-ts 7.1.5 (CVE-2026-40345, rated high) via the Prisma CLI — not reachable from request handling, but it blocks any audit gate
where: node_modules path `@prisma/client@7.9.1 > prisma@7.9.1 > @prisma/config@7.9.1 > deepmerge-ts@7.1.5`; pnpm-lock.yaml:4680-4684 (`@prisma/config@7.9.1` dependencies include `deepmerge-ts: 7.1.5`)
what: GHSA-ggr8-5vv4-36mx / CVE-2026-40345, CWE-674 stack exhaustion when merging recursive object graphs. Vulnerable `<8.0.0`, patched `>=8.0.0`; the tree has 7.1.5 and there is no route to 8.x without a Prisma release, because @prisma/config pins it. Reachability assessed rather than assumed: deepmerge-ts is used by @prisma/config to merge prisma.config layers, which runs only under the Prisma CLI (`prisma generate` at image build, `prisma migrate deploy` in the `migrate` one-shot). The inputs are the repo's own config files, not tenant or request data. The API's request path never loads @prisma/config.
impact: Real exploitability against Libriant: negligible — an attacker would need to control the Prisma config file, at which point they already control the build. The operational impact is different and real: this advisory is why `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` cannot be turned on as a blocking gate (supply-chain-08) without an ignore entry, and an ignore entry added on day one tends to become permanent.
evidence: RAN `pnpm audit --json`: `{"vulnerabilities":{"info":0,"low":0,"moderate":0,"high":1,"critical":0},"totalDependencies":895}`, sole advisory `deepmerge-ts <8.0.0 -> >=8.0.0`, six paths all rooted at prisma@7.9.1. READ pnpm-lock.yaml:4680-4684 confirming @prisma/config@7.9.1 -> deepmerge-ts 7.1.5 with no override available (an override to ^8 would break @prisma/config's expected API).
fix: Do not force an override. Record the reachability assessment above in the repo, set the CI audit gate to `--audit-level=critical` with a full non-blocking `pnpm audit --prod` report, and add a tracked item to re-run the audit on the next Prisma minor. Fixing supply-chain-04 (autoInstallPeers) removes this path from the production image entirely, leaving it dev-only.
verification: Re-ran the audit independently: `pnpm audit --json` -> metadata `{'info':0,'low':0,'moderate':0,'high':1,'critical':0}` over 885 dependencies; the sole advisory is GHSA id 1145093, `deepmerge-ts` high, vulnerable `<8.0.0`, patched `>=8.0.0`, 'DeepmergeTS has stack exhaustion when merging recursive object graphs', with paths `packages__db-control>@prisma/client>prisma>@prisma/config>deepmerge-ts` (and the db-tenant equivalents). READ pnpm-lock.yaml:4680-4686: `@prisma/config@7.9.1` -> `deepmerge-ts: 7.1.5`, no route to 8.x without a Prisma release. I specifically tried to refute the reachability assessment — i.e. to find a request path that loads @prisma/config — and could not: the API's runtime entrypoint is tsx over apps/api/src/main.ts and @prisma/config is a Prisma *CLI* dependency, exercised only by `prisma generate` (image build) and `prisma migrate deploy` (the migrate one-shot), both over repo-owned config files. The finding's own severity discipline is right: it correctly declines to force an override, and correctly identifies that the real cost is that it blocks `--audit-level=high` as a gate. This is the best-calibrated finding in the set.

title: The production deploy's SSH target list is produced by an unpinned PyPI install whose failure is swallowed
what: `python3 -m pip install --quiet pyyaml || true` installs the latest PyYAML from PyPI, unpinned and unhashed, on the runner. The python one-liner that follows parses infra/deploy/fleet.yml and writes `hosts=<json>` to $GITHUB_OUTPUT; that JSON becomes the `deploy` job's matrix, and `matrix.host.user` / `matrix.host.ssh` are interpolated directly into the `ssh` command lines at deploy.yml:232, 264, 347 and 399. The `|| true` means a failed or hijacked install is not surfaced here; the script either dies with an opaque ImportError or runs against whatever got installed.
impact: A compromised PyYAML release runs arbitrary code on the runner that immediately afterwards loads the production SSH key, and can rewrite the host matrix. Host-key pinning (deploy.yml:199-221) blocks redirection to an unknown host, but not code execution on the runner, and not deletion or duplication of legitimate hosts. Separately, `|| true` on a step whose output gates production is the wrong failure mode.
evidence: READ deploy.yml:161 `python3 -m pip install --quiet pyyaml || true` and :162-166 emitting `hosts=` consumed at :189 `matrix: host: ${{ fromJson(needs.plan.outputs.hosts) }}`. RAN `grep -rnE 'curl .*\| *(ba)?sh|pip install|apt-get install' scripts/ infra/ .github/` — this and verify.yml:346 (`apt-get install postgresql-client-16`, a distro package on a throwaway CI runner) are the only two remote-install sites.
fix: Drop the pip install: parse fleet.yml with `yq` (preinstalled on GitHub runners) or convert infra/deploy/fleet.yml to JSON and read it with `jq`. If Python is kept, use `pip install --require-hashes -r` a pinned requirements file, and remove the `|| true`.
verification: The mechanism is real — deploy.yml:161 is verbatim `python3 -m pip install --quiet pyyaml || true`, unpinned and unhashed, and its output at :162-166 becomes the deploy matrix consumed at :189. But the stated impact is FALSE and that is the whole severity.
