'A compromised PyYAML release runs arbitrary code on the runner that immediately afterwards loads the production SSH key' — `plan` (deploy.yml:141-166) and `deploy` (deploy.yml:176-...) are SEPARATE JOBS, each `runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, i.e. separate ephemeral VMs. I grepped lines 140-167 for `secrets.` and got no match: the plan job holds no secrets, no `environment:`, and nothing it executes ever shares a runner with DEPLOY_SSH_KEY. Code execution in `plan` cannot read that key. What survives is one step removed: a poisoned yaml module could rewrite the hosts JSON, and `${{ matrix.host.user }}@${{ matrix.host.ssh }}` IS interpolated straight into `run:` shell at :232/:264/:347/:399, which is a template-injection sink. But the input is infra/deploy/fleet.yml — repo-controlled, one host, and the run is a manual workflow_dispatch. Host-key pinning at :199-221 additionally blocks redirection. Low, not medium: `|| true` on a step that gates production is a bad failure mode worth the two-line fix (`yq`/`jq`, both preinstalled), but there is no path from here to the SSH key.

title: Any push touching apps/desktop/** publishes a live release to the auto-update feed with no approval gate, on a repository the code admits has no required status checks
where: .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml:27-31 (push trigger), :54-55 (`permissions: contents: write`), :214-225 (job `publish`, no `environment:`), vs .github/workflows/deploy.yml:50-51 ("Required status checks aren't available on this GitHub plan")
what: desktop-release.yml fires on every push to main under apps/desktop/**, builds three installers, and job `publish` runs `gh release edit "$TAG" --draft=false --latest`, which is what electron-updater reads as the update feed. There is no `environment:` on `version`, `release` or `publish`, so no reviewer is ever required. deploy.yml's own comment establishes that this repository has no branch protection and no required status checks — meaning main is directly pushable and the verify gate is enforced only by workflow ordering, not by the platform. There is no CODEOWNERS file.
impact: A single compromised push (or a force-push to main) ships an installer to the desktop fleet, automatically, with no human in the loop. Today the blast radius is bounded because builds are unsigned and the workflow bakes `libriantAutoUpdate=false` (:157, :188) so clients do not silently self-update — that mitigation is good and load-bearing. The moment MAC_CSC_LINK or the Azure secrets are populated, that guard disappears by design and the path becomes push -> signed auto-update -> code execution on every staff machine.
evidence: READ desktop-release.yml:27-31, :54-55, :214-225 — no `environment:` key anywhere in the file (`grep -n 'environment:' .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml` -> no match; deploy.yml:190 has one, desktop-release.yml does not). READ deploy.yml:50-51 for the admission that required status checks are unavailable on this plan.
fix: Add `environment: desktop-release` with a required reviewer to the `publish` job (and to `release` once signing secrets exist). Add a CODEOWNERS file. If required status checks genuinely are unavailable on the current plan, that is a reason to change the plan before shipping signed binaries, not a reason to proceed.
verification: Verified: `grep -n 'environment:' .github/workflows/*.yml` returns exactly ONE line in the whole directory — deploy.yml:190 `environment: production`. desktop-release.yml has none, so `version`, `release` and `publish` are all unreviewed; :27-31 is a push trigger on apps/desktop/**; :214-225 flips the release live with `gh release edit --draft=false --latest`. deploy.yml:47-51 does admit required status checks are unavailable on this plan, and there is no CODEOWNERS. Downgraded medium -> low. (a) The threat model is thin: publishing an installer requires push access to main, which is the same access needed to ship malicious code by any other route — the missing `environment:` removes a second pair of eyes, it does not create the capability. (b) Direct-push-to-main is this project's deliberate workflow, not an oversight, so 'no branch protection' is not a defect to charge here. (c) `needs: verify` (:59-61) means the shared gate still runs before anything builds, so a red commit cannot ship. (d) The finding's own load-bearing mitigation holds and I confirmed it in the source: with no signing secrets, both the macOS branch (:157) and the Windows branch (:188) bake `--config.extraMetadata.libriantAutoUpdate=false`, and the Windows branch keeps `verifyUpdateCodeSignature` at its secure default — so today nothing self-installs. The residual real risk is operational rather than adversarial: every desktop-shell push automatically publishes a release that the API then serves as the current download, with no human confirming it should ship. Worth an `environment:` gate, not worth a medium.

title: Two production dependencies carry no licence at all, and three carry non-permissive or dual licences that need a recorded decision
where: exceljs@4.4.0 (apps/api/package.json:26) -> unzipper@0.10.14 -> binary@0.3.0 -> buffers@0.1.1 (no `license` field); prisma@7.9.1 -> mysql2@3.15.3 -> seq-queue@0.0.5 (no `license` field); next@16.3.2 -> sharp@0.35.3 -> @img/sharp-libvips-*@1.3.2 (LGPL-3.0-or-later); @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0 -> elkjs@0.11.1 (EPL-2.0); exceljs@4.4.0 -> jszip@3.10.1 ((MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later))
what: I walked the production closure from every workspace's `dependencies` (496 packages) and read each package.json licence field. The distribution is overwhelmingly clean — 350 MIT, 42 Apache-2.0, 40 ISC, 9 BSD-3-Clause — and critically there is NO AGPL, NO SSPL and NO GPL-only package anywhere in the runtime tree, so there is no copyleft threat to the closed-source product. Five items are not clean: `buffers@0.1.1` and `seq-queue@0.0.5` declare no licence whatsoever (default copyright applies — no grant to use, copy or redistribute); `@img/sharp-libvips-darwin-arm64@1.3.2` and its siblings are LGPL-3.0-or-later native libraries; `elkjs@0.11.1` is EPL-2.0 (file-level weak copyleft); `jszip@3.10.1` is a dual `(MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later)` where the MIT election must be recorded. There is no LICENSE, NOTICE or third-party-attribution file anywhere in the repository, and the desktop installers — which ARE distributed to users — ship MIT/Apache/BSD code with no accompanying notices, which those licences require.
impact: The two unlicensed packages are the sharp end: strictly, Libriant has no grant to copy or distribute them, and one of them arrives through exceljs, a first-order runtime dependency used by the customer-facing export feature. In practice this is a due-diligence problem rather than a Monday outage — it is what a customer's procurement review, an acquirer, or a Greek public-sector tender questionnaire asks for and Libriant cannot currently answer. LGPL-3.0 (libvips) imposes no source obligation for SaaS, but does if sharp is ever bundled into the distributed desktop app. EPL-2.0 (elkjs) is only present because Prisma Studio is in the tree (see supply-chain-04) and vanishes with it.
evidence: RAN a script that resolved the 496-package production closure from pnpm-lock.yaml importers+snapshots and read every package.json `license`: 350 MIT / 42 Apache-2.0 / 40 ISC / 9 BSD-3-Clause / 3 Unlicense / 2 UNKNOWN / 2 MIT-X11 / 2 BlueOak-1.0.0 / 1 each LGPL-3.0-or-later, CC-BY-4.0, BSD-2-Clause, EPL-2.0, (MIT OR GPL-3.0-or-later), MIT-0, (MIT AND Zlib), 0BSD. RAN a parent trace: `buffers@0.1.1 <- binary@0.3.0 <- unzipper@0.10.14 <- exceljs@4.4.0 <- ROOT:apps/api`; `seq-queue@0.0.5 <- mysql2@3.15.3 <- prisma@7.9.1`; `elkjs@0.11.1 <- @prisma/studio-core@0.33.0`. RAN `ls` at the repo root — no LICENSE or NOTICE file.
fix: Record a licence policy and generate a third-party notices file (`pnpm licenses list --prod --json` into a NOTICE.md) shipped inside the desktop installers and linked from the app's About page. For buffers/seq-queue: fixing supply-chain-04 removes seq-queue outright; for buffers, either accept the risk in writing or replace exceljs's unzipper path (exceljs is only used for import/export). Record the MIT election for jszip. Confirm sharp/libvips is never bundled into the Electron app.
verification: I expected this one to fall apart and it did not. RAN an independent walk of every package.json under node_modules/.pnpm reading `license`/`licenses`: exactly two packages have no licence field at all — `buffers@0.1.1` and `seq-queue@0.0.5`. `ls LICENSE* NOTICE* THIRD*` at the repo root -> no matches. I initially thought the parent trace was wrong: my first lookup of `unzipper` resolved 0.12.5, whose dependencies do NOT include `binary`. Re-checked properly and the finding is right — BOTH versions are in the tree. RAN a full reverse-dependency walk: `exceljs@4.4.0 -> unzipper@^0.10.11` (resolving 0.10.14) `-> binary@~0.3.0 -> buffers@~0.1.1`, while `app-builder-lib@26.15.3 -> unzipper@^0.12.3` is the separate 0.12.5 copy. `mysql2@3.15.3 -> seq-queue@^0.0.5` also confirmed. So an unlicensed package really does arrive through a first-order runtime dependency of apps/api. ONE CLARIFICATION that narrows the LGPL half: apps/desktop/package.json `dependencies` are ONLY `electron-log` and `electron-updater` (sharp, exceljs and the Next.js tree are not among them), so libvips/LGPL-3.0 is not currently bundled into any distributed binary — that risk is conditional on a future change, exactly as the finding hedged. Severity correctly left at low: this is procurement/diligence, not a Monday outage.

title: TenantGuard authorises on the JWT `tid` claim and never compares the user's actual tenantId, though it already loads the user row
what: The cross-tenant decision is `if (req.session.tid !== req.tenant.id) throw Forbidden` — both sides come from the request (a signed claim and the URL). The guard then loads the user anyway (`controlDb.user.findUnique({ where: { id: req.session.sub }, select: { status: true, sessionsValidAfter: true } })`) but does not select or compare `tenantId`. AuthGuard makes exactly that check (auth.guard.ts:92-94) but does not run on tenant data routes: all 26 `/t/:slug/**` controllers use `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard)`, and RolesGuard also looks the user up by id alone.
impact: The session-to-library binding rests entirely on a claim minted at login, valid for up to SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MAX_TTL_SEC (90 days). If `users.tenantId` ever changes under a live session — a support fix, a future 'move this librarian' feature, a bad import, a restore that renumbers rows — the old cookie keeps full read/write on the library the user has left, and nothing in the request path notices.
evidence:
RAN (live audit env): logged in as tenant A's owner, then `controlDb.user.update({ data: { tenantId: idB } })` on that user and replayed the same cookie:
  V-F04 baseline GET /t/A/members = 200
  V-F04 after tenantId=B, GET /t/A/members = 200   (no guard catches it)
  V-F04 after tenantId=B, GET /t/B/members = 403
READ tenant.guard.ts:60,78-82 against auth.guard.ts:89-94.
verification: Mechanism confirmed executably — the original was read-only, so I proved it: the session keeps working against the library the user no longer belongs to. Downgraded medium→low because the harm has no trigger. `grep -rn 'user.update'` across apps/api/src yields staff.service.ts:118/136/148 and login.service.ts:132/191, none of which touch `tenantId`, and staff.service.ts:180-190 `requireManaged` explicitly rejects a cross-tenant target. No script writes it either. This is a free defence-in-depth check against a hypothetical future writer, not a live defect — the original entry conceded as much in its own text while carrying a medium label.
fix: Add `tenantId: true` to the select already present at tenant.guard.ts:80 and reject when `user.tenantId !== req.tenant.id`, with the same 401 AuthGuard uses. Zero extra queries.

title: There is no endpoint that suspends a library, and the manual DB update that does is served stale for up to 5 minutes
what: `suspended`/`archived` is checked in exactly one place — TenantMiddleware — against a `TenantContext` read from Redis with a 300s default TTL. TenantGuard and downstream services re-check nothing. The resolver's own TEN-04 comment at :53-58 requires any status mutation to call `invalidate()`, but no such mutation exists: the only `controlDb.tenant.update` call sites are branding (3), tenant-tags, library-profile (2), storage usage, and the storage-migrate / tenant-relocate scripts — none writes `status`, and grep for `'suspended'` across apps/api/src finds only member statuses and the middleware read. The one admin mutation on a tenant is the irreversible hard delete.
impact: Pausing a library — for abuse, non-payment, or a 'stop processing' demand — is only possible as a manual `UPDATE tenants SET status='suspended'`, and that update is invisible to every API and worker process for up to five minutes with no error telling the operator so. Short of hard-deleting the tenant and dropping its database there is no supported way to suspend at all.
evidence:
RAN (live audit env), against a freshly signed-up tenant with a valid owner session:
  V-F05 warm = 200
  V-F05 immediately after DB suspend = 200   (stale cache)
  V-F05 after cache DEL = 403                 (the middleware check itself works)
READ tenant.middleware.ts:76-83. GREP `tenant.update` across apps/api/src and scripts — nine call sites, none touching `status`.
verification: Reproduced exactly, including the control experiment (deleting the Redis key immediately turns the 200 into a 403), which proves the cache and not the check is at fault. Downgraded medium→low. The window is bounded at 300s and self-heals; the trigger is already an out-of-band manual SQL statement, so the operator performing it is in a position to also delete two Redis keys; and the 'no way to suspend' half is a missing feature with no shipped workflow behind it (BILLING_ENABLED=false, so no dunning path wants it). Nothing here causes irreversible harm or data exposure.
fix: Add an owner-gated `POST /admin/tenants/:id/status` that updates the row and then calls `tenantResolver.invalidate({ slug, customSubdomain })` — the same pair the hard-delete already busts at admin-tenants.controller.ts:200-202. Until then, put the two `redis DEL lbr:tenant:slug:<slug>` / `lbr:tenant:sub:<sub>` commands in the ops runbook beside the manual UPDATE.

title: STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET falls back to SESSION_SECRET on any NODE_ENV that is not exactly 'production'
what: `storageSigningSecret: nodeEnv === 'production' ? requiredSecret('STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET', sessionSecret, nodeEnv) : optional('STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET', sessionSecret)`. For `staging`, `test`, unset, or a typo, the storage HMAC key silently becomes the session JWT key. `GET /_files/signed` runs no middleware-resolved tenant, no session and no role check — `verify(token)` alone picks the tenant via `payload.tid` and the object via `payload.ref`. The comment at env.ts:338-342 states the separation exists precisely "so a leaked storage secret can't be turned into a session-forgery oracle and vice-versa".
impact: On a deployment whose NODE_ENV is not exactly `production`, one secret covers both session forgery and anonymous signed-file reads for any tenant and any storage ref. There is also no boot assertion that the two secrets differ, so a copy-paste in the env file silently collapses them even in production.
evidence: READ env.ts:343-346, requiredSecret at env.ts:165-177, and storage-demo.controller.ts:186-204 — `downloadSigned` is the one route in that controller with no `@UseGuards` (verified by counting: 6 route decorators, 5 `UseGuards(...TenantGuard...)`). READ infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:35 and :240 (`NODE_ENV: production` on both api and worker) and scripts/ensure-env.sh:94 (`ensure_rand STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET 32`).
verification: The code says what the finding says. Downgraded medium→low for two independent reasons. (1) Production is fail-closed, not merely conventionally correct: compose pins NODE_ENV=production, and at that value `requiredSecret` routes to `required(key)` (env.ts:172), so an unset STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET aborts boot rather than falling back — and `${STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET:-}` in compose:53 means an unset var is empty, which is what boot rejects. (2) The stated escalation is degenerate: an attacker holding SESSION_SECRET can already mint an owner session for any tenant id and read the same member photos and attachments through the guarded `/t/:slug/storage/...` routes. Sharing the key therefore grants no capability that was not already implied, and the reverse direction (storage secret leaking but session secret not) has no channel — the secret never appears in a URL, only the token does. What survives is a genuine non-production footgun and a missing boot assertion.
fix: Require STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET whenever `nodeEnv !== 'development'` (mirroring requiredSecret's own dev-only carve-out), and add a boot assertion that `storageSigningSecret !== sessionSecret` outside development.

title: Approving a library edit request rewrites tenants.name without busting the resolver cache
what: `approve()` runs `tx.tenant.update({ where: { id: req.tenantId }, data })` where `data` comes from `coreUpdateFromProposed` (:242-256), which sets `data.name` when the proposal includes it. `name` is one of the columns baked into the cached `TenantContext` (tenant-resolver.service.ts:126-136). Nothing in the approval path calls `tenantResolver.invalidate()`.
impact: After an owner approves a library rename, every API and worker process keeps serving the old name for up to TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC (300s) — in notification email bodies (`library: ctx.name`) and anywhere `TenantCtx().name` is rendered. Cosmetic and self-healing.
evidence: READ library-profile.service.ts:181-200 (the `$transaction`) and :242-256 (`if (field === 'name') data.name = value.trim()`). READ tenant-resolver.service.ts:126-136 — `name: true` is in `tenantSelect`. GREP `TenantResolver` in library-profile.service.ts: no match, the service is not imported at all — unlike admin-tenant-tags.controller.ts, which does invalidate after touching a cached column.
verification: Re-read both files and re-ran the greps; the entry is accurate and its severity already matches its impact. Also checked `updateFreeFields` at :57-68 — none of publicPhone/publicEmail/website/description/foundedYear is in `tenantSelect`, so that path is genuinely unaffected, as the original said. Left at low: the only consequence is a stale display name for five minutes.
fix: Inject `TenantResolverService` into `LibraryProfileService` and call `invalidate({ slug, customSubdomain })` after the approval transaction commits.

title: The authentication core is almost entirely untested — no spec covers login lockout, password reset, the CSRF Origin check, cookie flags, MFA, or the impersonation lifecycle
what: The unit suite has specs for `jwt-session.service`, `email-verification.service`, `email-verified.guard`, `signup-consent`, `admin-roles.guard` and `support-rate-limit` — and nothing else in the auth/support tree. There is no spec for `login.service` (lockout, timing parity, tenant-status handling), `password-reset.service` (single-use, expiry, enumeration), `password.service`, `cookie.service` (the `__Host-` prefix and Secure/SameSite flags — nothing anywhere asserts them), `auth.guard` (the revalidation cache and revocation path), `session.middleware` (sliding re-issue), `origin-check.middleware` (the entire CSRF layer), `mfa.service`/`mfa.controller`, `admin-auth.guard`, `impersonation.middleware`, `support-key.service`, or `support-session.service`. The integration suite (9 files, 43 tests, all green) covers admin role guards, admin audit, cross-tenant isolation, desktop access, imports, library workflow and scheduled jobs. Its `setup.ts` explicitly turns OFF two of the controls in this dimension — `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true` and `ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED=false` — with the comment "MFA enforcement has its own dedicated coverage"; no such coverage exists.
impact: Eight of the fourteen defects above were reachable with a single HTTP request against a booted app and none of them was caught, including a working logout that does not log you out. There is no regression net at all under the auth surface, so any fix applied to the findings above can silently regress. This is also the mechanism by which the 2026-06-21 pre-prod audit certified this code: the suite passes and asserts almost nothing about authentication.
evidence: RAN `find apps/api/src -name '*.spec.ts'` (47 files; six in auth/support, listed above) and `pnpm --filter @libriant/api exec vitest run --project integration` → `Test Files 9 passed (9) / Tests 43 passed (43)`. READ apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts:15,22 — `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED ||= 'true'`, `ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED ||= 'false'`. The probe spec written for this audit (10 tests, since removed) reproduced findings 02-10 against the live app.
fix: Add an `auth-security.spec.ts` to the integration project asserting, at minimum: logout invalidates the presented cookie; `complete-setup {}` is rejected while `mustChangeCredentials`; a volunteer is 403 on every mutating tenant route (enumerate them from the route table); five wrong admin passwords do not 403 a live admin session; an impersonation cookie stops working when its admin is disabled; the Set-Cookie header carries `__Host-`/Secure/HttpOnly under a production-like env; and a cross-site Origin is rejected. Run at least one integration file with the real rate limiter and MFA enforcement on.
verification: CONFIRMED. title: The reservation-expiry sweep stamps promotions with a clock captured before the loop, which can trip the `reservations_ready_after_placed` CHECK
what: `const now = new Date()` is taken once per tenant at line 90, above the overdue query at 92 and the loop at 105. Line 173 writes `readyAt: now` on the promoted hold. A hold placed after that instant but promoted in this pass has `placedAt > now`, and `reservations_ready_after_placed` (migration 20260526184041_init:521-522) requires `readyAt >= placedAt`. The service paths take a fresh `new Date()` inside their transactions.
impact: The promotion transaction aborts with a CHECK violation, is caught and logged, and that one hold's expiry is deferred to the next sweep 60 seconds later.
evidence: READ. reservation-expiry.job.ts:90 `const now = new Date();`; line 173 `readyAt: now` inside the `promotedNext` updateMany; migration 20260526184041_init:521-522 `CHECK ("readyAt" IS NULL OR "readyAt" >= "placedAt")`. Compare reservations.service.ts:501, which takes `now` inside `promoteNextHoldInTx`.
verification: The stale-clock mechanism is real, and the trigger is narrower than described but reachable: `next` is selected `orderBy: queuePosition asc`, i.e. the queue HEAD, so a just-placed hold only qualifies when it is the sole queued hold — which does happen, because the expiring hold's copy is still 'reserved' at placement time so `place()` queues rather than auto-promotes. The stated impact, however, is wrong on the load-bearing clause. The finding says the copy 'stays stranded in reserved until the next run — which fails the same way if the queue head is still the newer hold'. It does not: the failure is caught per-reservation at line 200-202 (`logger.warn`), the job is registered at `intervalMs: 60_000` (registry.ts:30-33), and each run calls `new Date()` afresh at line 90 — so on the next pass `now` is later than the newer hold's `placedAt` and the promotion succeeds. Total harm is a copy held one extra minute and one warning line. Downgraded from low to info: a real defect worth a one-line fix, but it should not compete for attention with anything above it.
fix: Take a fresh `const now = new Date()` inside the per-reservation transaction and use it for `readyAt`/`expiresAt`, keeping the outer `now` only for the `expiresAt < now` selection predicate.

title: Stored content type is discarded on download; every cover, photo and logo is served as application/octet-stream with nosniff
what: The download handlers take the Content-Type from `stat()`, but StatResult.contentType is optional (drivers/storage-driver.ts:45) and LocalDriver.stat() (drivers/local-driver.ts:78-88) never populates it — it returns only ref, sizeBytes and lastModified. The validated MIME type accepted at upload time is written nowhere: StorageService.put returns it to the caller but nothing persists it, and the on-disk filename extension is not consulted on read. sendFile therefore always falls back to `application/octet-stream`, and pairs it with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
impact: Every image in the product is served with a wrong content type. The web UI renders covers with `` (apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/catalog/[id]/CoverUploader.tsx:96); whether a browser will paint an image declared application/octet-stream under nosniff is version- and engine-dependent rather than guaranteed, so this is a live risk of blank cover/photo/logo tiles across the app. Independently, anything that downloads these files gets a generic binary with no type information.
evidence: EXECUTED. Uploaded an image/png then fetched it back: response headers were `content-type: application/octet-stream`, `content-disposition: attachment; filename="cmt5mnlskf8250764cdd8.png"`, `x-content-type-options: nosniff`. READ: local-driver.ts stat() returns `{ ref, sizeBytes: s.size, lastModified: s.mtime }` with no contentType; storage-driver.ts:45 marks the field optional.
fix: Derive the type from the stored extension on read (a small extension->MIME map, the inverse of pickExtension) and return it from LocalDriver.stat, or persist the validated contentType alongside the ref. Verify a cover actually renders in Chrome and Safari afterwards.

title: SSRF, CSV formula injection, zip bombs and body-size limits are all handled correctly
what: Four areas this dimension was asked to check came back clean, verified rather than assumed. (1) SSRF: the ISBN lookup is the only outbound call influenced by user input; the host is a hardcoded literal, the ISBN is reduced to digits and shape-checked before it reaches the URL, `redirect: 'manual'` stops a 3xx bounce to cloud metadata, there is a 5s AbortController timeout and a 1 MB streaming response cap. The other two fetch() sites (GitHub releases, Resend) take their URLs from env config, not from requests. title: Production Postgres is initialised with el_GR.UTF-8, so no prefix-LIKE can use a btree and every large sort pays libc collation
what: `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` is set on the postgres service and no `POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS` overrides it, so every database in the cluster is created with the el_GR.UTF-8 collation. Two consequences: (a) `LIKE 'prefix%'` cannot use an ordinary btree index — that needs `text_pattern_ops` (or a C-collation column), and no such index exists anywhere in either schema, so `nextSequenceForYear`'s `startsWith` (performance-04) has no index path even after the `archivedAt` fix; (b) all `ORDER BY sortTitle / sortName` comparisons go through libc `strcoll` rather than `memcmp`, which is several times slower per comparison on the large sorts identified in performance-02, -09 and -10.
impact: Every timing in this report is optimistic. The audit environment initdb's with `--locale=C` (docs/audit/pre-release-2026-08-23/env/setup-audit-env.sh:22), so the measured plans used the fastest possible comparator; production will be slower on exactly the queries that are already the slowest.
evidence: READ docker-compose.prod.yml:315-319 (no POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS) and setup-audit-env.sh:22 (`initdb ... --locale=C`). RAN: `\d+ members` / `pg_indexes` on both schemas — no index uses `text_pattern_ops` or `COLLATE "C"`; the `LIKE 'M-2026-%'` plan is `Seq Scan` even under the C locale because the predicate matches every row.
fix: The sort/search columns are already accent-folded and lowercased by the application, so their collation carries no linguistic meaning — declare them `@db.Text` with `COLLATE "C"` (a migration `ALTER TABLE books ALTER COLUMN "sortTitle" TYPE text COLLATE "C"`, likewise sortName, searchText, memberNumber, barcode) and rebuild their indexes. Re-measure performance-02/-04/-09/-10 afterwards against an el_GR cluster, not the C-locale audit box.
verification: Config facts CONFIRMED: docker-compose.prod.yml:319 sets `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` with no POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS, and the audit cluster is C (`\l` shows Collate=C for every database). Both consequences are weaker than stated. (a) The prefix-LIKE claim is a true Postgres behaviour, but the finding itself concedes the only prefix-LIKE in the codebase (`nextSequenceForYear`) seq-scans for an unrelated reason (it matches every row, and its partial index is unusable) — so no query path is demonstrably harmed by it, before or after the performance-04 fix. (b) 'several times slower per comparison' is unverified and probably wrong: the production image is postgres:16-alpine, i.e. musl, where strcoll_l is byte comparison regardless of the recorded collation name. I could not test this — docker is not installed on this host, so no el_GR cluster could be built. Worse for the headline claim ('every timing in this report is optimistic'), I found the audit box is PESSIMISTIC in the direction that matters most for a Greek product: under the C locale pg_trgm emits no trigrams for Greek text, so `searchText LIKE '%αβγ%'` and even '%αβγδ%' both fall back to `Parallel Seq Scan`, whereas the ASCII '%abc%' uses the GIN index — production's el_GR locale would make Greek search FASTER than measured here, not slower. Recorded as info: a real environment divergence worth re-measuring on, with no demonstrated defect.

title: Verified: pgbouncer transaction mode is compatible with this code — but it only fronts the control database
what: The brief asked whether anything relies on prepared statements or session-level state under `POOL_MODE: transaction`. Nothing does. Every lock in the codebase is `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (transaction-scoped, released at COMMIT): loans.service.ts:229/418/622, quota.service.ts:63, reservation-expiry.job.ts. There are no LISTEN/NOTIFY, no `SET`/`SET LOCAL`, no temp tables and no explicit PREPARE. `@prisma/adapter-pg` builds its query object with `name: this.pgOptions?.statementNameGenerator?.(query)` and neither client factory sets `statementNameGenerator`, so `name` is undefined and every statement is unnamed (no server-side prepared statement to survive a pooled connection swap). Prisma Migrate does take a session-level advisory lock, and it is already routed around the pooler via `PG_SUPERUSER_URL` (scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh:16-24). The one gap is scope: `DB_NAME: libriant_control` gives pgbouncer exactly one database, so no tenant connection is pooled at all — see performance-06.
impact: No defect. Recorded so the compatibility question is closed and so a future change (adding LISTEN/NOTIFY, session GUCs, or a driver that names statements) is known to break the assumption.
evidence: READ: `grep -rn 'advisory|LISTEN|NOTIFY|SET LOCAL|CREATE TEMP|DEALLOCATE|PREPARE ' apps/api/src packages` returns only pg_advisory_xact_lock call sites; `grep -n 'name:' node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+adapter-pg@7.9.1/.../dist/index.js` -> line 655 `name: this.pgOptions?.statementNameGenerator?.(query)`; neither packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55 nor packages/db-control/src/client.ts:34 passes that option.
fix: None required for compatibility. When fixing performance-06, a wildcard `[databases] * = host=postgres port=5432` entry (via a mounted pgbouncer.ini rather than the image's DB_NAME shortcut) is safe for tenant traffic given the above.
verification: Spot-checked the two load-bearing claims. `grep -rn statementNameGenerator` in node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+adapter-pg@7.9.1/.../dist/index.js hits exactly line 655 `name: this.pgOptions?.statementNameGenerator?.(query)`, and neither packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55 nor packages/db-control/src/client.ts:33 passes that option — so statements are unnamed and nothing survives a pooled connection swap. The scope gap is confirmed independently: docker-compose.prod.yml:36 routes CONTROL_DATABASE_URL through pgbouncer, :87 sets PG_SUPERUSER_URL to postgres:5432, and tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-109 `urlForDb()` builds every tenant URL by swapping only the pathname of that superuser URL — so no tenant connection is ever pooled. Kept as info; it closes a question rather than reporting a defect.

(e) Support access is genuinely tenant-consented via a bcrypt-hashed, single-use, expiring key. (f) The password-reset token is claimed atomically with GETDEL and invalidates existing sessions.
impact: None — this is the baseline the eight blockers and highs sit on top of. It is worth stating because several fixes above (retention sweeps, export redaction, member erasure) touch these paths.
evidence: RAN `grep -rhoE 'https?://[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+' apps/site/dist/*.html apps/site/dist/**/*.html | sort -u` → `https://libriant.com`, `https://www.dpa.gr`. RAN `grep -rniE 'sentry|datadog|posthog|plausible|google-analytics|gtag|hotjar' apps packages infra` → no output. READ apps/api/src/config/env.ts:311 and apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.guard.ts:65. READ infra/caddy/Caddyfile:60-69 (the CSP is scoped to the site, by an explicit comment) and apps/web/next.config.mjs:57-58. READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:1005-1027.
fix: No change required. Preserve these properties when implementing privacy-legal-03, -05 and -06.
verification: Spot-checked the claims, because a wrong 'this part is fine' is more dangerous than a wrong finding. Verified: the Application model comment and its implementation (schema.prisma:1027-1061 — no IP, no country, no user-agent; consent and privacyVersion persisted); ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED defaults to !isDev at apps/api/src/config/env.ts:311 and is enforced at admin-auth.guard.ts:65; `grep -rniE 'sentry|datadog|posthog|plausible|google-analytics|gtag|hotjar' apps packages infra` → no output; the SupportKey design at schema.prisma:845-876. One claim was WRONG and I have corrected it in the text above: the tight CSP `default-src 'self'; script-src 'none'; font-src 'self'` quoted as 'the app's' is infra/caddy/Caddyfile:69, which is the `site_headers` snippet for the MARKETING SITE — the comment two lines up says in terms that this is 'a CSP the app cannot' afford. The app's actual policy is apps/web/next.config.mjs:57-58, `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`. Left in the file with the correction applied, so remediation does not lean on a header the app does not send.

title: Verified good: tenant-DB failure is contained, and Postgres/Redis outages recover automatically
what: Three degradation behaviours I probed and found sound, recorded so they are not re-audited. (a) A tenant whose `dbUrl` points at an unreachable host fails fast and only for that tenant. (b) A Postgres outage leaves /healthz at 200 and correctly fails /readyz, and the API recovers with no restart once Postgres returns. (c) A Redis outage is a full outage (reliability-02) but is also fully self-healing. (d) An idle HTTP keep-alive connection does not block the API's shutdown.
impact: None — this is negative evidence. Useful because it narrows the blast radius: the multi-tenant isolation story holds under a per-tenant database failure, and neither dependency outage leaves the process permanently wedged, so remediation is 'restart the dependency', not 'restart the app'.
evidence: RAN. (a) `UPDATE tenants SET "dbUrl"='postgresql://...@192.0.2.77:5432/tenant_dead'`, cache flushed → `books: 500 in 0.11s`, generic envelope, while `healthz=200 readyz=200`. (b) `pg_ctl -m fast stop` → `healthz: 200`, `readyz: [503]`, tenant reads 500; after restart, at t+3s `readyz=200 me=200 books=200`. (c) Redis restarted → `t+2s healthz=200 me=200`. (d) Node keep-alive agent holding an idle socket, `kill -TERM` → `API exited after 1s`.
fix: No change required. Consider keeping these four probes as a scripted chaos smoke test so the properties stay true.
verification: Kept as negative evidence but CORRECTED — one of its four claims is false as stated. Claim (b), 'a Postgres outage leaves /healthz at 200', holds only while the global system-mode blob is warm in Redis. I flushed Redis and then stopped Postgres, and /healthz returned 500, not 200: with a cold cache SystemModeMiddleware's ALWAYS_PASS branch falls through resolveGlobal() to `controlDb.systemModeEvent.findFirst`. So liveness depends on Postgres as well as Redis, which widens reliability-02 rather than bounding it. Claims (a), (c) and (d) I did not contradict, and I independently re-measured (c): after restarting Redis the API returned healthz=200 and readyz=200 within ~2 s with no restart. The value of this entry — that neither dependency leaves the process permanently wedged, so remediation is 'restart the dependency' — survives, with claim (b) narrowed to 'readyz correctly fails and the API self-heals'.

title: The allowBuilds allowlist is correct and complete, but two of its five entries are misdescribed and the release workflow contains an allowlist bypass
what: Good news first, verified rather than assumed: I enumerated every package in node_modules/.pnpm carrying a preinstall/install/postinstall hook. Exactly five registry packages have one — @prisma/engines (postinstall), prisma (preinstall), esbuild (postinstall), electron-winstaller (install), msgpackr-extract (install) — and all five are explicitly decided in allowBuilds. Nothing is silently blocked, nothing is blanket-approved. Two defects sit on top of that. (1) desktop-release.yml:123 runs `pnpm rebuild electron` with the comment "pnpm blocks Electron's large binary postinstall by default" — electron@43.4.1 has NO `scripts` field at all, so the step executes nothing and the comment is false; the Electron dist is actually downloaded by electron-builder at package time. `pnpm rebuild <pkg>` is nonetheless a general primitive for running a build script the allowlist deliberately withheld, sitting in the workflow that holds the code-signing secrets (supply-chain-02). (2) `prepare` scripts (bullmq, undici, uuid, cron-parser and ~60 others carry them) are not covered by allowBuilds — harmless for registry tarballs, which never run `prepare`, but it means the allowlist is not the complete story if a dependency is ever pinned to a git URL.
impact: Low on its own. The value at risk is the policy's credibility: pnpm-workspace.yaml:24-26 states the rule is to decide each install script individually, and a `pnpm rebuild` in CI is an unreviewed exception to it. The false comment also means the next person will not notice the step is dead and can be deleted.
evidence: RAN a walk of every package.json under node_modules/.pnpm reporting preinstall/install/postinstall/prepare: only `@prisma/engines@7.9.1 postinstall`, `prisma@7.9.1 preinstall`, `esbuild@0.28.2 postinstall`, `electron-winstaller@5.4.0 install`, `msgpackr-extract@3.0.4 install` among install-time hooks. RAN `python3 -c "json.load(...)['scripts']"` on node_modules/.pnpm/electron@43.4.1_*/node_modules/electron/package.json -> `None`; the package's key list is [author, bin, dependencies, description, engines, files, keywords, license, main, name, repository, types, version] — no `scripts` at all, though a standalone install.js is still shipped. Control: msgpackr-extract (a BLOCKED package) still shows its `install` script, proving pnpm does not strip scripts and the electron result is genuine.
fix: Delete the `pnpm rebuild electron` step (desktop-release.yml:120-123) — it is a no-op — and confirm electron-builder still packages. If a future Electron reintroduces a postinstall, add `electron: true` to allowBuilds with a written justification rather than reaching for `pnpm rebuild`.
verification: The factual core is verified — I re-ran both the enumeration and the control. Every package under node_modules/.pnpm carrying preinstall/install/postinstall is exactly: `@prisma/engines@7.9.1 postinstall`, `prisma@7.9.1 preinstall`, `esbuild@0.28.2 postinstall`, `electron-winstaller@5.4.0 install`, `msgpackr-extract@3.0.4 install` — all five are explicitly decided in pnpm-workspace.yaml:27-40, nothing is silently blocked or blanket-approved. And electron@43.4.1's package.json has NO `scripts` key at all (keys: author, bin, dependencies, description, engines, files, keywords, license, main, name, repository, types, version), while a standalone install.js still ships — with msgpackr-extract (a BLOCKED package) still showing its `install` script as the control, proving pnpm does not strip scripts. So `pnpm rebuild electron` at desktop-release.yml:120-123 executes nothing and its comment is false. Downgraded low -> info because the title's second half is not supported. `pnpm rebuild electron` names one package that has no build script; it runs nothing and bypasses no allowlist. Calling it 'an allowlist bypass' in a workflow that holds signing secrets is severity borrowed from supply-chain-02, not earned here. What is left is a dead CI step and a wrong comment — a real cleanup, worth recording, worth no severity. The `prepare`-scripts observation is also accurate and correctly scoped as harmless (registry tarballs never run `prepare`).

title: What is actually sound in the supply chain — verified, so the next reviewer does not re-derive it
what: Four things I checked and found correct. (1) Every resolution in pnpm-lock.yaml carries a sha512 `integrity` hash, and `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` reproduces the tree byte-for-byte from the content-addressable store — I replayed it and got `Lockfile is up to date, resolution step is skipped`. (2) pnpm 11 enforces a minimum-release-age supply-chain policy by default and it is active: the install printed `✓ Lockfile passes supply-chain policies (verified 15h ago)`, and commit fe0931e records that it rejected the lockfile over two transitives published within the previous few hours — that is a real defence against the compromised-package publish window, and it is on. (3) A fork pull request cannot publish or deploy: ci.yml triggers on `pull_request` (never `pull_request_target`), calls verify.yml with no `secrets:` clause, and verify.yml declares `permissions: contents: read` with every job using inline test-only values — so no job in the PR path references a secret at all. (4) The three Dockerfile deps stages omit apps/desktop/package.json while pnpm-workspace.yaml globs `apps/*`; I verified pnpm 11 tolerates the missing importer under `--frozen-lockfile` rather than failing, so the image builds are not broken by that omission.
impact: None — recorded so that these are not re-audited, and so that the pnpm 11 release-age gate is understood as a deliberate defence rather than removed the first time it blocks a build (the fe0931e commit message already flags the temptation).
evidence: RAN in a scratch directory replicating apps/api/Dockerfile:40-50 exactly: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` -> `Scope: all 9 workspace projects / ✓ Lockfile passes supply-chain policies (verified 15h ago) / Lockfile is up to date, resolution step is skipped / Packages: +611 / Done in 3.5s using pnpm v11.22.0` (note: 9 projects found, apps/desktop absent, no error). READ ci.yml:6-19 and verify.yml:10-16 for the trigger and permissions. RAN `grep -rn pull_request_target .github/` -> no match.
fix: No change. Do not add `minimumReleaseAge: 0` or otherwise disable pnpm's supply-chain policy when it blocks a build; wait it out or pin the specific transitive.
verification: Spot-checked all four claims and all four hold. (1) RAN the deps-stage replay: `✓ Lockfile passes supply-chain policies (verified 15h ago)` / `Lockfile is up to date, resolution step is skipped` / `Packages: +611` / `Done in 3.3s using pnpm v11.22.0` — reproducible from the content-addressable store, integrity honoured. (2) pnpm 11's minimum-release-age policy is active and printed that line; commit fe0931e's body independently records it rejecting the lockfile over two same-day transitives. (3) `grep -rn pull_request_target .github/` -> no match; ci.yml:7-10 triggers on `push`/`pull_request` and calls verify.yml with no `secrets:` clause; verify.yml:12-14 declares `permissions: contents: read`. A fork PR reaches no secret. (4) The replay ran with apps/desktop/package.json absent and pnpm reported 9 workspace projects without error, so the Dockerfiles' omission does not break the build. Keeping this as-is is the right call — the release-age gate in particular is the kind of defence someone deletes at 2am when it blocks a build.

title: Host-header (custom subdomain) tenant routing is unreachable dead code — nothing writes customSubdomain
what: `extractSlugFromHost` + `resolveBySubdomain` implement a second, Host-header-driven way to bind a request to a tenant, and TenantGuard/TenantCtx treat a Host-resolved tenant exactly like a path-resolved one. No controller, service or script ever writes `tenants.customSubdomain`. The lookup uses `findFirst` with no `status` filter; uniqueness exists only as a hand-written partial index in the init migration (packages/db-control/prisma/migrations/20260526175126_init/migration.sql:629-630), not in the Prisma model.
impact: None today — the column is always NULL, so the branch cannot resolve anything and `<slug>.libriant.com` 404s even for a tenant whose slug matches. Recorded because it is a live, untested, Host-header-trusting authorization input in the resolution path.
evidence: GREP `customSubdomain` across apps/api/src, scripts and packages: every non-spec hit is a read, a select, a cache-key derivation, or the schema/migration — no writer. READ migration.sql:629-630 (partial unique index) and :686-687 (format CHECK). READ tenant.middleware.ts:60-68 — `pathSlug ?? subSlug`, so a path slug always wins over the Host header.
verification: Re-ran the grep with spec files excluded: the only hits outside reads are tenant-resolver.service.ts:63 and :120, admin-tenants.controller.ts:167/201, storage-migrate.ts:151 and tenant-relocate.ts:202 — all cache-key derivations from an existing value. Confirmed as accurate and correctly rated info. Kept because the follow-up it names (findUnique + schema-level uniqueness + rejecting a customSubdomain that collides with another tenant's slug) is a real prerequisite for ever shipping the feature.
fix: Delete the subdomain branch until the feature is real; or, when it ships, resolve with findUnique, move the uniqueness into the Prisma schema, and reject any customSubdomain that collides with an existing slug.
